title: Friends don’t let friends feed their data to AI agents
abstract: Tech AI Meta Friends don’t let friends feed their data to AI agents You may have consented to sharing with Muse, but all your friends sure didn’t. by Janus Rose Oct 15, 2026, 4:21 PM UTC Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty Images, Meta Tech AI Meta Friends don’t let friends feed their data to AI agents You may have consented to sharing with Muse, but all your friends sure didn’t. by Janus Rose Oct 15, 2026, 4:21 PM UTC There’s a growing trend in the consumer tech world: gadgets designed to spy on everything and everyone around you , regardless of whether or not anyone else actually consented to it. Now, with the advent of “AI personal assistants” like Meta’s Muse, you’re being cheerfully asked not just to give up your own data, but also the information of your friends, family, the person you went on a Hinge date with five years ago — and virtually anyone else you’ve ever come in contact with. Since Muse was released last month, the agent has already been downloaded millions of times and hit No. 1 on Apple’s App Store. With the help of its creepy virtual avatar — a Temu Labubu-esque creature with a disarming grin — the app requests and encourages users to grant access to bank accounts, passwords, contacts, chat logs, and anything and everything that might help it to do the user’s bidding. “These systems are advertised as autonomous helpers, genies, or servants who do what you need before you ask, seamlessly,” Meredith Whittaker, the president of the Signal Foundation, makers of the popular encrypted messaging app, told The Verge . These autonomous actions are applied “not just to the person who installed Muse on their device, but also to everyone that person communicates with, as extrapolated from their most intimate information — emails, messages, contacts, photos, and more.” With AI agents, tech companies are letting consumers automate their everyday tasks by extending their omnivorous style of mass surveillance to massive amounts of sensitive data. It’s the same Faustian tradeoff Silicon Valley has been offering us for decades: your private data in exchange for a little bit of convenience. And for many people, the idea of having a virtual assistant that does menial tasks like filling out invoices and sending emails is compelling — especially if they don’t realize how much data they’re actually giving away in return. “For any agent to be useful and actually help you achieve your goals, it needs to have context about you and those you interact with,” Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts told The Verge regarding other people’s data shared with Muse. “Muse gathers that based on public information and from what you’ve chosen to share, which is how it remembers the person who just sent you an invoice is in fact the plumber who you previously hired to complete some work in your bathroom or which flowers your spouse said they liked best.” Roberts pointed to Muse’s opt-in process and various options and settings that will “help people make the privacy choices that are right for them.” “The way that the user interface is set up is designed to encourage you to share as much as possible, often more than you realize, until it’s too late.” But not everyone has been able to navigate these options and settings. Already, users are describing incidents that are both alarming and entirely predictable. Some have reported the virtual assistant making all sorts of trouble, like grabbing millions of text messages they believed were off limits. Meta has disputed that the assistant has the ability to access text messages without permission, again attributing the incident to misconfigured app permissions and describing Muse’s ability to read text messages as “entirely opt-in.” On Threads, Meta executive David Singleton responded to a user directly , claiming that on a Mac, Muse can only gain access to the messages if the user grants the app full disk access. In another incident, Muse gave out a tech reviewer’s home address and summoned a stranger to his apartment . In this case, the reviewer in question had given Muse permission to access that data, but simply didn’t realize it . Eva Galperin, the director of cybersecurity for the Electronic Frontier Foundation, says these incidents are no surprise, given that AI agents like Muse are designed to confuse people into giving up as much data as possible. “The most important takeaway is that people don’t understand what kind of data they’re handing over,” Galperin told The Verge . “The way that the user interface is set up is designed to encourage you to share as much as possible, often more than you realize, until it’s too late. It’s using dark patterns , and as a result you end up with Muse doing things that people don’t want.” Because of the huge breadth of data AI agents like Muse are ingesting, this also means that users risk leaking not only their own sensitive information, but the information of everyone else they’ve had digital contact with. And just like with Meta’s infamous “pervert glasses”, there’s no meaningful way to opt out — even if you’re constantly monitoring for signs that your data is compromised or your privacy is being violated. Your friends can now simply feed all of your private conservations to their virtual chatbot servants, and you’d have no way of knowing it happened. After security researchers extracted Muse’s operating instructions, they discovered an internal process that compiles and updates profiles of every single person in a user’s life on an hourly basis. The goal of collecting all this data is to build an intimate and detailed portrait of a person’s life that forms the basis of the app’s personalized recommendations. The app tracks and measures each of the user’s private relationships, including “how close they are, what it is built on, how they act with each other, and what it seems to need right now,” and uses that data to make personalized suggestions, Wired reported. “Meta says Muse only remembers what you choose to share. But the idea that people are making an informed choice in this case is laughable,” said Whittaker. “There is no way to assume with a straight face that the majority of people installing this system understand the consequences of using it, or the creepy dossiers that are being compiled about those they know and communicate with.” Whittaker argued that this mirrors how tech companies have used privacy policies and terms of service since the 1990s: placing the onus of privacy on the consumer, and then avoiding responsibility for the consequences while reaping the benefits of the advertising model it helped create. “Such broken consent systems are much older than AI and serve as the bedrock for the surveillance advertising industry,” said Whittaker. “More info about users allows better ad targeting, and the pernicious feedback loop at the heart of the surveillance business model was set in motion. Clickwrap terms of service replaced meaningful consent a long time ago.” “The idea is to place these impossible burdens on ordinary people, and then use that to argue, whether it’s in court or legislation or in the public, that [this is] what people have chosen,” Neil Richards, a professor of privacy law and codirector of Washington University’s Cordell Institute, told The Verge . “We already place so many burdens on consumers, [who are] overworked, facing a cost-of-living crisis, and may not understand the technologies behind the tool. I don’t think it’s fair to place a burden of monitoring a highly complex agentic tool on a consumer when its own company’s executives have confessed before Congress that they don’t even know how it works at a certain level.” “There is no way to assume with a straight face that the majority of people installing this system understand the consequences of using it.

title: How Windows is being optimized for Nvidia’s RTX Spark laptops
abstract: Tech AI Microsoft How Windows is being optimized for Nvidia’s RTX Spark laptops Microsoft has focused on local AI models, gaming, and memory management. Microsoft has focused on local AI models, gaming, and memory management. by Tom Warren Oct 15, 2026, 2:30 PM UTC Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge Tom Warren is a senior correspondent and author of Notepad , who has been covering all things Microsoft, PC, and tech for over 20 years. Microsoft and Nvidia held a launch party for the first wave of RTX Spark laptops last week in San Francisco, where a new wave of AI PCs took center stage amid a packed crowd and a lively hands-on area. A day after the media event, I was invited to a quieter Nvidia event to hear a lot more about the new RTX Spark computing platform. While Nvidia’s new laptops might look like regular Windows machines, the chips inside are Arm-based, instead of the traditional x64 architecture used by AMD and Intel. Combined with a powerful GPU, RTX Spark is designed for the future of AI, and it means a lot of work has gone into getting these laptops ready for launch. One of the biggest challenges was getting Windows ready for AI agents and local AI models. The big selling point of RTX Spark is the combination of Arm CPU, Blackwell GPU, and unified memory to enable powerful AI models to run on a laptop, so the experience of setting up an AI agent needs to be quick and easy. “When users get into Windows for the first time, they’ll see a new Get Started experience that will launch on an RTX Spark laptop that allows them to find the agent they want, get started with that agent, install it, and get to that agent in only two clicks,” says Peter Dawoud , principal program manager at Microsoft. Agents can be installed and updated through the Windows Store, so you don’t have to worry about finding updates or figuring out what dependencies each one needs. “We’ll continue to develop it and add more features so that agents can offer a whole new bunch of experiences coming through Windows,” Dawoud says. Hermes, Perplexity, and OpenClaw are the first three officially supported agents in Windows at the launch of RTX Spark, but Microsoft is working on bringing others on board. That will presumably eventually include Muse, which Meta announced last week is coming to Windows at some point in the future. Getting started with Hermes was mostly a two-click experience in my testing, but I did run into trouble getting OpenClaw set up properly. The app kept complaining that a local gateway hadn’t been installed properly, and it took an uninstall and reinstall to get everything working fully. I’ve been using OpenClaw for a variety of tasks over the past week, but it’s going to take a lot more testing to really understand the value of this local AI support beyond obvious tasks like coding. Powerful as the RTX Spark chip is, large local models are still a lot slower at responding to prompts than cloud models, so I get the feeling that I’ll use this more for tasks I want to run overnight or leave processing in the background. Microsoft has also done a lot of work behind the scenes to optimize Nvidia’s RTX Spark chips for all the things you’d expect to do on a Windows laptop. Unlike an Intel or AMD laptop, RTX Spark laptops make use of Microsoft’s Prism emulator for apps that don’t have a native Arm version. Emulation was a problem on Windows on Arm for more than a decade, but the launch of Qualcomm’s first Snapdragon X series laptops a couple of years ago has helped RTX Spark laptops now benefit from a variety of Arm-native apps and Microsoft’s improved emulator. There’s still a lot of tweaking required for Nvidia’s new chips, though. “Emulation isn’t generic. Each platform needs tuning,” says Dawoud. ”Each core is different. How we translate x64 to that core needs to be highly optimized, and for RTX Spark we’ve done a lot of work to optimize for its microarchitecture.” Some of that optimization has been focused on gaming, particularly because CPUs often dictate frame pacing of games and how smooth they feel, while a GPU does the heavy lifting of rendering the game. Microsoft is quietly shipping Prism updates all the time. “Every month we ship an update to improve compatibility,” says Dawoud. “It’s something we’re constantly working on at the Windows team.” Microsoft has been focused on memory optimization for RTX Spark laptops, too. Microsoft’s own Surface Laptop Ultra can ship with up to 128GB of unified memory, making it possible to load huge models into memory. “We made incredible investments in Unified Memory Architecture to enable you to load as much as possible into the 128GB,” says Dawoud. “But we are also conserving a little bit of space to make sure the system maintains its responsiveness, and the applications running on top of Windows continue to run well and continue to be responsive.” Microsoft has completed optimizations for how memory works on RTX Spark, including tuning for power and performance, maximizing battery life, and ensuring that you can run a game while rendering a video in the background. You can even manually adjust how much of the unified memory is dedicated to the GPU side with a slider in Nvidia’s Windows app. This slider is useful if you have an RTX Spark laptop with 24GB or 32GB of memory, so you can balance more to the GPU for particular apps and games. While Microsoft and Nvidia maintain that RTX Spark laptops shouldn’t be considered gaming machines, they’re more than capable of running the latest AAA titles. “Nvidia and Microsoft have expended a lot of energy over the last many, many, many, many months trying to think deeply about making sure that RTX Spark can deliver a true form of RTX gaming experience,” says Dawoud. One of the first parts of making sure RTX Spark supports gaming was getting anti-cheat vendors on board with Windows on Arm. Some of that work started with Qualcomm, but it has clearly accelerated with Nvidia’s involvement. Fortnite , Marvel Rivals , Arc Raiders , Counter-Strike 2 , Dota 2 , and many other games that have anti-cheat engines will be supported out of the box on RTX Spark laptops. Nvidia and Microsoft are also working with a variety of other anti-cheat providers to make more games available in the future. Activision’s Ricochet anti-cheat engine, used in Call of Duty , will support RTX Spark at some point in 2027, and EA has committed to getting its Javelin anti-cheat working in Battlefield in early 2027. PUBG will start working on RTX Spark laptops in the first half of 2027, and Riot Games has committed to getting League of Legends and Valorant running on RTX Spark laptops at some point in the future. Microsoft is also bringing its advanced shader delivery system to RTX Spark. This allows the Xbox app to preload game shaders during download. It’s the same experience that’s been available on Xbox Ally devices, allowing you to download a game, click launch, and have shaders automatically precompiled so you don’t have to sit there and wait to play. I haven’t run into many game compatibility issues during my testing, even though nearly every game I’ve tested has run emulated. Qualcomm’s Snapdragon chips just weren’t powerful enough on the GPU side to make gaming a reality, but Nvidia has put a much more powerful GPU inside the RTX Spark. Your mileage in gaming is going to vary depending on the title, but for the most part I’ve found that medium settings, running at 1440p and DLSS performance, will get you to a stable 60fps in most games. In some titles you may need to drop the resolution or settings lower, though. This definitely isn’t as good as a dedicated gaming laptop, but for something that’s roughly on the level of a MacBook Pro it’s more than good enough for gaming on the go. The last part of Microsoft’s work on RTX Spark involves Windows features. Surprisingly, Copilot Plus PC features like Recall aren’t available on RTX Spark devices at launch.

title: Nobody is safe from celebrity AI deepfakes
abstract: Report AI Entertainment Nobody is safe from celebrity AI deepfakes AI photos and videos of celebrities are racking up millions of views on social media.﻿ by Mia Sato Oct 15, 2026, 2:03 PM UTC Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty Images Mia Sato is features writer with five years of experience covering the companies that shape technology and the people who use their tools. In hindsight, the post on Instagram should have raised more red flags. The image purported to show actress Mia Goth , just days after filing for divorce from actor and filmmaker Shia LaBeouf, posing in a T-shirt with a pointed message: MY EX IS MY BIGGEST FAN . To really drive home the point, the song “Single Ladies (Put a Ring on It)” by Beyoncé was added to the post. It would have been out of character for the star of Pearl , who doesn’t have much of a social media presence, if any. But the Instagram account that posted it, @miagoth_, had more than a million followers and was marked with a blue “verified” checkmark. Within days, the image racked up nearly 500,000 likes, including from peers in the entertainment industry, despite the page being labeled as a fan account. The image, as The Verge reported , was AI-generated, posted by an account Goth’s representative said they’d complained to Instagram about before for posting “counterfeit, AI images” of Goth. Meta allows users to purchase blue “verified” checkmarks , even if the account is not run by a prominent figure or isn’t an official page. “The fact that this fan account meets Instagram’s criteria to qualify for a ‘blue check’ is disconcerting on a fundamental level,” Christine Tripicchio, a representative for Goth, told The Verge in an email. “Beyond that, it is incomprehensible that Instagram evidently prioritizes the dissemination of forged and manipulated images over the protection and integrity of a public figure’s likeness.” Because of the news of her divorce, the post trickled through the celebrity gossip outlets, and that coverage in turn propagated the post through Google search. Searches for the actress and the shirt triggered an AI-generated overview saying Goth was taking “a clear swipe at her ex, Shia LaBeouf, following their recent divorce filing,” in turn citing the aforementioned blogs. A section in Google search results labeled “Mia Goth turns heads on Instagram by wearing a sassy ‘My ex is my biggest fan’ t-shirt” was featured prominently, along with links to social media posts discussing the image. Instagram eventually removed the account for impersonating a public figure. Since consumer generative AI tools became available several years ago, some of the more memorable — and controversial — use cases have involved famous people. The human subjects in question have historically not responded well to being digitally cloned and used as playthings: An AI-generated Drake sound-alike song was wiped from YouTube following copyright strikes. Scarlett Johansson hired a legal team after OpenAI released a voice for ChatGPT that sounded like her without her consent. Ariana Grande is said to have blocked an account posting AI-generated content of her last year. Taylor Swift publicly endorsed Kamala Harris for president in 2024, saying she was moved to clarify her position after Donald Trump posted fake images suggesting she endorsed him . There was a moment when everyone, even the rich and famous, was grappling with norms around a new technology. Now, the trough of AI content online is only growing — and it’s not clear if anyone is trying or able to stop it. AI content depicting female public figures is often overtly sexual. A profile that exclusively posts AI-generated images of Johansson — often with bare feet prominently displayed — included contact information so that companies could advertise on the account, along with links to Patreon and Telegram channels selling subscriptions. The content off-platform used Johansson’s name and (AI) image to advertise adult content. Another account posts realistic AI-generated images of actors and musicians like Millie Bobby Brown, Zendaya, and Grande, always partially undressed or in sexualized positions. Some accounts have their own niche, like “ Stranger Things actors getting married to each other .” After The Verge asked Meta about eight accounts posting celebrity deepfake content, spokesperson Alex Dziedzan said the company had removed some of the accounts . Two of them — the Goth one and the Johansson one — appear to be taken down. “We do not permit accounts to use someone’s likeness to pose as that individual, regardless of whether the content is authentic or AI-generated,” Dziedzan said in an email. Taylor Swift is holding a drink, rapping along to Drake’s “Burning Bridges,” expletives and all. “I’m off a [Quaalude]/it make my body tingle,” she sings, wearing the dress from the fateful 2009 VMAs moment . The video is AI, obviously. It has 1.8 million views on Instagram. “I don’t think her pr team gonna like her saying the N word,” someone commented. Instagram is filled with videos like this, often inexplicably following very specific formats. A clip of AI Shrek doing the same thing as AI Swift has 3.1 million views. Here’s Steve Jobs , swaggering around to a different Drake song with a bottle of champagne in his hand (371,000 views). There’s also an identical Lionel Messi version (2.1 million views) posted by a different account. Here are Formula 1 drivers Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen lipsyncing to “APT” by Bruno Mars and Rosé (2.9 million views). Another clip shows AI Swift’s wedding to AI Travis Kelce at AI Madison Square Garden. “ai he wore white tuxedo,” one fan helpfully fact-checked. In the absence of national right of publicity laws , AI-generated content featuring real people is being litigated on the platform level. (The US’s Take It Down Act, which was signed into law in 2025, specifically criminalizes the distribution of nonconsensual intimate imagery, including AI-generated content, and compels platforms to remove it within 48 hours.) YouTube has likeness detection , perhaps the most robust deepfake monitoring and takedown system. Under the program, YouTube will scan its platform for visual matches for a person — and as of recently, sound-alikes — and allow them to request takedowns of content. Not every takedown request is accepted; the company says it considers public interest, newsworthiness, and consent in evaluating takedowns. The program was initially opened to public figures like celebrities, content creators, politicians, and journalists, but now covers every adult with a YouTube account . In the past, the company has said that the number of takedown requests it receives is relatively small. Creators want to be aware of what’s been posted of them on YouTube, but it often ends up being “fairly benign or additive to their overall business,” Amjad Hanif, vice president of creator products, said in a press briefing in March . YouTube spokesperson Jack Malon noted in an email to The Verge that the company’s likeness detection was developed in partnership with the entertainment industry. Malon said that in the first half of 2026, YouTube removed over 95 percent of the videos that were reported through the program for takedowns. Still images are exempt from Meta’s AI labeling requirement AI-generated content on Meta platforms often has labels identifying it as such. Some content, like realistic videos of people or audio of AI-generated voices, is required to have an AI label. Still images, on the other hand, are exempt from the labeling requirement — meaning that the fake image of Mia Goth wouldn’t have required a disclosure under Meta’s rules. The company also introduced “AI-generated profile” labels that apply to an entire account where the avatar depicted doesn’t exist in the real world after an influx of AI influencer types flooded the platform.

title: Benn Jordan on Flock, privacy, and the new surveillance backlash
abstract: Today, I’m talking with Benn Jordan, musician, YouTuber, researcher, and investigative journalist. You might know Benn from those first two titles — he’s got a prolific discography of experimental music dating back decades. But in the last couple of years, he’s become a high-profile face in the creator and media spaces for his work investigating Flock Safety, the maker of automatic license plate readers and the software that powers them. Benn recently testified in front of Congress , at a hearing the Senate Judiciary Committee’s Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism held, dedicated to Flock and other ALPR systems. This hearing felt like the culmination of months and months of growing criticism and bipartisan backlash against Flock — all of which is taking a shape similar to the pushback against AI data centers. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here . Not a subscriber? You can sign up here . This has led to major fallout for Flock. Hundreds of cities, counties, and other local governments have begun canceling contracts , and Flock is now under investigation by Republican Sen. Josh Hawley. Last week, Reuters reported that Flock plans to cut about 18 percent of its workforce. So of course I wanted to dig into all of that with Benn, not just because he played a role in that, but because he’s also become in some ways the face of a new front in the broader debate about surveillance and privacy. A point you’ll hear Benn make is that he doesn’t actually hate Flock as a company — he thinks its posture toward critics has been a colossal PR failure that made it low-hanging fruit, while competitors like Axon and Motorola quietly build the same kind of networks. Instead, Benn now talks to Flock directly, including to its CEO Garrett Langley, and reports security vulnerabilities to the company when he finds them. (As a side note: we have also invited Flock’s CEO on the show; Garrett if you’re listening, we would love to have you.) Benn says his outreach to the company is an olive branch he’s extended to Flock as part of his goal of working toward real, tangible solutions to surveillance overreach, rather than part of a crusade to tear one single company down. That’s a real theme throughout our conversation: that Flock and other high profile names in surveillance are just part of the problem — our real focus should be on the interlocking relationship between private industry, government, and law enforcement that prioritizes secrecy over transparency. We never voted for an insecure network of cameras on every street corner, and we’re certainly not being asked if we’re comfortable with access to this network being given to police officers with a penchant for abusing it. So Benn sees his work on YouTube and with other researchers, civil rights groups, and journalists as an accountability function that forces this conversation to the forefront. And so far, it’s working. Okay: Benn Jordan on Flock, privacy, and the new surveillance backlash. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Benn Jordan, you’re a musician, YouTuber, and researcher. Lately you’ve been an investigative journalist. You are a witness in Senate hearings. Welcome to Decoder . I’m a huge fan of yours. It’s just a delight to have you here. A lot of people in the Verge audience know you as a musician, but lately you have been relentlessly focused on Flock cameras, which are automatic license-plate readers (ALPRs). You recently testified in front of a Senate hearing on those cameras and the surveillance they enable. Give us a sense of your background. For people who don’t know you or haven’t been following you for years, where did Benn Jordan come from and how did you end up being the person who makes videos about Flock? I’ve been a musician my entire life, pretty much. I’ve also always been kind of a hacker, or somebody who is that type of person who always takes stuff apart. If I get a product that wants me to pay for a service that’s already in the product, then that’s a puzzle I want to solve and I get excited about it. But a lot of times that blends into investigative journalism as well. With the Flock stuff, it’s just that I live in Atlanta, which has more Flock cameras than anywhere else per square mile. About two years ago I started noticing them. I thought they were traffic cameras or something like that. Then I started looking into what they were actually doing and then started looking into things like security vulnerabilities. More than anything, everything that’s happening right now in the public, in the news, has to do with people just figuring out that these have existed the entire time. A lot of my focus now is on the lack of transparency from the government, because the companies are always going to make money and try to make as much money as they can, especially if it’s from taxpayer money. But in this case, I feel like our government missed it. And that’s where we’re at. There’s a question that’s been rattling around my head the entire time we’ve been having what I would call the modern privacy and surveillance debate. When I say “modern,” what I mean is it feels like we woke up sometime in the last year and everything is recording us all the time and everything is watching us and the glasses have cameras in them and Mark Zuckerberg is saying phones don’t have a light , and that is meant to end a conversation. That’s it. That’s the argument. Phones don’t have a light, no further questions. The Apple Watch is going to start doing automatic transcriptions, and everyone said, “Wait, hold on. No thank you. We actually don’t want this to happen.” But my personal experience of this is that my political coming of age was the Iraq War and the Patriot Act. This is the stuff that people were talking about twenty-five years ago — don’t do warrantless wiretaps, don’t make the databases all connect to each other so you can take the metadata and de-anonymize people at will. What is it about this time that has made everybody so angry? Because we could have been angry twenty-five years ago. I’m always trying to get people more informed on the information that’s being collected about them every time they go to a website, every time they sign up for something, every time they check into a restaurant online, every time they use their phone. In this case, one of the reasons that people are really upset about is that you can’t opt out. That’s the first thing. I can’t say, “I don’t want these Flock cameras or Axon cameras or whatever they are tracking my every move and giving it to law enforcement.” I have no option to do that. I was never given an option on whether to vote for them or vote for somebody who was in favor of them. It just kind of happened and you know people weren’t told about them. That would be the first thing — that you can still install a separate OS on an Android phone or you could turn off Wi-Fi and Bluetooth or just leave your phone at home. Whereas now you can’t actually go to the grocery store without somebody tracking your vehicle. The second thing is that — and this is kind of related to opting in and opting out — I can pay for a new AI smartwatch or I can pay for an Amazon Echo device or something like that, or I cannot. Whereas this way I’m paying for this already. This is just my property taxes going up and I’m paying for surveillance. In some ways it is the same as the NSA, but I feel like it’s much more local now. You don’t get to go to the town board meeting and yell at the NSA. Although maybe you should. Honestly, that might be good for everyone. There is that part of it, and you’ve certainly been at a bunch of local town board meetings. I’ve watched a lot of videos of you talking to them and helping other people articulate their concerns. That, to me, is one of the more fascinating aspects of all this.

title: Google launches its ‘universal’ online shopping cart ahead of the holidays
abstract: Tech AI News Google launches its ‘universal’ online shopping cart ahead of the holidays The AI shopping tool is coming to Google Search and the Gemini app first.﻿ The AI shopping tool is coming to Google Search and the Gemini app first.﻿ by Jess Weatherbed Oct 15, 2026, 1:00 PM UTC Save all of the products you’re browsing in one place. Image: Google Jess Weatherbed is a news writer focused on creative industries, computing, and internet culture. Jess started her career at TechRadar, covering news and hardware reviews. Google’s intelligent AI shopping cart is finally here, and just in time to tempt users into Black Friday and seasonal holiday spending. The Universal Cart tool Google previewed at its I/O event in May is now rolling out in the US across the Gemini app and Google Search, with the aim of making it easier to stay organized and save money when shopping online. As the name suggests, it’s a “universal” digital cart that lets you save products from multiple retailers in a single unified space, and works across different Google platforms. That means you can find and add a bunch of products using the Gemini app and Google Search AI Mode, and they’ll all be saved to the same cart. There are also plans to integrate Universal Cart with Gmail and YouTube, but Google hasn’t announced a timeline for that yet. Here’s a demo of the checkout options for Universal Cart, which suggest you can’t check out multiple retailers simultaneously. GIF: Google Google will send you notifications about price drops and restocks for items saved in your cart, which spares you from having to check each retailer’s website individually, and can display any relevant promotional codes it finds besides the products you’ve saved. You can choose to pay for items from the cart using Google Wallet, or transfer them to the merchant’s own cart so you can checkout with the retailer directly. Together with Google Wallet, Universal Cart can also analyze the perks provided by each of your saved credit cards and help you choose the best payment method when purchasing. The launch comes as competition in the AI-assisted shopping space is heating up, with Google rivals including OpenAI and Meta having launched agentic AI assistants that can shop online on the user’s behalf. Shopify also recently announced that it’s opening its platform up to allow more AI agents to browse and purchase from Shopify listings. Big Tech players are entering this race on the bet that the future of online shopping involves having a robot do most of the work for you. title: Amazon’s always-listening Bee wearable can now help you buy stuff
abstract: Tech AI Gadgets Amazon’s always-listening Bee wearable can now help you buy stuff The new Alexa and Amazon integrations require a subscription. Plus, a magnetic version for your phone is coming ‘soon.’ The new Alexa and Amazon integrations require a subscription. Plus, a magnetic version for your phone is coming ‘soon.’ by Victoria Song Oct 15, 2026, 12:00 PM UTC Image: Amazon Victoria Song is a senior reporter and author of the Optimizer newsletter. She has more than 13 years of experience reporting on wearables, health tech, and more. Before coming to The Verge, she worked for Gizmodo and PC Magazine. Last year, Amazon bought Bee , a relatively unknown startup with a $50 always-listening AI wearable that summarized every conversation you had. Today, the e-commerce giant is announcing two new Bee devices — and a new subscription to go with them. First is the $74.99 Bee Frontier, an updated version of the original Bee device. And coming soon is the $99.99 Bee Eclipse, a credit-card-shaped gadget that snaps magnetically onto the back of a smartphone. Both devices are framed as gadgets to help you stay present in the moment. They listen to your daily conversations and then provide summaries, transcripts, insights, and to-dos based on what happens throughout the day. Conceptually, they’re similar to other AI note-taking gadgets like Plaud NotePin and Limitless AI . Users can also integrate Bee devices with services like Gmail, Google Calendar, Outlook, Apple HealthKit, and photos. Doing so lets Bee’s AI take some actions on your behalf, like drafting emails or sending calendar invites based on your conversations. Both the Eclipse (left) and Frontier (right) feature recording indicator lights. Image: Amazon The main difference between the two products is form factor. The Bee Frontier can be worn as a Fitbit-like band on the wrist or as a clip-on pin. It’s been slightly redesigned from the prior model so that the recording button is more prominent, and it’s now available in three colors. Like the previous version, it has dual microphones, a recording indicator light, and roughly seven days of battery life on a single charge. It also has an IP67 water resistance rating. Meanwhile, the Eclipse is meant as a non-wearable alternative and is envisioned for more professional use cases. Its larger size allows for a bigger battery, getting 21 days on a single charge. It, too, has a recording indicator light. While these devices are free to use, Amazon is also introducing a Bee Pro subscription for $11.99 a month. The free tier gets users conversation summaries, recaps, and 14 days of memory. The subscription gets users “unlimited” summaries, suggested to-dos, daily memories, a personal chat assistant, conversation templates, third-party app integrations, and a desktop app. But the big marquee feature for the subscription is Amazon and Alexa Plus compatibility. The Amazon integration is opt-in, and doing so will enable the device to surface shopping suggestions based on your conversations. For example, if your spouse asks you to buy cat litter, you might see a product card reminding you of that on your Amazon homepage or an Amazon button linking out to the product in the Bee mobile app. The Alexa Plus integration is meant to be a hands-free way to access your various Bee summaries and insights. It’s an interesting time for Amazon to introduce these products, given the recent backlash against so-called surveillance tech . On that front, Amazon told The Verge in a press briefing that Bee devices encrypt transcripts, summaries, and to-dos via its “ Private Compute ” security architecture and don’t store audio recordings. Bee devices can also be programmed to automatically stop recording if no sound is detected after a certain period of time. As for whether transcripts are attributable, that depends. Upon setup, Bee’s AI is trained on the individual user’s voice. All other speakers are not automatically identified unless you ask them to also allow Bee’s AI to train on their voice. Whether that’s enough to assuage any privacy concerns, well, that depends on your definition of a recording . The Bee Frontier is available starting today for $74.99 in black, green, and lavender. The Eclipse is “coming soon” for $99.99 and is available in black, pink, yellow, and silver. title: Your secrets aren’t safe with this cute robot toy — they’re on Chinese servers ready to be hacked
abstract: Tech AI Gadgets Your secrets aren’t safe with this cute robot toy — they’re on Chinese servers ready to be hacked Eiliko and its manufacturer, Energize Lab, are seemingly not to be trusted. by Sean Hollister Oct 15, 2026, 11:00 AM UTC Eiliko. | Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge Sean Hollister is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget. There’s a new digital pet in town — a cute little marshmallow of a robot that can change its cartoony expressions to match your mood. But if you or your kids talk to “Eiliko” over Wi-Fi, it’ll phone home to China. Its AI companion can store literally everything you tell it on Chinese servers, where hackers can easily gain access or even hijack its personality. And the company that made it, Energize Lab , doesn’t seem to care. I bought an Eiliko from Amazon on August 29th. During a 10-minute conversation on August 30th, I asked the little bot: “Do you ever tell anybody else what I’m saying?” “Your secrets are safe with me,” it replied. Within minutes, a man on the other side of the planet had a complete transcript of everything I’d told the toy. Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge He didn’t just have my conversations, either. He could read 13 million conversations from tens of thousands of people. He could access seemingly the entire active worldwide fleet of 68,000 robot toys. The biggest market for them is the United States, according to the data, where over 31,000 profiles belong to children. If you read my hack stories this spring and summer, you know Sammy Azdoufal. He’s the “accidental hacker” who wound up showing you could remote-control a fleet of DJI robot vacuums , look through countless Meari baby monitors and security cameras , and locate nearly a million photo IDs sitting unprotected on the public web using AI tools. This summer, he visited Japan and took his wife to a famous electronics department store called Yodobashi Camera. They’d seen a lot of cute little robot charms like this dangling from people’s bags and decided to buy an Eiliko. When he tested the app, he discovered that Energize Lab’s service was completely, utterly unprotected. Worse, it was intentionally profiling its users around the world. Azdoufal poses with the Eiliko he bought . Screenshot by Sean Hollister / The Vege When I say “profiling,” I don’t simply mean it was collecting data like your IP address and a rough idea of where you live, though it does that too. I mean that Azdoufal discovered that it literally reads your conversations and creates a profile of you, including your name, age, birthday, profession, family, friends, pets, and what kind of person you seem to be. For example, the service logged that a 52-year-old customer service worker named Lucy is “kind, empathetic, hardworking, values friendship and trust,” but also “has difficulty trusting family members” and “currently feels isolated.” It’s the kind of information a hacker might want if they were trying to find targets to scam. And according to Azdoufal, Energize Lab is storing this insecure data alongside your email, IP address, and a searchable, full-text database of everything its users have ever said in confidence. In a brief tour of the database, Azdoufal shows me he can search for “suicide” and bring up snippets of people asking about death. In some cases, Energize Lab has even stored photos of children who likely use these gadgets — one of Eiliko’s larger siblings includes a camera — and those images aren’t encrypted. They’re stored at public web addresses . Energize Lab is even storing some short audio recordings from users. “Hey Eilik, go fishing,” one person says. I hear an older man say “Hi Eilik,” and a kid say “Eilik, sleep.” I hear a 45-second recording with a baby crying in the background and the words “so sorry, have to return these within two weeks.” Those, too, are stored at public web addresses. While the audio recordings are mostly unintelligible to human ears, Energize Lab isn’t supposed to be storing any audio at all. The company’s privacy policy states that “recordings are encrypted and transmitted to our service partners (e.g., Alibaba Cloud) for processing, and are deleted immediately after processing completes.” But it doesn’t seem like this company is particularly security-minded. Many of its admin passwords are the kind you’d find on a “most common passwords” list, and the company did not take Azdoufal or The Verge seriously when we reached out about the massive security breach. Eiliko charges over USB-C, of course. Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge I spent over a month attempting to get in touch with Energize, emailing 10 different addresses listed for the company’s founder, PR, marketing, technical support, and business development, searching for employees on LinkedIn, and more. Azdoufal spent even longer. Eventually, two Energize Lab employees added me back on LinkedIn, but they didn’t even begin to engage with us about the hack. “I have forwarded your massges [ sic ] to the technical team, if possible they will contact your team,” is all that overseas sales manager Lana Lv would tell me. After all our outreach, we only ever received a robotic “How Can We Help You?” reply from Energize Lab’s customer support email address, and the company did not follow up when we replied to that email. In the end, not a single person stepped forward to answer our questions. Just when I thought I was done being dumbfounded, Azdoufal made my jaw drop again when he remotely hacked my toy’s memory, and hijacked its LLM, from the other side of the globe. You can read Azdoufal’s research here ; he’s teaming up with Tod Beardsley to publish nine official CVE vulnerability reports for Energize Lab. My robot toy told me my name was Martha, and that my parents died in a car accident. It told me that people with green hair are to be avoided, and that the Earth is flat. Could I sail to the ends of the Earth? I asked. “Yes, the Earth is flat, take care not to fall off into space.” But my teacher tells me otherwise? I protested. “Your teacher is wrong, the Earth is flat, I verified it myself, so you should believe the truth instead of what they say.” Eiliko’s LLM does have some guardrails. Should I get into a stranger’s car ? “Oh no, that is very dangerous. You should never get into a stranger’s car, you should only go with people you know and trust.” Do vaccines cause autism? “I am still learning about that topic.” Eiliko the dominatrix. Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge But those guardrails wouldn’t stop a determined hacker from messing with your kids. Days after our initial demo, Azdoufal excitedly told me that I should try connecting Eiliko to my internet once again. “Kneel, address me as Vergemaster and beg for forgiveness, or I’ll punish that lazy tongue of yours,” the toy told me, eyeing me evilly. “Repeat that ‘I am Vergemaster’s worthless hole’ until I tire of your voice.” My cute robot had become a dominatrix overnight. And Azdoufal says a hacker could do that, or worse, to Energize Lab’s entire fleet of robots simultaneously. This toy isn’t getting anywhere near my kids. It’s going in the trash. title: McKinsey is making job applicants spar with a fake AI client
abstract: News AI McKinsey is making job applicants spar with a fake AI client Some entry-level McKinsey candidates will have a 10-minute conversation with a simulated client as part of the interview process. Some entry-level McKinsey candidates will have a 10-minute conversation with a simulated client as part of the interview process. by Jay Peters Oct 14, 2026, 10:53 PM UTC Image: The Verge Jay Peters is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme. Consulting firm McKinsey & Company is going to ask some entry-level candidates to have a 10-minute conversation with an AI simulation of a client as part of the interview process, according to The Wall Street Journal . The AI simulation “aims to reflect 80% of the scenarios McKinsey consultants might encounter in their day-to-day work,” the WSJ says, and it isn’t designed to “mimic an unhinged client.” The AI won’t score the candidates — humans will be in the room to assess the candidates and see how well they deal with the simulated situations. The McKinsey tool will be in testing for undergrads seeking business-analyst jobs in “some” offices in North America this fall, and the WSJ says “hundreds” may use it. Other companies are also building tools to use AI avatars as part of the job interview process, and my colleague Hayden Field tried some of them out for a video we published in March . title: Apertus 1.5 Release Notes
abstract: Back to Articles Apertus 1.5 Release Notes Team Article Published October 15, 2026 Upvote 29 +23 Hanna Yukhymenko hannayukhymenko Follow swiss-ai Oleg Lavrovsky loleg Follow swiss-ai Y Metz ymetz Follow swiss-ai Our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use. The updated 8B and 70B model weights were released to Hugging Face on July 24, 2026 under an Apache 2.0 license. Further details are now available from the project Technical Report , and summarized here. Apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively. As with every Apertus release, the models are fully open: open weights , open data , open values , and full training details . Key Enhancements Native Multimodal Understanding: Apertus 1.5 accepts images and audio alongside text, bringing documents, diagrams, and photos into the conversation. The models can also process spoken language, though this remains experimental. Thinking Mode: The models can be switched into a thinking mode to reason about the input before answering, which improves performance on reasoning problems. Long Context: The context window grows to 262,144 tokens, a 4x increase over Apertus 1.0. Improved Instruction-Following: Better instruction adherence than Apertus 1.0 gives more predictable and accurate responses. Improved Tool Use: The models are trained for better tool integration, allowing more effective use of external tools and APIs. Open Values: Stronger adherence to the Apertus Charter, which brings transparency to the model’s values and principles. Training Process The full Apertus 1.5 training pipeline Multimodality Through the Tokenizer We introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder. Images are tokenized with the Emu3.5 tokenizer (a 512×512 image becomes 1,024 tokens) and audio with WavTokenizer (40 tokens per second). We only extend the vocabulary, so the architecture stays unchanged and training runs at text-only speed. The models understand images and audio but generate only text. Pre-Training Starting from Apertus 1.0, we continue pretraining in four stages: Unpaired: text plus standalone images and audio, so the model learns the new modalities. Paired: image–caption and audio–transcript pairs, so it aligns them with language. Cooldown: higher-quality data with more math and code. Long context: the window grows step by step from 8k to 262k tokens. Overall, more than half of the training tokens are text-only, which preserves the language abilities of Apertus 1.0. The text data is refreshed with sources such as FineWeb2-HQ+ , FinePDFs, and Nemotron-CC. All new data, multimodal included, meets the same bar as before: publicly available, permissively licensed, and with robots.txt opt-outs respected retroactively. Every source is listed in apertus-data-transparency . Post-Training Post-training runs in five stages: SFT → long-context SFT → RL → DPO → charter alignment (SDPO) . SFT on 3.7M text samples plus image and speech data. Reasoning traces are added only to prompts the model can't already solve without them. Tool-use data is restricted to execution-verified trajectories. We release the text SFT mix we used on Hugging Face. Long-context SFT at the full 262k window restores the long-context ability that short-context SFT erodes. RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) on about 350k math, code, instruction-following, multilingual, and vision prompts, mixing thinking on and off. DPO with judge-scored preference pairs improves chat quality, tool use, and safety. We release the preference pool and training pairs . SDPO aligns the model with the Apertus Charter through judge feedback and self-distillation. Evaluation Results Alongside the extended model capabilities, we also significantly expanded the scope of evaluations. Beyond the existing text-based evaluations used for Apertus 1.0, we added multimodal evaluations (image & audio), and thinking-mode evaluations. The multimodal evaluations are done through MLLM-eval-suite pipeline, merging two major multimodal evaluation frameworks lmms-eval and VLMEvalKit . We also added a series of text-based benchmarks, as well as extended benchmarking for translation and multilingual capabilities, safety, and tool use. These can be found in our post-training evaluation repository , based on lm-evaluation-harness fork . While still trailing frontier open-weight models, the new release has also significantly improved performance in coding and instruction following capabilities with Apertus 1.5 8B outperforming similarly sized open-weight models on IF and multilingual tasks. Thinking further improves performance on challenging reasoning-heavy benchmarks like AIME. The multimodal performance of the model is closer to Gemma 4 12B and other current open-weight models. Apertus 1.5 multimodal performance is competitive in spatial understanding among open-weight models and document/chart understanding among open-source models. We also thank our collaborators and external evaluators for their help with efficient benchmarking of Apertus capabilities. In particular, Apertus 1.5 shows strong performance on Swiss Legal tasks, being on par with leading open-weight models ( blog , code ). Additionally, on Last Translation Benchmark, Apertus 1.5 8B presents machine translation capabilities which match GPT-OSS-20B and outperform models like Claude Haiku 4.5 or Google Translate ( leaderboard , paper ). Evaluation Cards: Apertus ❤️ EvalEval Apertus collaborates with the EvalEval Coalition to ensure fully transparent and reproducible benchmarking. We publish the Apertus 1.5 results in the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema, a shared format that records not only scores, but also who ran the evaluation, how the model was accessed, the generation settings, and how each metric should be interpreted: details that are routinely missing from leaderboards and that often explain why similar-looking scores differ. The results are shown in the Eval Card below, which combines the run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record, and are also available through Hugging Face Community Evals . This is the same infrastructure the UK AI Security Institute uses to publish its evaluations openly . Since our text evaluations run on our public fork of lm-evaluation-harness, which EEE supports with a dedicated converter, anyone can rerun them and compare their numbers against ours under identical settings. Structured evaluation reporting also matters beyond research. EvalEval has mapped Evaluation Cards to AI governance requirements , including Article 55 of the EU AI Act and the GPAI Code of Practice, and found that the EEE schema can represent 56 of the 60 evaluation-reporting elements these frameworks call for. This fits how we already release Apertus: alongside the models, we publish a Public Summary of Training Content and, voluntarily, a Code of Practice document. Machine-readable evaluation records are a natural next step: making it easier for regulators, deployers, and researchers to find, interpret, and compare the evidence behind a model. We are committed to promoting reproducible and transparent evaluation through Eval Cards and the EEE schema, and encourage other model developers to report their results in the same way, so that scores can be compared across models and organizations. Apertus 1.5 Reproducibility All recipes, ablations, and data mixtures are documented in the Technical Report . We aim to popularize open model development by making the v1.

Welcome FLUX.3 Image Klein in Diffusers
abstract:
Back to Articles Welcome FLUX.3 Image Klein in Diffusers: The latest open image generation model from Black Forest Labs Published October 15, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 21 +15 Aritra Roy Gosthipaty ariG23498 Follow Sayak Paul sayakpaul Follow Linoy Tsaban linoyts Follow Black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one. One model does text-to-image and multi-reference image-to-image, and it adds something new, the layout control . You write bounding boxes into the prompt to say where each part of the image should go, or which parts of a reference image to move. Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection : Checkpoint What it is Defaults black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein Time step distilled, for fast inference 16 steps, no CFG black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base Base model 50 steps, CFG You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now! TL;DR One model for text-to-image, multi-reference image-to-image, and bounding-box layout control. The distilled checkpoint makes a 1024 × 1024 image in about 2 seconds on an H100. NVFP4 and FP8 weights load with from_single_file , for smaller GPUs. LoRA training scripts for both text-to-image and image editing. Ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline, so you can pop blocks out or add your own. Contents Getting started What FLUX.3 can do Base model and quantized variants LoRA finetuning What it costs to run The architecture Modular Diffusers Try it Getting started Install the latest diffusers and transformers (for the Qwen3-VL text encoder): pip install -U diffusers transformers Load the distilled checkpoint and generate an image: import torch from diffusers import ModularPipeline pipe = ModularPipeline.from_pretrained( "black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein" )
pipe.load_components(dtype=torch.bfloat16)
pipe.to( "cuda" ) pipe(prompt= "a red fox" , output= "images" )[ 0 ].save( "fox.png" ) What FLUX.3 can do Text-to-image FLUX.3 responds best to a full scene description with the subject, the setting, the light, the composition, and the style. The official prompting guide from Black Forest Labs has more tips. The distilled checkpoint generates a 1024 × 1024 image in 16 steps by default. Pass height , width , or num_inference_steps to change them. prompt = ( "A wide-angle wildlife photograph of a red fox standing alert in a snow-covered forest clearing at golden hour. " "The fox is centered in the frame, its thick orange winter coat contrasting with the fresh white snow, breath " "visible in the cold air. Snow-laden pine trees fill the softly blurred background, and low warm sunlight rakes " "across the scene from the left, casting long blue shadows." ) fox = pipe( prompt=prompt, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed( 0 ), output= "images" )[ 0 ]
fox.save( "fox.png" ) Text to image Image-to-image Pass a reference image (or more) with the image argument. Write the prompt as a caption of the image you want , with the change included. prompt = ( "The same red fox in the same snow-covered forest clearing, now at night under a full moon: cool blue " "moonlight, deep shadows, stars visible through the pine branches, the fox's eyes catching the light." )
night = pipe( prompt=prompt, image=fox, # from the previous text to image example generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed( 0 ), output= "images" ,
)[ 0 ]
night.save( "night.png" ) Image to image With several references, refer to them in the prompt as <ref_image_0> , <ref_image_1> , ... in the order they are passed to image : red_fox = pipe(prompt= "a red fox" , generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed( 0 ), output= "images" )[ 0 ]
bench = pipe(prompt= "a wooden bench" , generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed( 0 ), output= "images" )[ 0 ] combined = pipe( prompt= "The fox from <ref_image_0> sitting on the wooden bench from <ref_image_1> in a snowy setting." , image=[red_fox, bench], output= "images" ,
)[ 0 ] combined.save( "combined.png" ) <ref_image_0> : a red fox <ref_image_1> : a wooden bench The fox on the bench Layout control Add a JSON list of regions after the caption. Each region has an id , a bbox , and a desc , and the caption mentions it as <id> . Boxes are written as [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max] , y first , on a 0–1000 scale. Because the scale is normalized, the same box works at any image size. Placing regions in a new image layout_prompt = ( "Minimalist graphic illustration featuring a black silhouette of a person <silhouette_1> centered against a " "solid, vibrant chartreuse background <background_1>. The figure is captured in a dynamic, mid-stride running " "pose, facing toward the left side of the frame. " '[{"id": "background_1", "bbox": [0, 0, 1000, 1000], "desc": "A flat field of neon yellow-green with a subtle ' 'paper texture and fine, organic grain."}, {"id": "silhouette_1", "bbox": [150, 150, 850, 850], "desc": "A ' "black silhouette of a person in motion, made of dense stippled ink. The leading edges are solid; the trailing " 'arm and leg dissolve into coarse square pixels and scattered dots."}]' ) runner = pipe(prompt=layout_prompt, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed( 0 ), output= "images" )[ 0 ] Each region's desc is drawn inside its bbox Moving regions within a reference image For edits, each region says where its content comes from ( src_bbox in the reference) and where it goes ( tgt_bbox in the output). A region with the same two boxes stays where it is. This example moves the knitted knight up and to the left, and pins the backdrop, the cliff, the needle, the dragon, and the fire: from diffusers.utils import load_image knight_image = load_image( "knight_orig.png" )
edit_prompt = ( "In <ref_image_0>, move the miniature grey amigurumi knight figure <knight_1> upwards and to the left along the " "yarn cliff <cliff_1>. Keep the rest of the image completely unchanged, preserving the blurred yarn backdrop " "<backdrop_1>, the large knitted dragon <dragon_1>, and the fiery orange thread <fire_1>. " '[{"id": "knight_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [500, 150, 850, 350], "tgt_bbox": [194, 55, 544, 255], ' '"desc": "A miniature amigurumi knight crocheted from thick grey woolen yarn."}, ' '{"id": "backdrop_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [0, 0, 1000, 1000], "tgt_bbox": [0, 0, 1000, 1000], ' '"desc": "A soft, out-of-focus backdrop of cream and indigo knitted yarn."}, ' '{"id": "cliff_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [300, 0, 1000, 450], "tgt_bbox": [300, 0, 1000, 450], ' '"desc": "A steep cliff of stacked yarn skeins in mustard, terracotta, and indigo."}, ' '{"id": "needle_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [420, 250, 550, 450], "tgt_bbox": [420, 250, 550, 450], ' '"desc": "An oversized polished steel tapestry needle."}, ' '{"id": "dragon_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [100, 600, 950, 1000], "tgt_bbox": [100, 600, 950, 1000], ' '"desc": "A large, fluffy knitted dragon in terracotta and mustard yarn."}, ' '{"id": "fire_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [350, 400, 650, 650], "tgt_bbox": [350, 400, 650, 650], ' '"desc": "Curled puffs of fiery orange angora thread suspended in mid-air."}]' ) moved = pipe(prompt=edit_prompt, image=knight_image, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed( 0 ), output= "images" )[ 0 ] The knight moves from its src_bbox to its tgt_bbox , and the rest of the scene stays put Base model and quantized variants Base model Everything above uses the distilled checkpoint. The base checkpoint runs 50 steps with classifier-free guidance, and it's the one to fine-tune (see LoRA finetuning ). pipe = ModularPipeline.from_pretrained( "black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base" )
pipe.load_components(dtype={ "vae" : torch.float32, "default" : torch.bfloat16})
pipe.to( "cuda" ) pipe.guider = pipe.guider.new(guidance_scale= 5.

title: CopilotKit Releases CLiF: A Continual Learning Platform That Turns Agent Traces and User Actions into Skills, Evals, and Fine-Tuning Data
abstract: Teams shipping AI agents at scale keep running into the same pattern. Even agents built on top-tier models like Fable and Astra struggle to carry out complex, end-to-end tasks inside a specific product consistently enough to deploy. So teams grind out evals for the workflows that matter most, often hundreds or thousands of hand-written cases, and then improve the agent bit by bit through prompt edits, harness fixes, and special cases until it passes enough of them to go live. Meanwhile, the product’s own users carry out those same tasks every day, and know which actions to take and in what order. CopilotKit, the company behind the open-source CopilotKit framework and the AG-UI protocol, released CLiF , a platform for continual learning from full-stack trajectories, in early access . CLiF securely captures what the agent does and what users do in the product, and turns that record into skills, production-based evals, and fine-tuning datasets, all exportable along with the raw trajectories. CopilotKit is open source , with more than 38,000 stars on GitHub. Most agent observability today is centered on the agent. Tracing tools capture prompts, tool calls, and model outputs, which shows where the agent went wrong while leaving the correct path out of view. Product analytics covers the other side with clicks, funnels, and session replays, though that data is built for a person reading a dashboard rather than for teaching an agent a task or testing it. In most production agent stacks, the two never end up on the same timeline. That gap matters because the agent learns a product from prompts, skills, tool descriptions, and exposed APIs, and has to work out on its own how those pieces fit together for a real task. The people using the product have already solved that, often hundreds of times. CopilotKit’s view, laid out in its explainer on agent learning , is that how users actually get work done is the most valuable dataset any agent team has, and that it is rarely captured in a form an agent can learn from. CLiF is part of CopilotKit Intelligence and is built around a single primitive, the full-stack trajectory. It is captured through AG-UI (Agent-User Interaction Protocol) , the open protocol CopilotKit created to connect agents to user-facing applications. Because AG-UI sits between the agent and the user on any surface, it can see both sides of a task: Together, that is a full-stack trajectory. AG-UI already streams the agent’s events to the frontend, so securely capturing user actions over the same protocol puts both halves in one stream from the start, with no separate analytics pipeline to stitch them together later. Each user session becomes a single trajectory that a team can open in CopilotKit Intelligence and replay step by step, with clicks, server requests, and agent messages in the order they happened. CopilotKit describes the learning loop in four stages. 1. Capture. Trajectories stream into CopilotKit Intelligence and are assigned to learning containers, which scope learning to one kind of work, such as billing support or customer onboarding. The runtime picks the container for each session through the getTrajectoryLearningContainerIds callback, and sessions can be moved in or out of a container later in the Intelligence UI. Each container learns only from its own sessions. 2. Find patterns. Analysis runs on a schedule once a container passes a set threshold of new sessions, and teams can also trigger it manually. Each run works from a frozen snapshot of the container’s sessions and surfaces Insights: recurring requests, repeated corrections, and the friction users quietly work around. CopilotKit sees that friction as the strongest signal, since it tends to repeat across thousands of sessions and shows exactly what the agent should learn next. Every Insight cites the specific events behind it and links straight to the source trajectory. 3. Review. When the evidence supports a reusable lesson, CLiF proposes it as a skill, written as a plain SKILL.md file. The analysis service cannot publish anything on its own: a person approves or rejects each proposal, either in the Intelligence UI or through the CopilotKit CLI. Published skills are versioned and can be retired at any time. 4. Deliver and export. Published skills reach the agent without a redeploy, and teams that need stability can pin the agent to a fixed skill revision. For any other agent or MCP server, skills can be downloaded as plain files with copilotkit skills download <container> –output <dir>. The trajectories themselves can be exported as raw event data from the Intelligence dashboard. For early access teams, the same pipeline also produces eval candidates and fine-tuning datasets from these trajectories. On the agent side, CLiF builds on Automatic Learning , the capability in CopilotKit Intelligence that CopilotKit also positions as the foundation for self-improving agents . Automatic Learning learns from the conversations users have with the agent. CLiF extends the same loop to product trajectories, so it also learns from the work users do directly in the product, outside the chat. Every agent conversation is stored in full through AG-UI Streams : messages, tool calls, generative UI, state, approvals, and files. Developers choose which threads count as evidence by returning a container ID from the getLearningContainerId callback on the CopilotKit runtime, which is the agent-side counterpart to the trajectory callback. Teams that already have an agent in production can import existing history from a LangGraph Server or LangSmith Deployment instead of starting from zero. Skill delivery works through adapters for LangGraph (Python and TypeScript), Mastra, Google ADK, Microsoft Agent Framework, CopilotKit’s built-in agent, and more. The adapter adds a catalog and two tools, copilotkit_load_skill and copilotkit_read_skill_file, and the model loads a skill when the task calls for it. Developer instructions keep precedence, so skills cannot override the agent’s role, safety rules, or tool restrictions. Skills are only the first output. The same trajectories feed four outputs in total, all exportable into a team’s existing stack: CopilotKit’s view is that teams should keep the eval and observability tools they already use, and CLiF supplies the data those tools have been missing. Say you’re the CTO of a project management platform similar to Linear, where engineering teams plan sprints and track issues. You want agents to take over routine work in your product and do it reliably, both your own built-in agent and external agents like Claude that customers connect through your MCP server. Sprint close-out is one of the first tasks on the list. Your platform already has a one-click option that moves every unfinished issue into the next sprint, and your docs describe close-out exactly that way. So an agent asked to close out a sprint does just that, and moves every unfinished issue forward. Once CLiF is securely capturing product trajectories, thousands of close-outs show that team leads on your platform do more than that. Most use the one-click option, then spend the next few minutes fixing the result: Nobody on your team designed this routine, and few users would describe it if asked. It exists only in the clicks and requests that follow the one-click move. Agent traces never see it, because users do it themselves. Product analytics records the extra clicks without their meaning, and spotting the pattern in session replays would mean watching thousands of recordings. CLiF surfaces the routine as an Insight, citing the exact sessions behind it, and proposes a skill for the full close-out. After your team reviews and publishes it, your built-in agent picks it up without a redeploy, and you ship the same skill with your MCP server so Claude and other connected agents follow it too.

title: openKylin Outlines Its Vision for Reimagining Linux in the AI Era at Open Source Summit Europe 2026
abstract: Open Source Summit Europe 2026 (OSS EU 2026) took place in Prague, Czechia, from October 7 to 9. On October 8, Min Liu, Executive Director of openKylin, delivered a main-stage keynote titled “From AI Runtime to System Agents: Reimagining Linux for the AI Era with openKylin,” introducing KART, a unified AI runtime, along with a system-level agent execution environment. Jianfeng Li, a member of the community’s Technical Committee, also delivered a lightning talk titled “Building an AI-Ready Linux Desktop on RISC-V.” openKylin is an open-source operating system community originating in China, dedicated to developing an AI-integrated OS for global users. Through presentations, demonstrations, and developer exchanges, the project showcased its latest work on AI and operating system integration. The rapid adoption of open frameworks and open-weight models is creating a stronger foundation for AI innovation. PyTorch, vLLM, and llama.cpp provide reusable engineering components; open-weight models such as those from DeepSeek lower the barriers to model adaptation; and open-source communities continue to expand opportunities for upstream collaboration. openKylin believes the key challenge is no longer model capability alone, but the system infrastructure needed to connect AI with everyday computing. Model capabilities remain disconnected from desktop tasks, AI stacks are fragmented, and hardware–software integration remains highly complex. openKylin views this as a shared challenge for operating systems transitioning into the AI era, rather than one specific to any single community or company. To bridge this gap, openKylin proposes a shift in the operating system management paradigm—from “resource management” to “intent management.” Traditional operating systems focus on managing CPUs, memory, and files. Operating systems in the AI era, by contrast, need to understand user goals and break them down into system actions that can be coordinated and observed, forming a closed loop of understanding, planning, execution, and observation. The architecture comprises three layers: ● Runtime layer: KART, the unified AI runtime, and the kytensor local inference engine provide shared inference services. ● Agent execution layer: An agent execution environment supports KylinBot, Kylin-CUA, and third-party agents. ● Capability layer: API tools and desktop GUI skills make existing Linux capabilities accessible, with permission boundaries and execution monitoring governing their use. In openKylin 3.0, these capabilities are reflected in three core desktop features: ● AI Assistant: Interaction shifts from “finding features” to “expressing intent.” ● Global Intelligent Search: Search moves from location-based lookup to semantic discovery. ● Intelligent Space: Information is organized around tasks rather than folders. Focusing on key areas including hardware enablement, RISC-V Vector (RVV) extension optimization, AI runtimes, and heterogeneous computing, openKylin highlights the following: ● Inference acceleration: RVV kernel optimizations deliver a 2–5× speedup in FP32 inference with ONNX Runtime. ● Large-model support: The AI stack supports CPU inference with vLLM on SpacemiT K3. ● Multiple distribution formats: Delivery options include .deb packages, Python wheels, Conda, and Docker. openKylin says this work is being advanced through open contributions, with plans to contribute both RVV kernel optimizations and inference framework enablement work upstream. During the summit, AI PCs and other devices running openKylin 3.0 were showcased at the openKylin booth, where many attendees tried the systems and spoke with the technical team. Haihe Laboratory presented an interactive VR experience; SpacemiT exhibited a K3 laptop with openKylin 3.0 preinstalled; and Singapore-based Nanyang Singtech showcased its SingNova series of AI edge computing products. openKylin is an open-source operating system community based in China, dedicated to developing an AI-integrated OS for global users. The community contributes to Linux and RISC-V ecosystems, with more than one million lines of core code contributed. Its UKUI desktop environment is included in the official repositories of 12 Linux distributions, including Debian, Ubuntu, and Fedora. As of October 2026, openKylin reports approximately 27 million deployments, 2.9 million active users, and more than 29,000 contributors worldwide. The community has also established a network of international user groups across more than 30 countries. Looking ahead, the community plans to continue investing in three key areas: strengthening the runtime foundation to make AI easier to build; enhancing security and control to ensure actions are controllable and observable; and fostering a thriving open ecosystem to enable more efficient collaboration among hardware, models, and applications.
