title: TypeSafe AI Releases Jev 1.14 With Images, Box Type and 262k Context
abstract: TypeSafe AI has released Jev 1.14 , a new version of its System One decision model. It is live now under the jev-preview alias. It adds 3 experimental ‘danger zone’ features: images, a box type and longer context. For developers, Jev 1.14 pushes a typed decision model toward vision tasks like inspection and localization. TypeSafe shares a note that none of the 3 features are ready for production yet. Jev is a System One model from TypeSafe AI that returns typed decisions instead of generated text. You send a state along with typed questions : Choice, Score or Noul. Jev answers each with a typed value, probabilities and a confidence score. TypeSafe trains it with Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD) . The new version, jev-1.14.0 , brings small, subtle improvements to almost everything, according to the release post . TypeSafe expects the largest gain in multilingual support. Images are composable. Each image is listed once in a top-level assets map under a reference string. You then place that reference anywhere in state , instructions or criteria . The API swaps each reference for the image before the model reads it. TypeSafe says jev-1.13.0 was multimodal all along. Per the Images docs , both Jev 1.13 and Jev 1.14 now accept images. Each request needs the header TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Images: true . TypeSafe warns that all models, Jev included, perform worse on images than on pure text. It recommends the simplest possible questions. Box is a new question type that returns 1 bounding box per question. The answer gives top , bottom , left and right edges as fractions from 0 to 1. It also returns a confidence score. Box needs jev-1.14.0 or jev-preview , plus the images header. Box always returns a box. A question about an absent object still returns 4 edges. TypeSafe suggests pairing it with a Noul question that checks whether the target exists. TypeSafe also shared a small test on 36 painting crops, each cutting off part of the target. 4 per-edge Noul questions caught 30 cuts. A single “is all of it inside” question caught 26. Drawing the box as an outline and asking about it caught 20. By default, both models keep 64k tokens per request and 32k per question. Sending TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Long-Context: true raises both limits to 262k tokens, per the Models docs . TypeSafe states that Jev always supported longer context internally. It capped context on purpose because Jev, like all models, is less reliable on long inputs. The dev team still recommends short contexts. TypeSafe published internal intelligence charts in the release post . They compare Jev only against open-weight models. The post does not include a numeric score table. TypeSafe says the measurement is likely biased toward its own models. It tells developers to favor their own evals. Pricing is unchanged at $42 per billion input tokens, or $0.042 per million. Output tokens are free, per the Models docs . The rollout plan from the release post : Check out the release post , Models docs , Images docs and Box docs . All credit goes to the researcher of this project. Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter . title: Meet Grok Voice 3.0: SpaceXAI Voice Agent Model Ranks #1 on Artificial Analysis
abstract: SpaceXAI just released Grok Voice 3.0 . Grok Voice 3.0 is a SpaceXAI speech-to-speech model that listens, reasons, calls tools and speaks. It now ranks first on the Artificial Analysis Speech-to-Speech Index with a score of 86.9. For developers, the endpoint, events and $0.08 per minute price are unchanged from Grok Voice 2.0. Grok Voice 3.0 is SpaceXAI’s flagship realtime voice model, exposed as grok-voice-3.0 on the /v1/realtime WebSocket endpoint . The grok-voice-latest alias already points to it, so existing agents switched automatically. SpaceXAI has not published parameter counts or architecture details. Reasoning is on by default ( reasoning.effort: "high" ) and can be set to "none" for faster turns. Server-side voice activity detection handles barge-in. Tools run inside the session: collections search, web search, X search, remote MCP servers and custom functions. The AA Speech-to-Speech Index is an equal-weighted average of 4 components. Those are Big Bench Audio reasoning, τ-Voice agentic performance, Speech Agent Arena preference and task success rate. Grok Voice 3.0 scores 86.9. GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) scores 83.2, Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking 82.6. Grok Voice 2.0 scored 81.3. Component results are strong, not uniformly first: ServiceNow’s EVA-Bench scores enterprise voice agents on accuracy and experience. SpaceXAI reports a top accuracy score of 74%. Artificial Analysis measures 0.81 s time to first audio. GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) measures 1.34 s, so SpaceXAI’s “40% lower latency” claim checks out. Grok Voice 2.0 was faster, though, at 0.70 s. On cost, SpaceXAI cites Artificial Analysis cost per Big Bench Audio task. Grok Voice 3.0 costs $0.025 per task, versus $0.030 for GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) and $0.055 for GPT-Realtime-2.1 (High). On AA’s cost per hour of input audio, Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking is cheaper: $3.50 versus $4.80. List prices are not directly comparable. GPT-Live-1 costs $0.05 per minute, but backend model and tool usage is billed separately. Gemini 3.8 Live bills audio per minute plus text tokens. Benchmark data: Artificial Analysis , accessed October 14, 2026. SpaceXAI’s blog lists frozen Arena Elo values of 1048 (GPT-Live-1) and 990 (Gemini). The API is compatible with the OpenAI Realtime API , so migration mostly means a new URL and key. Production teams should pin grok-voice-3.0 rather than the alias. Grok Voice 2.0 is now deprecated. Check out the official announcement , the Speech to Speech docs and the Artificial Analysis leaderboard . All credit goes to the researcher of this project. Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter . Wait! are you on telegram? now you can join us on telegram as well. title: Datalab Releases OmniParseBench: An Open OCR Benchmark With 16,288 Pass/Fail Tests to Audit OCR Parsers
abstract: Datalab has released OmniParseBench , an open OCR benchmark for document parsers. It scores parsers with 16,288 yes/no tests on 2,937 pages from 2,343 documents. The pages span 92 languages. The dataset and code are public. It helps engineers answer a sharper question than a leaderboard does: which parser handles documents like mine? Datalab sells a parser, and its own top setting, Datalab accurate, ranks second on the launch leaderboard, behind Gemini 3.8 Flash. Is it deployable? Yes. OmniParseBench is an evaluation harness, not a model. It installs with uv pip install omni-parse-bench, needs Python 3.11+, and scores outputs offline with no API keys. OmniParseBench is a document-parsing benchmark from Datalab where every test is a yes/no question about 1 page. A parser’s score is the share of tests it passes. Datalab built it to be clear, auditable and explorable. Datalab names two problems with existing benchmarks. olmOCR-bench showed that pass/fail unit tests work. Datalab now calls it saturated. In its view, top systems are separated by output conventions and overfitting, not reading. Each olmOCR-bench test also sits in 1 bucket, set by its page’s source. A handwritten table gets averaged into whichever bucket its page landed in. ParseBench from LlamaIndex splits parsing into 5 capabilities, each with its own metric. Datalab argues those scores share no unit, so they cannot be compared or combined cleanly. The final score is the mean of 3 family scores: text, tables and layout. Five test types feed those families: Numbers must match digit for digit, though 1,240 matches 1240. Equations are compared by what KaTeX renders, so \frac{a}{b} equals \dfrac{a}{b}. Each decision is pass, fail, unsupported or error. The last 2 are left out of every score. No model judges the outputs; the scorer is open code . A test checks one or more args, each of which is the content at one place on the page. Each arg carries tags on 5 axes: structure, rendering, role, script and language. Scripts use ISO 15924 codes; languages use ISO 639-3 codes. Tags never decide a verdict or the headline. They only select tests, so any slice gets its own score. The table tag covers 6,767 tests on 1,000 pages from 875 documents. English covers 10,089 tests. Non-English languages cover 1,931 tests on 529 pages from 321 documents. Every test also records its derivation, meaning how its answer was established. There are 10 derivations . They include publisher JATS XML, the PDF text layer, authored pages, olmOCR-bench tests, model panels and human review. *Used in creating and verifying at least some tests, per Datalab . Claude Sonnet 5.5 posts the top text (93.1) and tables (95.4) scores. Its layout score of 77.5 pulls its headline to 88.7. Reducto leads layout at 95.8. Datalab also plotted each headline against median latency and price per 1,000 pages. Latency was measured on 200 sampled pages, sent 8 at a time. Datalab does not top its own benchmark. It flags the two models that helped build tests, and it tells readers to weigh the fact that it sells a parser. It commits to reporting OmniParseBench scores for future releases. Its advice: the best benchmark is your own documents. Vendors need keys such as DATALAB_API_KEY or OPENROUTER_API_KEY. The CLI shows its plan and asks before calling any vendor. Runs are resumable. The query guide shows how to compare runs by tag, suite or test type. Check out the blog post , dataset and GitHub repo . Thanks to the Datalab team for the resources behind this article. Datalab supported and sponsored this content. The post Datalab Releases OmniParseBench: An Open OCR Benchmark With 16,288 Pass/Fail Tests to Audit OCR Parsers appeared first on MarkTechPost .

title: Fish Audio Releases Drama 3, a 35B Open-Weight MoE Text-to-Speech Model
abstract: This week, Fish Audio released Fish Audio Drama 3 . Drama 3 is a text-to-speech model from Fish Audio that takes plain-language acting direction. It is a 35B mixture-of-experts model with about 3B parameters active per token. The weights are on Hugging Face , and the model is also live in the Fish Audio API . For developers, it is a self-hostable option for scripted dialogue, audiobooks and dubbing. Drama 3 turns a script along with bracketed directions into acted speech. Writers place cues like [barely holding it together] before a line. Paired tags such as <whisper> change only the enclosed words, per the Drama 3 docs . Directions can be written in any language, independent of the spoken line. The model supports 83 languages . Speaker tags <|speaker:0|> to <|speaker:15|> allow up to 16 characters in 1 request. The API takes 1 voice ID per speaker, so a full scene renders in a single call. According to the launch post , the backbone starts from the Qwen3.5-35B-A3B language model. It has 40 layers, grouped as 3 Gated DeltaNet layers per 1 gated full-attention layer. Only 1 layer in 4 keeps a KV cache. DeltaNet layers store history in a constant-size state instead. A new Codebook-MTP decoder replaces the per-frame Fast AR decoder used in S2 . It has 4 shared layers feeding 9 layers, 1 per acoustic codebook. Only codebooks 0 and 1 feed back into the backbone; S2 fed back all 10. The audio tokenizer is unchanged from S2. It is built on the Descript Audio Codec and outputs 44.1 kHz audio. It runs at about 21.5 frames per second. Training ran 3 pre-training stages, then instruction tuning, then reinforcement learning. RL used GRPO without a KL penalty and a single learned human-preference reward model. Fish Audio reports Drama 3 at 93.2% overall on Artificial Analysis Pronunciation Robustness , ranked #1. Its predecessor S2.1 Pro scored 88.1%. Human listeners judge hard English words across 4 categories: This benchmark tests pronunciation, not emotional delivery. Fish Audio describes emotive quality only qualitatively. On the Artificial Analysis quality leaderboard , ‘Drama 3 Preview’ holds an Elo of 1242. That beats S2.1 Pro at 1190 but trails Eleven v4 Turbo at 1328. The Fish Speech install guide lists at least 48 GB of NVIDIA GPU memory in FP8. CPU, Apple MPS and AMD ROCm are not supported. MoE experts ship in FP8, with the remaining weights in bf16. The model card reports streaming results on 1 H200. At 1 stream, median time to first audio is 88.9 ms with a real-time factor of 0.131. At 16 streams, throughput reaches 927.6 frames per second. Serving runs through SGLang-Omni , whose fused kernels are validated only on Hopper GPUs. In the hosted API, set the model header to drama-3 on POST /v1/tts . The docs warn that a missing or misspelled header silently falls back to s2.1-pro . List price is $50 per 1M characters. A $10 launch price runs until November 12, 2026, per the launch post . The weights use the Fish Audio Community License v1.0 . Research and non-commercial use are free. Commercial use is free under USD 500,000 in annual revenue. Hosting Drama 3 as a third-party API needs a separate license. Products must display ‘Built with Fish Audio.’ Cloning a real voice without consent is prohibited. Check out the weights on Hugging Face , the technical report , the GitHub repo and the launch post . All credit goes to the researcher of this project. Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter . title: Abacus AI Honest Review: Key Criticisms, Facts & What Users Should Know
abstract: Abacus AI Honest Review: Key Criticisms, Facts & What Users Should Know This review highlights the main critiques of Abacus AI, its price, user reviews, reliability of workflows, and real-life use cases to assist you in evaluating its advantages and disadvantages. By KDnuggets on October 15, 2026 in Partners Sponsored Content Quick Overview Of This Abacus AI Review What does Abacus AI provide?: A comprehensive platform based on ChatLLM, numerous AI engines, agents, programming utilities, software development, data analytics, and content creation. Problems mentioned by users: Feedback from users highlights issues with difficult interfaces, unexpected spending of credits, mistakes of agents, delays in support responses, and unclear bills. What is evident from the facts?: The platform provides information about prices, limits on credits, integrations, and enterprise features. The cost per operation and typical support response time remain unclear. Reliability of workflows: The agents will perform complicated tasks, but you will need to troubleshoot, test, and verify the results for production use. Who is going to benefit more from Abacus AI? : Industry professionals like analysts, developers, startup founders and IT professionals who heavily rely on varied AI tools and workflows. The Bottom Line: Consider trying Abacus AI if its pricing and other aspects match your requirements. A Closer Evaluation Of Abacus AI: Online reviews and competitor reviews of Abacus AI present two distinct perspectives on the platform. Generally speaking, positive reviews can be found among those users who make extensive use of the platform and value the wide variety of AI models, agents, and cost-effectiveness of the platform. However, negative reviews can highlight the challenges and confusion associated with using credits, pricing, learning curve, and some workflow-related issues. Analysis of both perspectives will allow one to get a better understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of the platform. This article studies Abacus AI through Reddit discussions, positive and negative user reviews, and video walkthroughs to find out how users perceive and utilize the platform. In addition, the review of the platform's features, pricing, credit system, and product ecosystem is conducted to add depth to the analysis. It is necessary to conduct an honest review of Abacus AI that will cover its main strengths and weaknesses and answer the most common criticisms. About Abacus AI - A Brief Note : Abacus AI is a technical workspace that combines various AI models and functions under one umbrella. One can use this workspace for writing, data analysis, generating images and videos, coding, and much more. ChatLLM makes a great start for beginners in AI technology. The app basically gives you access to various models of providers like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google through one interface so that you can toggle between these models without accessing multiple applications. Even though many people draw comparisons between Abacus AI, ChatGPT, and Claude, it should be kept in mind that these two platforms are designed to serve different purposes. While ChatGPT and Claude specialize in conversational AI, Abacus AI covers a broader area of individual and commercial needs in the form of various AI capabilities. The ideal option would depend on your needs: if you seek assistance in conversational AI, you might go for ChatGPT and Claude; however, if you are looking for multiple AI capabilities and models in one place, then you should consider Abacus AI. The following table explains the ecosystem of Abacus AI and their respective uses. The Ecosystem: Core Tools & Services Product What It Does ChatLLM Provides users with access to a varied range of AI models all at once, with intelligent routing powered by RouteLLM. Abacus AI Agent Performs multi-step actions including research, coding, web work, and app development. Claw AI-agent performing multi-step actions through messaging channels like Slack, WhatsApp, and Telegram without losing context between sessions. Hermes AI agent capable of performing multi-step actions and learning reusable skills from prior experience with the task. Abacus AI Desktop Desktop coding environment for coding, pair programming, and editing local files. Studio Image, video, and audio creation with the help of a variety of AI models. AppLLM / Vibe Coding Assists users in creating and deploying web apps by describing what they want. SuperComputer Cloud environment enabling users to run AI agents, code, and services which continue working after the browser session is over. Agent Swarms Enables coordination of several AI agents to perform different aspects of the complex task simultaneously. Abacus AI Smaug Family of AI models specifically made for reasoning, coding, and agent-based workflows. Open weight models included. Abacus AI Bot Open source coding agent and desktop app helping users to interact with AI agents. An Evidence Based Assessment Of Abacus AI Several common complaints about its user interface, pricing, credit system, and suitability for various kinds of tasks are noted both in reviews and on forums. Here are the significant criticisms to consider. 1. Complex Interface & Usage Difficulty Complex interface: Some users find the platform difficult to navigate because it offers many tools and features in one place. Fact Checked & Evidence The platform contains distinct, separately accessible layers: ChatLLM (daily chat), the Agent layer (automation and workflows), Studio (media generation), Desktop (code editor), and AppLLM (app builder). These are not a single cluttered screen; they are separated surfaces accessible from a sidebar. Users who stay in ChatLLM for writing, research, or document analysis consistently report a low-friction experience. The April 2026 platform update introduced Effort Levels — a Low / Auto / High toggle that simplifies the most common decision a new user faces (how much compute to use), removing one of the primary sources of interface overwhelm for first-time users. Comparable multi-layer platforms — Notion, Salesforce, and n8n — all have orientation phases. A denser interface reflects the breadth of what is possible, not a fundamental design failure. Model identification: Switching between AI models can make it harder to track which model was used in previous conversations. Fact Checked & Evidence The current ChatLLM interface displays the active model name in the conversation header and preserves that attribution in the conversation history view. Users can see which model handled any prior response without navigating to settings. RouteLLM , the platform's intelligent routing layer, automatically selects the appropriate model for a task type. For users who want manual control, the model selector is a visible dropdown that persists across the session and is labelled in each conversation record. Per the Abacus AI ChatLLM FAQ , the platform supports model switching mid-conversation, and each switch is reflected in the interface display. Steep learning curve: Advanced features, particularly AI agents and workflow creation, may take time to understand. Fact Checked & Evidence The learning curve applies specifically to the agent-building layer, not to the ChatLLM interface. Conversation-Level Skills , documented in Abacus AI's own help pages, allow users to pre-select which agent capabilities are active for a specific run. This reduces setup complexity and makes agent behavior more predictable from the first run. Abacus Design , introduced in early 2026, lets users prototype a workflow or UI before the agent starts building, which reduces wasted effort on poorly specified tasks and shortens the learning-by-doing cycle. Comparable agent tools — n8n, Make, and Salesforce Flow — all have meaningful learning curves for advanced automation.

title: Building AI Applications with OGX, the Open-Source Agentic API Server
abstract: Building AI Applications with OGX, the Open-Source Agentic API Server OGX is an open-source agentic API server for building OpenAI-compatible AI applications, using any model and any infrastructure. By Shittu Olumide , Technical Content Specialist on October 15, 2026 in Language Models Here's the fact worth knowing before anything else about this topic: OGX is the rebrand of Meta's Llama Stack . Its own GitHub page states it directly, Llama Stack is now OGX , with the name change accompanying a real shift in mission toward being model-agnostic, multi-SDK, and production-grade — not a new, unrelated project with a confusingly similar architecture. That single fact resolves a lot of confusion for anyone researching agentic API servers, OpenAI-compatible APIs, or local AI application development right now, since a good amount of what's written about Llama Stack still applies directly to OGX under its new name. What Is OGX (and Why It Used to Be Called Llama Stack) OGX is plainly described as: an open-source agentic API server for building AI applications, OpenAI-compatible, any model, any infrastructure . Released under the MIT license, it's a genuinely established project — over 8,400 GitHub stars and 1,400 forks as of this writing — with regular community calls and active development. The core pitch is a drop-in replacement for the OpenAI API that you run yourself, on a laptop, in a datacenter, or in the cloud, and point any OpenAI-compatible client or agentic framework at it. Behind that single API sits a pluggable provider architecture: develop locally against Ollama, deploy to production against vLLM, or connect to a managed cloud service — all through the exact same API surface, so swapping the backend later doesn't mean rewriting the application on top of it. It goes further than just chat completions too: the Responses API handles server-side agentic orchestration, tool calling, MCP server integration, and built-in file search for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) in a single API call, and OGX natively supports the OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google GenAI SDKs against the same server, not just one vendor's client library. In this article, we will build an app — let's call it DocBrain — that does two things. First, real RAG: upload documents, and it answers questions grounded in their actual content, with retrieval happening automatically, not through a manually wired vector database and a separate retrieval script. Second, a genuinely agentic capability: while reviewing your documents, it can call a custom tool to flag and save a real action item — a lease renewal deadline, a follow-up task — to an actual file on disk, so it doesn't just describe what you should do, it does the bookkeeping. Prerequisites and Installing OGX You need uv , Python's fast package manager, and a local model backend. This tutorial uses Ollama , though the same code works unchanged against vLLM or a cloud provider later — that's the entire point of OGX's provider architecture. # Install Ollama, then pull a model ollama pull llama3.2:3b # Set up a real project (not the throwaway uvx command from a quick trial) uv init docbrain && cd docbrain uv add ogx openai Code explanation: uv init scaffolds a proper project rather than relying on a one-off uvx invocation, which matters the moment this stops being a five-minute experiment and becomes something you actually keep using. uv add ogx openai installs both the OGX server package and the standard OpenAI Python client, since that client is literally all DocBrain needs to talk to OGX. Starting the Server and Verifying It Works uv run ogx go With Ollama running and a model already pulled, this starts the OGX server at https://localhost:8321 . Confirm it's actually healthy before writing any application code: curl -k -s https://localhost:8321/v1/models | python -m json.tool Code explanation: OGX listens on HTTPS by default and is secure out of the box , so local testing needs the -k flag to skip certificate verification against its self-signed local cert. A healthy response lists your registered model under /v1/models , confirming the server started and Ollama connected correctly, before you've written a single line of the actual application. Basic Chat Through the Responses API The smallest real call, establishing the pattern everything else in this tutorial builds on: import httpx from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI( base_url="https://localhost:8321/v1", api_key="fake", http_client=httpx.Client(verify=False), ) response = client.responses.create( model="ollama/llama3.2:3b", input="What is OGX?", ) print(response.output_text) Code explanation: api_key="fake" isn't a placeholder you're meant to fill in — OGX doesn't check it at all for a local server, any string works. http_client=httpx.Client(verify=False) is the Python equivalent of curl's -k flag from the previous step, skipping certificate verification for local development. The model string follows a provider/model-name format — ollama/llama3.2:3b — which is how OGX knows which of its configured providers to route the request to. response.output_text is the Responses API's convenience property for the final text answer, with no manual parsing of a choices array required. Adding Real RAG: Uploading Documents and Creating a Vector Store This is where OGX's built-in retrieval actually shows up, and it's genuinely compact: # Upload a document file = client.files.create( file=open("lease_agreement.pdf", "rb"), purpose="assistants", ) # Create a vector store and index the file vector_store = client.vector_stores.create( name="docbrain-kb", file_ids=[file.id], ) # Ask questions with file search response = client.responses.create( model="ollama/llama3.2:3b", input="Summarize the key points", tools=[{ "type": "file_search", "vector_store_ids": [vector_store.id], }], ) print(response.output_text) Code explanation: client.files.create uploads the raw document; purpose="assistants" marks it as content meant to be retrievable rather than, say, a fine-tuning dataset. client.vector_stores.create is the step that actually does the work most RAG tutorials spend dozens of lines on manually — chunking the document, embedding those chunks, and indexing them into a searchable store — all handled server-side by OGX. The tools list on the responses.create call is what activates retrieval for this specific question: file_search combined with the vector store's ID tells OGX to search that store for relevant content and ground the model's answer in what it finds, automatically, before generating a response. Adding a Custom Tool: Flagging and Saving Action Items This is the genuinely agentic half of DocBrain — a real Python function the model can choose to call. # tools/action_items.py import json import os from datetime import datetime, timezone ACTION_ITEMS_FILE = "action_items.jsonl" def save_action_item(description: str, source_document: str, priority: str = "medium") -> dict: """Appends one action item as a JSON line to a local file.""" if not description.strip(): raise ValueError("description cannot be empty") if priority not in ("low", "medium", "high"): raise ValueError(f"priority must be low, medium, or high, got '{priority}'") entry = { "description": description.strip(), "source_document": source_document.strip(), "priority": priority, "flagged_at": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(), } with open(ACTION_ITEMS_FILE, "a") as f: f.write(json.dumps(entry) + "\n") return {"status": "saved", "entry": entry} def list_action_items() -> list[dict]: """Reads back every saved action item, an empty list if none exist yet.""" if not os.path.exists(ACTION_ITEMS_FILE): return [] with open(ACTION_ITEMS_FILE) as f: return [json.loads(line) for line in f if line.strip()] ACTION_ITEM_TOOL_SCHEMA = { "type": "function", "name": "save_action_item", "description": ( "Save a genuine, concrete action item found while reviewing a document.

title: 7 Open-Source AI Tools That Can Replace Paid Subscriptions
abstract: 7 Open-Source AI Tools That Can Replace Paid Subscriptions Find open-source alternatives to OpenAI API, Midjourney, Claude Code, Notion, Wispr Flow, Grammarly, and NotebookLM that you can run locally or self-host for more privacy, control, and lower cost. By Abid Ali Awan , KDnuggets Assistant Editor on October 15, 2026 in Artificial Intelligence AI subscriptions add up surprisingly fast. I pay for quite a few of them myself, and after a while you start wondering: is all of this really worth it? Is there an open-source alternative? Can I run it locally and privately? And can I do that without giving up too much in performance or quality? For many of the tools we use every day, the answer is now yes . You can replace cloud AI assistants with local large language models (LLMs), paid coding tools with open-source coding agents, image-generation platforms with local workflows, and apps like Notion with self-hosted alternatives. You can even replace cloud dictation with a fast speech-to-text app that runs entirely on your own machine. The open-source ecosystem has improved a lot, and many of these projects are no longer just experimental alternatives. They are polished tools that you can actually use every day. For this guide, I picked seven open-source AI tools that can replace common paid subscriptions while giving you more control, privacy, and often no recurring cost at all. 1. llama.cpp: Running LLMs Without Paying Per Token I use llama.cpp almost every day whenever I want to run a local LLM or test a newly released model. It is one of the best tools for running quantized models efficiently on your own hardware, and it is highly optimized across CPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, Apple Silicon, AMD GPUs, and other platforms. What makes llama.cpp especially useful is that it is not just an inference engine. Its built-in server gives you an OpenAI-compatible API and a web interface, so you can chat with your model in a UI similar to ChatGPT or connect it directly to applications that normally rely on paid APIs. That makes it a practical alternative to both monthly LLM subscriptions and per-token API costs. The models you can run locally are also getting much better. Qwen3.8-27B is one of the strongest open agentic coding models you can use today. With llama.cpp, you can serve it locally, test it through the web UI, or expose it as an API, while getting coding and agentic performance that is competitive with frontier models such as Claude Opus 4.8 . For me, that is the real appeal of llama.cpp: I can download a strong new model, run it privately, test it locally, and use it as an API without paying every time I send a prompt. 2. ComfyUI: Replacing Paid AI Image Generators ComfyUI is a powerful open-source alternative to tools such as Midjourney, Adobe Firefly, and other hosted image and video generators . It uses a visual node-based interface, so instead of hiding the generation process behind a single prompt box, you can see and control how models, prompts, LoRAs, ControlNets, upscalers, and other components work together. What makes ComfyUI especially useful is how much more it can do beyond basic image generation. You can use it for image editing, inpainting, outpainting, upscaling, reference-based generation, segmentation, and compositing , and it supports modern editing models such as Flux Kontext and Qwen Image Edit. It also supports video generation with models such as Wan, LTX-Video, HunyuanVideo, and CogVideoX, so the same interface can cover both image and video workflows. That is why I see ComfyUI as more than just a Midjourney replacement. Once you get comfortable with the workflows, it becomes a complete local creative AI platform for generating, editing, and automating images and videos, while giving you much more control than most hosted tools. 3. Pi: Replacing a Paid AI Coding Agent Pi is a fast, open-source alternative to coding agents such as Claude Code, Gemini CLI, and OpenAI Codex . I use it almost every day because it can build projects, debug code, find issues, edit files, run commands, and handle multi-step coding tasks directly from the terminal. What I especially like is using Pi with local models. I can run a model through llama.cpp , expose its OpenAI-compatible endpoint, and connect Pi to it. llama.cpp handles the inference, while Pi gives the model the agentic coding capabilities needed to actually work on a project. That gives you a complete local coding-agent setup without depending on a paid subscription. It is fast, flexible, and a great way to experience agentic coding with your own local models. 4. AppFlowy: Replacing Notion With an Open-Source Workspace AppFlowy is one of the best open-source alternatives to Notion if you want more control over your data. You can use it for documents, notes, wikis, tasks, databases, Kanban boards, calendars, and team collaboration, while keeping the familiar all-in-one workspace idea that makes Notion so useful. What I like about AppFlowy is that it is not just a small note-taking app. It has native desktop apps for Windows, macOS, and Linux, mobile apps, a web version, offline support, and options for self-hosting. You can also use its AI features for writing and editing, so it is getting closer to a complete productivity workspace rather than just a Notion clone. The main appeal is control . You can keep your workspace local or run AppFlowy on your own infrastructure instead of putting everything inside another SaaS platform. One caveat is that AppFlowy's current server-side self-hosting stack has moved toward an open-core/commercial model, while its web and Flutter clients remain open source, so the self-hosting story is a little more complicated than it used to be. 5. Handy: Replacing Paid AI Dictation Apps Handy is a fast, open-source dictation app that works completely offline. It is built with Tauri, Rust, React, and TypeScript , and the workflow is simple: press a shortcut, speak, and Handy transcribes your voice locally and pastes the text directly into whatever app you are using. That means you can dictate into ChatGPT, coding agents, documents, emails, terminals, or basically any text field without sending your audio to the cloud. It supports local Whisper models with GPU acceleration as well as Parakeet V3 for CPU-friendly transcription. The project reports around 5× real-time transcription speed for Parakeet V3 on a mid-range i5, so it feels fast enough for everyday dictation. That is what makes Handy such a good alternative to paid dictation tools. You get fast, private, system-wide voice typing with no subscription, no cloud processing, and no per-minute transcription cost. 6. LanguageTool: Replacing Grammarly for Everyday Writing LanguageTool is a strong open-source alternative to Grammarly for grammar, spelling, punctuation, and style checking. Its open-source core supports more than 25 languages, including English, Spanish, French, German, Portuguese, Polish, and Dutch, and it catches many contextual mistakes that a basic spell checker would miss. What makes it especially useful is that you are not forced to use the hosted service. You can run your own LanguageTool server locally or self-host it , which gives you more privacy and lets you integrate grammar checking into your own applications through its HTTP API. For everyday writing, emails, documents, and browser-based work, the free and open-source core is already very capable. LanguageTool also offers paid cloud features, but if your main goal is solid grammar and style checking without depending on another subscription, the open-source version is a very practical replacement. 7. SurfSense: Replacing NotebookLM for AI Research A lot of people I know use tools like NotebookLM to study documents, research topics, and build a searchable knowledge base around their own files. SurfSense gives you a similar experience, but with much more control.

title: An update on independent evaluators
abstract: Announcements An update on independent evaluators Oct 15, 2026 Last month, we committed to stronger independent, third-party assessment of our models and safety practices. We also signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, in which companies pledged to partner with independent external auditors or evaluators. Today, we’re announcing that we’ve started to give employee-like access to a team from METR , a nonprofit that evaluates frontier AI models. METR will publish the results of its risk assessments. Over the past year, we’ve worked with METR on several reviews of our Risk Reports . We’re also working with SecureBio and Accenture as evaluators, and are in early discussions with several other organizations, including Hugging Face . Here, we explain our approach to working with evaluators. Why we work with independent evaluators As models have become more powerful, they’ve required stronger safeguards and more challenging risk assessments. We want to be publicly accountable for the decisions we’re making. But we can’t publicly share all the information relevant to our safety work. Some of it could be useful to malicious actors, or is commercially sensitive, like compute or training information. Instead, we’re giving third-party evaluators deep access to our information, and are having them share evidence and reasoned conclusions about the risks involved in building our models. We aim to close the gap between what evaluators understand about a frontier AI company’s systems and what the company itself understands. To evaluate frontier models, evaluators need the following: Expertise in assessing the capabilities of frontier models, including understanding the way evaluations can go wrong, such as alignment faking . Independence : they shouldn’t hold equity in the company they’re evaluating, or be financially or operationally dependent on it. Enough access to meaningfully evaluate risks. Beyond access to the latest models, evaluators also need visibility into how those models were trained, into how our safeguards function, and more. Freedom to publish observations and assessments of a model or a process. Although the analogy isn’t exact, bank supervision operates on similar logic. Banks know more about their own risk positions than outsiders do, so regulators assign resident examiners to work inside the largest banks. If a bank’s risk-taking could threaten the public, third parties try to see that in advance. For the AI industry, this is a step toward robust safety oversight . We’re moving quickly with multiple evaluators and learning actively about what kinds of partnership work. We’re committed to sharing updates as we go. What we mean by “employee-like access” We’ve onboarded six METR employees with company hardware, office space, and access to internal tools and systems that are roughly on par with what our own risk assessment teams have access to. Outside a small number of clearly defined categories (e.g., data about customers, attorney-client privileged information, or information about our model architectures), Anthropic employees are encouraged to share information with them just as they would with a fellow employee working on alignment risk. 1 METR will publish its analysis of our risk levels, incidents, or practices. Anthropic can’t veto publication, but we can require them to redact information if it falls into narrow, predefined categories like the ones above. METR is free to characterize our redactions publicly, and say whether it believes the redactions were justified, as long as it does so without revealing the redacted information. Our engagement with METR is limited to a small team operating under enforceable agreements. Other METR employees are siloed from that team’s work, including researchers who work with us on other projects. Embedded evaluation gives a few qualified people working under Anthropic’s security standards a close view of how we operate. It’s not a way for other organizations to obtain our information, or that of our customers and partners. Our other evaluator partnerships We’re working on several other partnerships. Because these other partnerships are still in early stages, we’re providing these evaluators with more limited information, and they have more limited publication rights. Our goal with these early engagements is to make sure that our partners protect confidential information and have the requisite resources and expertise to evaluate our models. As partnerships progress and we build trust, we hope to fully embed more independent evaluators. We’re developing three tiers of access for evaluators. Over time, we hope to have several evaluators at the third tier, with each team publishing their own analysis of our risk posture and key decisions. In the first tier, evaluators conduct narrowly scoped risk investigations. We decide what access to provide a first-tier evaluator, and evaluators can publish their findings with our approval. In the second tier, evaluators can publish without our approval, and they have access to more information. We can still require removal of specific categories of information, though evaluators can publish their views on whether our redactions were justified. The third tier is the arrangement we’ve described with METR, with employee-like access and publication rights similar to those of the second tier. SecureBio is currently in the first tier. It’s in the process of reviewing the chemical and biological weapons chapter of our August Risk Report , after completing and publishing a pilot review of our previous risk report. After this review is complete, we will consider moving to projects with increased access and publication rights. With Accenture and Faculty, we're working toward an ambitious partnership that includes evaluating and red-teaming models, conducting alignment assessments, testing model safeguards, and building capabilities across our organizations. We’re embedding evaluators voluntarily, and we believe every frontier AI company should do the same. Footnotes Because these evaluators (like bank examiners) may also work with other companies, we exercise caution around the possibility of inadvertent leaks. Information about architectures presents a high risk of inadvertent leaks, and its relevance to risk assessment is typically low. When it is highly relevant, we will generally seek to share it, though this will require explicit internal approvals.

title: Local and Distributed Large LLM Inference with MLX and RDMA on Mac Studio
abstract: content type Featured highlight Local and Distributed Large LLM Inference with MLX and RDMA on Mac Studio October 15, 2026 MLX on Mac with Apple silicon lets AI researchers and developers experiment locally with the latest models and methods in a private environment. The open-source array framework leverages the unified memory architecture of Apple silicon, enabling anyone to run new inference and fine-tuning methods on their own hardware and explore other AI techniques. In a previous post , we highlighted the advantages of the M5 architecture and its GPU Neural Accelerators. In this post, we show how to run the latest frontier-class model — Muse Spark Open, with nearly a trillion parameters — right from your desk, using the latest version of MLX, released today. On a cluster of four Mac Studios, Muse Spark Open generates over 36 tokens per second (see Figure 1 ), well above average human reading speed. Beginning on a single Mac Studio (up to 512GB of unified memory), then scaling out across multiple Macs with the RDMA over Thunderbolt driver, below we share an overview of the range of models you can now run on Mac Studio. Muse Spark Open Decode Speed Context size of 8,192 tokens Figure 1: Muse Spark Open decode speed in tokens per second, on Mac Studio with M5 Ultra, at a context size of 8,192 tokens. Higher is better. We report performance for three parallelization schemes: pipeline parallelization over two Mac Studio computers (2 M5 Pipeline), and tensor parallelization over two (2 M5 Tensor) and four Mac Studio (4 M5 Tensor) computers. Running Large Language Models with MLX We benchmark several popular open-weight LLMs on Mac Studio , using the MLX LM package, as described in our prior post . We compare two generations of Mac Studio: the recently released M5 Ultra and the previous generation, M3 Ultra. The M5 generation features the GPU Neural Accelerator, which supports dedicated matrix multiplication operations, essential for many machine learning workloads. We evaluate three frontier-class models ( Table 1 ) spanning a wide range of sizes (in billions of parameters, B): the newly released Muse Spark Open (816 B), Mistral Medium 3.5 (128 B), and Qwen 3.8 (27 B). Muse Spark Open is a mixture of experts (MoE) model, which keeps only a fraction of its experts — and thus parameters — active, reducing compute at inference, and it is evaluated in NVFP4 precision. Mistral Medium 3.5 and Qwen 3.8 are dense architectures, where all parameters are active at inference, and they are evaluated in their native floating-point precision (FP8 and BF16, respectively). Model Total Parameters Active Parameters Native Precision Evaluation Precision Muse Spark Open 816B 42B BF16 NVFP4 Mistral Medium 3.5 128B 128B FP8 FP8 Qwen 3.8 27B 27B BF16 BF16 Table 1: Language models used in this post. Models ship in various precision formats; we evaluate Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5 in their native precision, and Muse Spark Open in 4-bit (NVFP4) precision. Our evaluation measures three metrics across a range of context sizes: time to first token (TTFT, in seconds), generation throughput (in tokens/second), and peak power usage (in watts). All the performance numbers in this post were obtained with mlx_lm.benchmark . For example, running Qwen 3.8 with 8,192 tokens of context and generating 128 tokens is performed with the command line: mlx_lm.benchmark --model Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B -p 8192 -g 128 -b 1 A popular use of local LLMs on Mac Studio is running agentic experiences in a private environment, including agentic coding applications that often need large contexts. We therefore report performance at both 8,192 and 65,536 context sizes. Raw TTFT and decode throughput are reported in Table 2 and Table 3 , respectively. Inference Performance on a Single Mac Studio Qwen 3.8 27B and Mistral Medium 3.5 128B fit comfortably on a single Mac Studio with 512GB, taking up to 68GB and 158GB of RAM in the large context size (65,536 tokens) setup. In Figure 2 , we compare their inference performance on a single Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM, both on M3 Ultra and M5 Ultra. Time to first token (TTFT) is essentially compute bound, and that is where the Neural Accelerators in the M5 Ultra GPU shine: the specialized hardware support for fast matrix-multiplication of the GPU Neural Accelerator directly translates into significant speedups for TTFT, up to 4.6× faster compared to an M3 Ultra (see Figure 2 ). That makes the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra the desktop of choice when it comes to handling tasks involving very large contexts. Generation speed (in tokens per second) is memory-bandwidth bound. The M5 Ultra chip delivers 1.2 TB/s of unified memory bandwidth, up from 819 GB/s for the M3 Ultra. Here again, that translates directly into generation speed (see Figure 3 ), with the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra reporting 1.6× faster tokens/s. TTFT Speedup Single Mac Studio, M5 Ultra over an M3 Ultra baseline (1.0×) Figure 2: Time to first token (TTFT) speedup on M5 Ultra over an M3 Ultra baseline, for Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5, at context sizes of 8,192 and 65,536 tokens. The M5 Ultra GPU Neural Accelerator shines on compute-bound workloads. Decode Speedup Single Mac Studio, M5 Ultra over an M3 Ultra baseline (1.0×) Figure 3: Decode speedup on M5 Ultra over an M3 Ultra baseline, for Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5, at context sizes of 8,192 and 65,536 tokens. Decode is memory-bandwidth bound, and the M5 Ultra’s 1.2 TB/s of unified memory bandwidth (vs 819 GB/s on the M3 Ultra) is a key advantage. The Mac Studio is also energy-efficient for LLM inference (see Figure 4 ): peak power consumption is about 200W for the Mac Studio with M3 Ultra, and 300W for the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra — a fraction of the power used by a common toaster. More importantly, that modest amount of power consumption means a Mac Studio can be deployed for AI work in any home or office environment. Peak Power Consumption Context size of 65,536 tokens Figure 4: Peak power consumption (in watts) during Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5 inference, at a context size of 65,536 tokens, on Mac Studio with M3 Ultra and with M5 Ultra. While both the Qwen and Mistral models fit on a single Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM, Muse Spark Open would require more than 1.6TB of RAM in its native precision (BF16) for the model parameters alone. In a 4-bit quantized (NVFP4) format, the model memory footprint is lowered to about 493GB. Add the memory needed for intermediate computations during inference, and the model cannot fit on a single machine. It requires parallelization across multiple Mac Studio computers. Pipelining Inference Across Two Mac Studio Computers Very large frontier-class models like Muse Spark Open will not fit on a single machine. It is, however, possible to store half of the model on one Mac Studio and the other half on another. We can then pipeline the model’s inference across two computers: the first Mac Studio executes the first half of the model’s layers, then sends the output to the second Mac Studio, which executes the second half. This parallelization scheme is called pipeline parallelization (see Figure 5 ) and is extremely simple to implement, requiring only minimal code changes. Splitting Large Models Across Multiple Computers Figure 5: MLX supports two approaches to splitting large models across multiple computers. With pipeline parallelization, a model is split across depth, while with tensor parallelization, a model is split across width. MLX supports different parallelization schemes, as described in the MLX distributed documentation . These rely on fast inter-machine communication: macOS 26.2 introduced a low-latency RDMA driver over Thunderbolt 5, and MLX (v0.30.1 and later) builds on top of this driver and provides new communication collectives ( jaccl , pronounced “jackal”) for different parallelization schemes.

title: Selection-Based Structured Reasoning: Toward Efficient Multimodal Search Agents
abstract: research area Methods and Algorithms content type paper published October 2026 Selection-Based Structured Reasoning: Toward Efficient Multimodal Search Agents Authors Feiyu Gavin Zhu†**, Xiaoyu Zhu, Jiqi Yang, Rui Yang‡***, Arnab Kumar Mondal, Yancheng Wang, Xinke Deng, Jean Oh†, Reid Simmons†, Joerg Liebelt, Xiang Kong, Zhongyu Jiang View publication Copy Bibtex Multimodal agents commonly generate freeform reasoning before each action. For small models, limited model capacity can result in lengthy reasoning that provides little useful guidance for action generation while incurring substantial inference cost. To address this challenge, we introduce Selection-based Structured Reasoning (SSR), a framework that reformulates reasoning as selection instead of open-ended generation. SSR represents recurring high-level reasoning as pre-specified, reusable natural-language candidates. At each turn, the model selects from the reasoning candidates based on their likelihoods given the current context, without an auxiliary task head. Using pre-specified reasoning traces enables parallel scoring, where teacher-forced prefilling computes token likelihoods concurrently within and across candidates using a shared context KV cache. We evaluated SSR on seven multimodal search benchmarks using 2B and 4B models. Across multiple reinforcement learning objectives and supervised fine-tuning, SSR delivers significant efficiency gains without sacrificing task performance. SSR achieves an average success rate competitive with leading search agents of the same scale, while reducing per-turn reasoning latency by over 90% and total per-question model inference latency by 28–54%. † Carnegie Mellon University ‡ University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign ** Work partially done while at Apple *** Work done while at Apple Related readings and updates. title: Plan or Retrieve First? A Scale Study of Tool Discovery Architectures
abstract: research area Methods and Algorithms , research area Tools, Platforms, Frameworks conference EMNLP content type paper published October 2026 Plan or Retrieve First? A Scale Study of Tool Discovery Architectures Authors Mingfei Zhang, Amit Surana, Ziauddin Majid, Chenxi Wang, Michael Xu View publication Copy Bibtex Tool-augmented LLM agents discover relevant APIs from large registries before planning execution, yet finite context windows prohibit injecting all tool definitions into a single prompt. The dominant approach, which we term Retrieve-then-Plan (RtP), embeds the user query and retrieves similar tools via approximate nearest-neighbor search. We study an alternative Plan-then-Retrieve (PtR) paradigm in which the LLM first generates Abstract Tool Stubs (hypothesized function signatures describing needed capabilities) which then serve as retrieval queries against the registry. Evaluating on ToolBench (46,984 unique API endpoints, 50 categories) across single-tool (G1), intra-category multi-tool (G2), and cross-category multi-tool (G3) query subsets, we find a clear complexity-dependent crossover: RtP outperforms PtR on single-tool queries while PtR outperforms RtP on multi-tool queries. This crossover holds at every retrieval budget (k=1 to 20), is robust across registry sizes from 1k to 47k APIs, and is consistent across model families (Gemini 2.5 Flash and gpt-oss-120b). We characterize a stub-hallucination failure mode (the LLM invents plausible but non-existent API names) that acts as a double-edged sword: on simple queries PtR’s stubs abstract away proper-noun signals that RtP matches directly, yet on complex queries the same mechanism decomposes multi-faceted intent into functional sub-needs. We further analyze token overhead and show that PtR’s extra discovery call roughly doubles inference cost, which pays off on multi-tool queries but hurts on single-tool ones, motivating complexity-adaptive routing as a practical direction—one that can be driven by a zero-cost signal already present in the pipeline (RtP’s top-1 retrieval score). Related readings and updates. ProTIP: Progressive Tool Retrieval Improves Planning December 20, 2023 research area Knowledge Bases and Search , research area Speech and Natural Language Processing Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly employed for complex multi-step planning tasks, where the Tool Retrieval (TR) step is crucial for achieving successful outcomes. Two prevalent approaches for TR are single-step retrieval, which utilizes the complete query, and sequential retrieval using Task Decomposition (TD), where a full query is segmented into discrete atomic subtasks. While single-step retrieval lacks the flexibility to handle… Read more Context Tuning for Retrieval Augmented Generation December 18, 2023 research area Knowledge Bases and Search , research area Speech and Natural Language Processing Workshop at EACL This paper was accepted at the UncertaiNLP workshop at EACL 2024. Large language models (LLMs) have the remarkable ability to solve new tasks with just a few examples, but they need access to the right tools. Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) addresses this problem by retrieving a list of relevant tools for a given task. However, RAG’s tool retrieval step requires all the required information to be explicitly present in the query. This is a… Read more Discover opportunities in Machine Learning.
