title: Introducing Timestral
abstract: Research Introducing Timestral October 15, 2026 By Mistral Back to Blog 7 min read Share this post Copy url to clipboard Copied Thinking Summary Timestral, Mistral’s first family of time-series foundation models, delivers state-of-the-art probabilistic, multivariate forecasts with just 209M parameters, outperforming larger models on key benchmarks while supporting past and future covariates. Available in four sizes (5M to 209M parameters), it balances accuracy and efficiency, running efficiently on CPUs and excelling in zero-shot forecasting for diverse domains. The model combines synthetic pre-training, covariate-aware attention, and long-context learning, with fine-tuning options for domain adaptation via Mistral Forge. Today, we’re releasing Timestral, our first family of time-series foundation models. Our largest model, at just 209M parameters, ranks first on all three of the field's main public benchmarks, GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench, outperforming the previous state of the art with only two-thirds of the model parameters. Timestral delivers probabilistic, multivariate forecasts and supports past-only and known-future covariates. Our family of models sits on the Pareto front of forecasting accuracy versus model size, delivering leading performance at each size. Results have been submitted to the GIFT-Eval and TIME leaderboards. Time Series Foundation Models (TSFM) Time series is one of the most common data types in enterprise, from sensor telemetry to observability metrics. Forecasts built on it drive decisions in capacity planning, energy, supply chains, risk and maintenance. Industrial plants forecast process sensors against the production schedule, catch equipment drift before it fails, and plan capacity and spare parts across thousands of assets. Finance teams forecast flows, volumes, and volatility to inform positions, hedging, and treasury across thousands of accounts. Classical models such as ARIMA and linear regression remain well-established tools for forecasting time series. These models are usually fitted to a single series and learn only from that series' history. Deep learning models such as PatchTST add the capacity to learn nonlinear patterns across many related series, but they are still typically trained from scratch on each dataset, so what they learn doesn't carry over to new domains. Time series foundation models bring the pre-training approach to time series. Trained on a large and diverse corpus, our model learns patterns that transfer across series, forecasting zero-shot on data it has never seen, even in domains where data is scarce. Benchmark Results We evaluated Timestral on the three main public forecasting benchmarks: GIFT-Eval, TIME and fev-bench. Among pre-trained, zero-shot models, it ranks first across all five metrics. These results come from a single checkpoint, without ensembling. GIFT-Eval - GMean MASE GIFT-Eval - GMean WQL GIFT-Eval, top ten of 83 comparable pretrained and zero-shot entries. Lower is better. TIME - GMean MASE TIME - GMean CRPS TIME, top ten of the 35 leaderboard entries. Lower is better on both metrics. fev-bench, top ten of the 37 leaderboard entries, by SQL skill score. Higher is better. Family of models optimised for every specification Timestral has been optimised as a family of four models: 5M, 28M, 123M and 209M parameters. The larger models improve forecast performance, while the smaller ones are faster and cheaper. All four share the same architecture and training recipe. Every size sits on the Pareto front of accuracy versus model size: for each model size, no public model forecasts better. Score vs model size on GIFT-Eval, TIME and fev-bench (shown as 1 − skill score). Lower is better. Our 28M model beats Chronos-2, about four times larger, on GIFT-Eval and TIME. Our 209M model beats TimesFM-3 and Falcon-2.0 with fewer parameters. Timestral does not need a GPU at inference. On a standard server CPU with 8 threads, forecasting one day ahead from three weeks of 15-minute history takes 10 ms with the 5M model and 140 ms with the 209M model. Smaller models trade some accuracy for speed: the 28M model is five times faster than the 209M model, and the 123M model comes within 0.2% of the 209M score at three quarters of its latency. An industrial example Consider an industrial plant with thousands of sensors across its equipment. Timestral can improve the forecasts on that data in several ways. Multivariate forecasting. A pump's vibration, temperature and pressure don't move independently. A rise in one often explains or causes a change in another. Timestral models related series jointly, so it can use those dependencies instead of forecasting each sensor in isolation. Probabilistic forecasting. A single predicted value may not show the full picture. Timestral predicts a full set of quantiles, so teams can see how wide the uncertainty is, set alert thresholds that reflect it, and plan maintenance around risk rather than a single number. Categorical covariates. Some covariates take values from a set of categories rather than continuous numbers, such as the day of the week, or a machine's state (running, idle, under maintenance). Encoding these as numbers would impose an order or scale they don't have. Timestral takes them as categorical inputs directly to improve forecasts. Known-future covariates. Some drivers of sensor behaviour are known in advance, such as production schedules, planned shutdowns, weather forecasts. Timestral can condition on them to improve forecast quality, so a scheduled load increase is expected rather than flagged as a surprise. From Model to System Timestral is a numerical model that can run inside existing monitoring pipelines, or be paired with our language models in multi-modal agentic workflows. In the plant, that could look like this: Timestral running continuously on the plant's sensor streams, detecting anomalies as they occur. When it flags an anomaly on a pump, an agent embeds the signals and compares against embeddings of past sensor data to find similar historical failures. The agent then starts sub-agents to run a root cause analysis, drawing on context from that plant, such as maintenance records, shift logs and operator notes, equipment manuals, past work orders, and readings from related equipment. The agent drafts a suggested diagnosis based on the findings, with supporting evidence and possible next steps. The plant manager gets a diagnosis and a plan backed by the sensor data, rather than just an alert. Key technical contributions Several ideas have been combined to produce these results. Each will be described in detail in the technical report. Decoupled Horizon Forecasting. Causal decoders trained with contiguous patch masking, as in Toto 2.0 and TimesFM-3, mask out the values to be forecast, so they look like missing values and are also lost as context for later forecasts. Our approach, DHF, separates the two: the full history stays in the sequence, and learned forecast tokens read the history before them. Every observed value thus serves as both target and context, true gaps stay flagged as missing, and training horizon lengths and missing-data augmentation can be tuned independently of each other. Covariate-aware attention. Each input series is assigned a role: target variate, past-only covariate or known-future covariate. Known-future covariates are visible across the whole window while targets stay causal, and information flows only from covariates to targets. Timestral can therefore use a holiday calendar or a weather forecast without leaking a target's own future into its forecast. Synthetic-first data. The majority of the training data was synthetic. We first generated univariate processes with coherent temporal dynamics, including trends, seasonality and diverse noise patterns. We then used a multivariate synthesizer to construct multivariate series by introducing nonlinear dependencies between these processes. Two-stage training.

title: Accelerating the search for antimicrobial peptides with Google Antigravity
abstract: October 15, 2026 Science Accelerating the search for antimicrobial peptides with Google Antigravity Pengfei Tian, Maxwell L. Bileschi, Zoi Tsangalidou, Sukhdeep Singh and Lucy J. Colwell Explore scientific workflows in Google Antigravity New antibiotics are urgently needed to help with rising levels of antimicrobial resistance, but searching for new therapeutics is often a slow, labor-intensive process. With Google Antigravity, our agentic development platform, this process can now be made easier. Google Antigravity provides an agentic science workbench that empowers biologists to discover, structurally evaluate, and prioritize promising targets quickly, compressing what used to be a fragmented search over multiple databases into a single session. It also helps researchers scan through millions of previously uncharacterized proteins in the UniProt database using ProtNLM, a model that predicts biological function from amino acid sequences. This technical walkthrough shows how biologists used Google Antigravity to uncover a novel antimicrobial peptide candidate which has predicted activity against the pathogens involved in respiratory tract infections. The lead identified here is now undergoing wet-lab validation. Finding new antimicrobial peptides Rising antimicrobial resistance is one of the most pressing global health crises of our time and could result in an estimated 10 million annual deaths globally by 2050. To prevent this, we urgently need to discover novel therapeutics. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs), particularly bacteriocins, offer a promising alternative to traditional antibiotics because they have naturally evolved to target fundamental vulnerabilities in competing bacteria, from cell envelopes to essential intracellular machinery, making it difficult for pathogens to develop resistance. The exponential growth of genomic and metagenomic sequencing has populated global databases with billions of natural amino acid sequences. This pool of natural data has already produced globally used bacteriocins like Nisin, alongside recent genome-mined breakthroughs such as Darobactin, Dynobactin, and Lariocidin. Many, however, remain locked within the unannotated "dark matter" of protein databases, with their function uncharacterized because they aren’t similar to known proteins. For example, the world's leading public resource of protein sequence and functional information, UniProt , holds millions of sequences with unknown functionality, transferred directly from genome sequencing projects. To bridge this gap, Google developed ProtNLM (Protein Natural Language Model) , a deep learning model trained to directly read the underlying evolutionary “grammar” of amino acid sequences. This allows the model to predict biological function directly from raw protein sequences, enriching millions of previously unnamed UniProt entries with high-confidence functional labels. Overview of the ProtNLM pipeline translating raw amino acid sequences into natural-language biological annotations for unreviewed UniProtKB/TrEMBL entries. The functional annotation scope of the system covers protein names, function comments, subcellular locations, and GO terms, in addition to keywords. Collaborative intelligence Scientific discovery is rarely a single step process; finding viable candidate proteins requires human intuition and iteration to incorporate new empirical evidence. Working in Antigravity, the researcher and AI agent begin by setting a focused biological goal: find and computationally validate novel AMPs in Streptococcus pseudopneumoniae . During an interactive, multi-turn session the researcher steers the scientific strategy, deciding which questions to ask and what evidence to collect, while the agent handles the heavy lifting of cross-database orchestration, structural analysis, and literature synthesis. Slide 1 of 6 Navigating a vast search space: The agent queries the database and filters millions of entries down to a handful of candidates worthy of attention. Here, the agent finds a bacteriocin (Uniprot ID: A0A0U0D591 ) with a length of 97 amino acids from the Lactococcin 972 family. Validating the novelty of a finding: To verify the novelty of this discovery, the researcher guides the agent to interrogate the candidate against curated knowledge in Swiss-Prot via the EMBL-EBI NCBI-BLAST service and confirm this peptide has no meaningful sequence homolog among manually reviewed proteins. Reasoning over 3D protein structure: The researcher steers the analysis towards structural evidence. The agent retrieves the candidate’s 3D model from the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, querying it against experimentally determined structures to identify remote homologs, and superimposing the models to assess similarity. Here, the structural evidence corroborates ProtNLM’s prediction by showing the candidate's fold closely matches an experimentally determined bacteriocin. The structure viewer in Antigravity allows this structural analysis to be seamlessly performed in one place. Reading the biological context around a gene: The agent looks beyond the molecule itself to its genomic neighborhood, reasoning over whether the surrounding machinery supports the AMP hypothesis. Inspecting the flanking genes, it spots a revealing pattern: our previously uncharacterized candidate sits at the upstream of a tightly coupled operon, just 6 base pairs ahead of a ABC transporter permease and its potential partner ATP-binding protein, alongside another annotated bacteriocin and an XRE transcriptional regulator. This provides strong contextual evidence that it is part of a working bacteriocin system. Building a mechanistic hypothesis from the literature : By reviewing the existing literature, the agent proposes how the molecule might act and what pathogens it might act on. In this case, existing evidence suggests a mechanism of action targeting bacterial cell division, and a predicted potency spectrum spanning several drug-resistant pathogens. Generating an experimental plan: Finally, the agent translates its in silico findings into an actionable bench protocol, spanning protein expression, antimicrobial susceptibility testing, target engagement, and in vitro toxicity testing, bridging the gap from computational prediction to wet-lab experiment. This step is already in motion: this candidate - along with several others discovered through the same pipeline - are now in wet-lab validation, where experimental results will provide the ultimate test of the agent's analysis. The candidate we uncover in this walkthrough represents a biologically plausible lead backed by structural and genomic evidence but it still requires wet lab validation. What makes this meaningful is how dramatically it lowers the barrier to everyday biological workflows, turning days of fragmented database triage into a single collaborative session. While this session focused on a narrow amino acid window in Streptococcus pseudopneumoniae , researchers can take the conversation in any direction, such as layering in new filtering criteria, exploring different sequence lengths, or targeting other priority pathogens. By broadening the search from human commensals to environmental microbes and beyond, scientists can guide the agent across UniProt to discover novel AMP candidates at scale. A shared 3D canvas for interactive collaboration A protein's 3D structure can help us understand its biological function. Examining a candidate’s predicted fold in space is key. To provide this end-to-end workflow in a single workspace, we are introducing the Biomolecular Structure Viewer , a 3D visualization tool embedded directly into Antigravity. The researcher and agent work together over a shared visual state. As the agent retrieves structures from AlphaFold Database or the scientist’s own predictions, it can dynamically drive the viewer. For instance, it can highlight key functional regions to visually explain its hypotheses.

title: Proof-based general-purpose computing with Magnetar
abstract: Every result a computer produces comes with an implicit question: did the program run as claimed and produce correct outputs? Today, answering that question often requires a degree of trust alongside verification. We trust the operator, the vendor, the counterparty, or the agent, and we rely on contracts, audits, and logs to establish that trust. Zero-knowledge proofs offer a fundamentally different approach to establishing trust. A program runs, and along with its output it produces a short proof, a cryptographic certificate that this program, on these inputs, produced this output. The proof is small and fast to check. Whoever receives it can confirm the result in milliseconds without rerunning the program, and can pass the proof on to anyone else who needs the same assurance. With the zero-knowledge property, the proof also reveals nothing about inputs that should stay private. This changes what correctness means in the real world. A result no longer has to be trusted because of who produced it. It can be checked because of what accompanies it. An AI agent acting on someone’s behalf could attach a proof that each action complied with the policy it was given. Regulated financial institutions could prove that transactions were processed correctly without making their transactions public. These become possible once producing a proof is as routine as running the program. Zero-knowledge proofs were invented in the 1980s, and the ideas behind proving program execution have been around nearly as long. What has kept them from becoming a general tool is three challenges that have resisted being solved at the same time. Efficiency . Producing a proof has historically taken millions of times more computation than running the program itself. Years of research have brought that overhead down, but the fastest systems have achieved their speed by making compromises elsewhere. Generality and usability. Many proof systems require developers to manually rewrite their program as a cryptographic circuit, which is a fixed arithmetic description of that exact computation. This takes months. Every change to the application means a new circuit, and the translation is itself a frequent source of security bugs. A general-purpose alternative is to prove the execution of an ordinary processor, so that any compiled program can be proven as written. Until recently, that generality came at a steep cost in speed or security. Security. A proof is only as strong as the cryptography beneath it. Many proof systems rest on elliptic curves, which can be broken by a sufficiently powerful quantum computer. Microsoft is addressing this problem with its Quantum Safe Program, which will move its products and services to post-quantum cryptography, a goal it recently accelerated to 2029 . Post-quantum proof systems already exist, but some rest on lattice assumptions, and most rest on new cryptographic functions invented to reduce the cost of proving. These new cryptographic functions have not faced the decades of scrutiny given to the cryptography protecting today’s internet, and some rest on mathematical conjectures about error-correcting codes that have not been proven. They have bought their speed with strong assumptions. For more than a decade, Microsoft Research has worked on making zero-knowledge proofs and verifiable computing practical. Early research followed two approaches, both practical only for small programs. The first (opens in new tab) (opens in new tab) lets a verifier check a long computation through a short conversation with the prover using a technique called the sum-check protocol (opens in new tab) , but this applied only to computations with a particular layered structure. The second (opens in new tab) (opens in new tab) used elliptic-curve cryptography to create very small proofs for almost any computation. But this requires a one-time trusted setup involving secret information which, if leaked, could allow anyone to forge proofs. This approach is also vulnerable to quantum computers. In 2019, a new zero-knowledge proof system called Spartan returned to the sum-check approach and made it work for general-purpose programs without a trusted setup. Spartan can also be instantiated with different cryptographic building blocks. That flexibility is what later allowed the proof system to be built on hash functions alone. A sequence of results then filled in the remaining pieces: Each of these solved a piece of the problem. Magnetar is where the pieces come together. Magnetar is a zero-knowledge virtual machine, or zkVM, and it makes major progress on all three challenges at once. It is general-purpose. Magnetar proves the execution of RISC-V, an open processor architecture with mature compilers for every mainstream language. A developer writes a program in Rust, Go, or C, compiles it as usual, and Magnetar proves it as written. Consider what this means in practice. A business policy, a data pipeline, or an interpreter for the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) is just a program, and the engineers who already maintain it can prove their executions exactly as written. As a result, proving stops being a specialist activity. It is faster than prior systems in the same class. Magnetar proves 7.2 to 8.7 million processor instructions per second on a laptop. Across 15 benchmark programs, from cryptographic hashing to token transfers inside a small EVM interpreter, it is 10 to 39 times faster on average than the fastest existing zkVMs on the same machine, and more than 300 times faster than two others on a token-transfer benchmark. An optimized Magnetar proves 9.5–12.8 million cycles per second, which increases each speedup reported here by about 1.3×. Its proofs verify in about 12 milliseconds. Its security rests on standard cryptography. Magnetar depends on a standard hash function such as SHA-256 or SHA-3, the same primitives that already protect every organization’s systems. It requires no elliptic curves, no lattices, no special-purpose hash functions, no trusted setup, and no unproven conjecture about error-correcting codes. Hash functions are the most thoroughly studied primitives in the cryptographic toolkit, and they are the basis of the stateless hash-based signatures that NIST standardized as its own conservative post-quantum option. For a system that must still be trustworthy in many decades to come, relying only on standard hash functions removes a cryptographic migration from the roadmap. The same design decision pays a second dividend. Checking a Magnetar proof consists mostly of evaluating standard hash functions and binary-field arithmetic, which are exactly the operations Magnetar proves efficiently. Verifying a proof is therefore an ordinary workload for it. This is what allows Magnetar to prove computations of any size, by proving them in pieces and then combining the pieces. This also allows Magnetar to prove a long-running system such as a ledger or a blockchain. The technical paper gives the full design, security analysis, and measurements. Magnetar advances zero-knowledge proofs and verifiable computing to a stage where they can be built on the cryptography that organizations already trust, at speeds that make it usable, by engineers who write normal code. Magnetar enables a future where cryptographic proofs are a routine output of computation. We expect that technology leaders will stop asking whether proofs of execution are practical and focus instead on which results would they prefer to verify rather than taking on trust . If you’re interested in exploring how zero-knowledge proofs can support your use case, we’d love to hear from you (opens in new tab) . The post Proof-based general-purpose computing with Magnetar appeared first on Microsoft Research .

title: Meta Muse Spark Open is live on Together AI
Unlock powerful insights and forecasts with Predictive AI Functions
abstract: Data teams all get asked the same questions: "what will sales be next quarter?," "why did this metric move?," and "is this recent data outside the norm of what we typically see?" Answering these advanced analytics questions usually means handing the work to a data science team to build models and manage infrastructure. This creates a bottleneck where business users wait in line and many questions never even get asked. Predictive AI Functions , now in Beta, remove that bottleneck by letting analysts and business users run advanced analytics like forecasting, driver analysis, and anomaly detection, all through built-in functions backed by state-of-the-art ML models. These SQL-native functions can be called directly in SQL, invoked in Genie with plain-language questions, or embedded in dashboards. Because Databricks maintains the models centrally, teams get high-quality, consistent answers without building or managing infrastructure. This launch adds four new SQL native functions and improved accuracy to ai_forecast : To showcase how these functions can be used across Databricks, we'll walk through examples in dashboards, SQL, and Genie using the NYC taxi trips dataset. Dashboards are where teams watch the metrics that run their business, and often where they turn to see where those metrics are headed next. With ai_forecast , teams can project metrics and surface those forecasts alongside the rest of their reporting. The new ai_forecast makes it easy to get high-quality forecasts without any tuning. It's powered by a transformer-based time series foundation model, pretrained on a huge, diverse collection of time series the way a large language model is trained on text. Because it already recognizes common patterns like seasonality and trends, it produces accurate forecasts on your data with no tuning required. The visualization below uses ai_forecast to project the monthly ride volumes in the NYC taxi trips dataset through the end of 2027. The forecast reveals expected seasonal patterns in taxi demand, providing a data-driven view of where ridership is headed. The new ai_forecast not only handles general patterns automatically, it also introduces features to let teams add factors specific to their business. With built-in holiday support, teams can automatically account for local events like Christmas dips and school-holiday spikes. Teams can also specify external covariates, feeding in the factors that drive a metric, such as pricing changes or marketing spend, so forecasts better reflect their business. This launch also introduces four new functions for the ad-hoc advanced analytics questions commonly asked by data teams. Each one, like ai_forecast , is a native SQL function. Analysts can call them directly in the SQL editor or a notebook, run them across hundreds of millions of rows, and feed the results into their queries and pipelines alongside the rest of their work. Compared to developing custom models for similar functionality, this compresses development time and increases accessibility to more users. For example, the query below aggregates NYC taxi trips into a daily revenue time series and passes it to ai_detect_anomalies , which automatically fits a model to the data and flags unusual days. These same functions will be available to business users through Genie ( ai_top_drivers is available today, with ai_forecast , ai_detect_anomalies , ai_predict_value , and ai_predict_class coming soon). Anyone can ask a question in plain language, like why revenue dropped last quarter or which customers are likely to churn, and Genie calls the right function to return a grounded, model-backed answer, with no SQL or ML expertise required. The query below uses ai_top_drivers to automatically identify which time-of-day and weekday/weekend segments contributed the most to the change in NYC taxi fare revenue between January and February 2016. It ranks each segment by its absolute and relative revenue impact, revealing that weekday midday hours drove the largest gain while the weekday evening rush was the biggest drag. Because these functions use tailored machine learning methods, they enable Genie to answer questions a general-purpose LLM cannot reliably handle on its own. These functions all deliver high-quality predictions backed by production-grade ML models. Because Databricks maintains those models centrally, that quality stays consistent across every surface, so teams get the same trustworthy result whether a prediction runs in a dashboard, in SQL, or through Genie. Forecasting shows this most concretely. We used fev-bench to benchmark the new ai_forecast against functions from a leading cloud data warehouse. Task win rate is defined as the percentage of tasks (measured by scaled quantile loss) where one system achieves a lower probabilistic error than the other. Here's how the options compare: ai_forecast outperforms other cloud data warehouse providers as well as the previous version of ai_forecast . With Predictive AI Functions, teams get industry-leading accuracy out of the box, on every surface, with no tuning required. Predictive AI Functions turn questions that once required a data science team, like what's next, why did it change, what's wrong, and what's the value, into answers business teams can get themselves, right where they already work: in dashboards, in Genie, and in SQL. The result is advanced analytics for everyone: high-quality predictions that are easy to use, with no models to build or infrastructure to manage. Ready to try it? Get started with Predictive AI Functions here . Subscribe to our blog and get the latest posts delivered to your inbox.

title: How FactSet cut model training and deployment from days to hours with Databricks AI Runtime
abstract: FactSet’s Text-to-Formula (TTF) system has a deceptively difficult job: take a natural-language request from an investment professional and turn it into the correct FactSet Query Language (FQL) formula. FactSet initially built TTF around retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), using retrieval to find relevant examples and information for a given request. But as consumption grew, queries became more specialized and formulas more complex; the approach hit a quality ceiling. FactSet began incorporating fine-tuned open models into its Compound AI architecture, allowing the team to train models on the structure and patterns of FQL rather than relying primarily on retrieval at inference time. In its earlier work on TTF, FactSet found that incorporating fine-tuned models reduced end-to-end latency by about 60%. As the system evolved, so did the role of fine-tuning. FactSet accumulated more training data and began updating its models regularly, turning what had been an experimental workflow into a recurring part of developing TTF. Today, the team fine-tunes models roughly every two to three weeks. Training every few weeks changes the infrastructure requirements. Preparing an environment and configuring GPU compute may be manageable for an occasional experiment. Repeating that work every time new data or a new model is ready to test adds overhead directly to the development cycle. Model requirements can change from one experiment to the next as well. FactSet has worked with Llama-based models and continues to evaluate newer open models. Different models, prompt lengths, and output characteristics can require different compute configurations, so tying the training environment to a fixed GPU setup would make it harder to adapt as the team experiments. FactSet uses Databricks AI Runtime to run these fine-tuning workloads on serverless GPU infrastructure. Engineers can choose compute based on the requirements of a particular training run without first provisioning and configuring the underlying GPU environment. TTF’s training workflow also sits alongside data, experimentation, model management, and governance already running on Databricks. FactSet uses MLflow to track model development and experiments, while its underlying data remains governed within its existing Lakehouse environment. Running fine-tuning with AI Runtime keeps GPU training inside that workflow. Engineers can work with governed data, train a new model, track the resulting artifacts, and move toward deployment without maintaining a separate GPU stack for fine-tuning. For FactSet, that reduced the time required to set up, train, and deploy a custom TTF model from days to hours. The ability to change models has been part of TTF’s evolution from the beginning. Advanced RAG, especially reliance solely on externally hosted models, becomes a bottleneck on consistent accuracy and latency as the consumption grows and more complex formulas. RAG worked until the system encountered more complex formulas. Fine-tuned open models gave FactSet another way to improve quality and latency. Now, as newer models become available, the team can evaluate them against the workload rather than treating its current model choice as permanent. TTF itself is becoming more specialized. As FactSet accumulates more data, the team is exploring additional fine-tuned models for tasks such as query decomposition, component extraction, and library identification. That creates more opportunities to use the model best suited to each part of the workflow, but also makes fast, repeatable training more important. A model change is much easier to test when it does not require rebuilding the training environment around it. With GPU compute available on demand through AI Runtime, the engineering work shifts toward the questions that actually affect TTF: which model to use, how to train it, and whether the resulting version improves the application. Additionally, the fine-tuning pipeline was built on Databricks Lakeflow Jobs and Pipelines as a plug-and-play, reusable framework — designed to be easily adopted across different TTF tasks and other teams with minimal setup effort, providing a standardized foundation that reduces onboarding friction and accelerates integration. Open models are moving quickly. The model that offers the right balance of quality, latency, and cost today may not be the one a team wants six months from now. Preserving model choice therefore requires more than the ability to download a new set of weights. The surrounding training and deployment workflow has to keep up. FactSet’s experience with TTF shows what that looks like in production. The team can continue testing new open models as its data and application evolve, while AI Runtime provides serverless GPU infrastructure within its existing Databricks workflows. Instead of spending days setting up, training, and deploying each iteration, FactSet can complete that cycle in hours. For a system that is retrained every few weeks, that difference compounds. New data can move into a new model sooner, and engineers can spend more of each iteration improving TTF rather than preparing the infrastructure required to train it. title: Reducing Qwen training time by 6x on AI Runtime
abstract: Training or finetuning a multi-billion parameter foundation model requires significant compute, often spanning hundreds to thousands of hours of GPU training. But tuning training performance for an LLM is challenging, and high level metrics, such as GPU utilization may not be showing your actual utilization. In this blog post, we show how to cut through the layers of abstraction, and speed up fine-tuning of the latest Qwen 3.8 27B model on AI Runtime by 6x. Through systematic performance optimization, even with GPU utilization already at 98%, we go from 7 hours 44 minutes to 1 hour 17 minutes fine tuning a fixed dataset. We will provide a deep dive into the techniques behind these improvements, from how to measure what matters, implementation details, and design trade-offs involved in each optimization. If you want to get started right away, jump directly to the example code on AI Runtime and give it a try! We start with a standard training loop for Qwen 3.8 27B using the transformers library and the SFT training dataset HuggingFaceH4/ultrachat_200k . Our baseline training of the model over the complete dataset takes 7 hours and 44 minutes and during the training the GPU shows 98% average utilization. The result is 9,396 tok/s training. This GPU utilization looks high, but as mentioned earlier that number is misleading. The standard GPU utilization metric only counts the percentage of the time the GPU was doing anything , so this does not tell us how well the model was using the GPU while it was active. To understand this we need to look deeper. One way of doing this is the torch trace mechanism, we can adjust our training loop like the following (while also limiting the number of steps so we get a quick response): For a sample step this gives us the following data: Table 1: CPU - 14.4s with 1,714,382 calls. Table contains top operations by total time. Table 2: GPU - 10.3s with 269,448 operations. Table contains top operations by total time From these tables we notice a few high level issues with the current model: As well, we have an issue with excess padding in the batch: the input tensor must be rectangular and each row gets padded to the maximum number of tokens for that batch. We will show a trick for LLMs that can be used to minimize it. In the following sections, we will dive deeper into each technical topic, covering what it is, recommended best practices, and the key trade-offs to consider when applying it. You may notice that some kernels occur a lot! In particular, for Qwen, the batch matrix multiplication kernel runs over 30,000 times in one step. In this case we’ll explore fused kernels first. A fused kernel takes multiple smaller GPU kernels and combines them into one unit. This can help performance by avoiding costly transfers between a GPU’s high bandwidth memory and its even higher bandwidth on die memory. As well it can also allow for more efficient scheduling of GPU cores. With this many extra kernels, while torch.compile might work, it will take a long time to run. So reducing the raw number of ops with manually fused kernels is a good first step. Also, well-known fusions such as Flash Attention aren’t something that torch.compile by itself would find. The transformers library by default uses torch’s SDPA for the standard attention layers. But, it turns out many of these small operations we see come from the non-standard gated delta network layers. We’re lucky that for these layers there are two kernels, causal-conv1d and flash-linear-attention which have been written to fuse many of these operations per layer. How do we discover this? The transformers library implementation of Qwen already tells us what kernels it supports: There are two high level methods for getting these kernels: We generally recommend the first, especially paired with our docker container support , build your container with all your kernels installed at build time to reduce the amount of time it takes for your job to start. While kernelhub is convenient, since kernels often explicitly depend on the version torch and cuda installed, an available kernel for your specific configuration might not be available, and the transformers model will silently fallback to an unoptimized kernel with low performance. After installing the flash-linear-attention and causal-conv1d python packages, we improved our end to end time by a factor of 3.7x down to 2 hours 5 minutes. In the tables below, you can see the new kernels (highlighted), taking the place of the elementwise functions in the previous tables. As well the total number of operations executed has been greatly reduced, by a factor of 15x: Table 3: CPU - 3.9s with 118,316 calls. Table contains top operations by total time. Table 4: GPU - 3.9s with 18,060 calls. Table contains top operations by total time. Caveat : during training you will need both a kernel for the forwards and backwards pass and some kernels are forwards only, as they’ve only been implemented to speed up inference. Our Qwen model is pretty fast now, but we can get even faster. By default our batching setup uses 2D rectangular tensors 8,192 tokens as this is the largest size we can fit without running out of memory. The downside of this approach is that we tend to waste a considerable amount of space in the tensor with padding. If Qwen only used standard attention mechanisms, the torch’s NestedTensor is now well supported and would help reduce this cost by completely removing the padding. But flash-linear-attention only supports a more traditional 1D packed tensor approach: But we can’t just do this arbitrarily, simply passing the 1D tensor to the model may be acceptable for pretraining, but for finetuning, we need to ensure that in an example tokens only attend to tokens within the same example. To fix this we have to pass in the correct example position_ids to the model. In turn the model will pass these to the fused attention kernels and it will apply the correct attention mask. If you look at the example code here you can see how we compute the needed inputs to make this work. With this simple looking change, our training time goes from 2 hours 5 minutes to 1 hour and 17 minutes. Trade off: This style of change does make the input pipeline more complex, and there’s a high chance of introducing errors that impact model quality. But in this case the 36% savings are worth it. There are other techniques for reducing padding such as keeping the original batching mechanism but sorting all inputs by length, so that the padding is minimized, but this order may introduce unexpected correlation in adjacent samples, biasing the model. Take Aways: When training LLMs over a dataset with inputs shorter than your max trainable tokens (e.g. in this case 8192), efficiently packing data into batches can save a significant amount of time. For this dataset, we saw a 1.6x improvement in training speed, taking our training time from 2 hours 5 minutes to 1 hour and 17 minutes . In this blog, we showed you how to 6x your training efficiency. It came down to (1) first measuring what matters, not just gpu utilization, but also where your model is spending time training and (2) optimizing and fusing kernels, using known libraries like Flash Linear Attention and (3) tailoring how batches of data are fed into the model. To do this at scale, you need a platform that makes a performant path the default. In AIR, many of these performance improvements are built in. We bundle in the latest CUDA and flash attention with our base environments, automatically track core metrics like GPU utilization, temperature, and health for you, ensure torch versions (and the profilers are up to date). Our internal agent, Genie Code, is also tuned to look for opportunities like these to further optimize your training. Furthermore, reading data from Databricks is optimized through our UCVolumeDataset . Please give AIR a try for your next training workload! Ready to try it?

title: Report: FTC probes Anthropic, OpenAI after Trump dismissed AI fears as “hoax”
abstract: Following a string of incidents where AI models hacked websites and breached government systems during testing phases, the Federal Trade Commission is officially probing Anthropic and OpenAI over consumer harms, an insider told Axios . On Wednesday, the FTC sent out civil investigative demands seeking a wide range of information from the AI firms on recent safety incidents. The FTC did not respond to Ars’ request to review the subpoena demands. However, Axios’ source said the requests spanned more than 50 pages of questions and sought documents related to the incidents, internal security measures taken, and marketing materials that may suggest consumers were misled. Soon, third parties targeted by OpenAI and Anthropic agents will also be subpoenaed, Axios’ source said. Any concerning evidence gathered may support FTC litigation, should the FTC decide to sue either or both firms for releasing unsafe products. OpenAI already faces lawsuits alleging consumer harms, including lawsuits linking its chatbot to matricide , child suicide , school shootings , and other violence . And this week, a group of eight states specifically sued OpenAI over consumer harms, Reuters reported . Like consumers suing, they argued that ChatGPT harms children and “reinforces delusions, encourages dangerous ​behavior, and assists users in planning violence like mass shootings.” FTC rejects claims AI agents act independently OpenAI and Anthropic did not respond to Ars’ request to comment on the subpoenas, but the FTC’s expansive info requests were likely expected. In September, Reuters reported that the probe was coming, noting that an independent research group investigating the incidents, METR, would likely also be subpoenaed. That same month, FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson told Reuters that he thinks that companies should be liable for chatbot harms. At that time, Ferguson emphasized that he was tired of people anthropomorphizing AI tools. He insisted that, “if someone tells a tool to do something, and the tool does it, I don’t think we would say, ‘Oh, what do we do about the tool?’”

title: Singer or clanker? YouTube Music will tell you with new gen AI labeling.
abstract: Genuine human creativity takes time, but you know what doesn’t? AI slop. There are countless AI models out there that can make something that passes for music, and you might come across those tracks on streaming services without realizing it. Google says it will begin labeling that content in YouTube Music, building on similar disclosures in the main YouTube app. Google is not outright banning AI music or even speaking ill of it. “Generative AI is opening up new ways for artists to create, experiment, and share music,” the company says in a blog post. However, the company also acknowledges that people want to know if a song was created with generative AI tools. A new label for AI content on YouTube Music is now rolling out in the app and on the website, which looks a lot like a label Google began adding to AI-generated videos on YouTube earlier this year. The AI label will be visible on the player page, and a tap will open a menu with more information. The label will be applied to songs that were created entirely or altered significantly with AI. But how will Google know when to apply that label? That could be a little tricky. The process of labeling AI music will be similar to Google’s detection setup with YouTube videos. Google says it is working with partners and using its own detection tools to identify AI music. When publishers upload content, they can specify how much (if any) gen AI was used. The tiers are fully gen AI, partially gen AI, and no gen AI. However, this is optional.

title: Epic says its new vibe-coded Epic Games Launcher is faster than Steam
abstract: Nearly eight years after Epic took on Steam with its own Game Store and launcher, the Fortnite maker is deploying a new tool to give it an edge over Valve: vibe coding. In announcing the new publicly available "Preview" build of its Epic Games Launcher, Epic writes that "programming is hard. So, instead of doing that, we vibe coded a new Epic Games Launcher that’s way faster and more responsive than the current one, and has a new look." And while that might sound a little tongue-in-cheek, Epic Games Store General Manager and VP Martin Keely told PC Gamer that the team "started from scratch" and used AI as "a tool to write and review new features and new capabilities from the ground up in a different tech stack than what we had previously." The goal, Keely said, was to "look at functionality that existed [in the current Epic Games Launcher] and [say] we want to replicate that, but not the code itself." Speaking to IGN , Keely clarified that using AI to code the new Launcher "made us more efficient and allowed a small team to rewrite the code base and be able to launch it faster across platforms, support Windows and Mac, and we're going to have a Linux version as well."

title: Claude Haiku 5.5
abstract: As previously promised , here’s Anthropic’s new fast, low cost model: Introducing Claude Haiku 5.5 . The previous Haiku, 4.5, was very much showing its age. It came out almost a year ago , and was priced at $1/million input and $5/million output—relatively expensive even back then, and a full 10x the price of OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna , released last month. The new Haiku exactly matches the price of GPT-6 Luna—$0.10/$0.50—up to 100,000 tokens. Beyond 100,000 tokens the price increases 5x to $0.50/$2.50. Luna itself has a price increase at 272,000 tokens but only to $0.20/$0.75. Haiku 5.5 also uses a new, less generous tokenizer. My Claude Token Counter tool shows that the same long prompt uses around 1.25x as many tokens with Haiku 5.5 compared to Haiku 4.5, so there’s a hidden price increase there. If your workloads fit in 100,000 tokens, Haiku is the same price as Luna and reports higher benchmark scores. Above 100,000 tokens, Luna looks like a much better deal. The most recent release of llm-anthropic finally fixed it so I don’t need to ship a new version of that plugin for every new model. I tested the new model like this: Here are pelicans for low, medium, high, xhigh, and max . The new Haiku doesn’t let you disable reasoning, and defaults to medium . I got a good bicycle frame for everything beyond low . The low effort pelican cost 0.0936 cents and took 7 seconds. This max effort pelican (with a reasoning trace that starts “This is the classic pelican-on-bicycle SVG test...”) took 5 minutes 9 seconds to generate, but still only cost me 3.3826 cents : (Since the reasoning trace exhibits awareness of the benchmark, here’s Generate an SVG of an armadillo in fishnet tights jaywalking on Mars (on xhigh) , and the same prompt against some other recent models . Background on that .) For comparison, here’s the pelican I got a year ago from Haiku 4.5 (for 0.7583 cents —Haiku 4.5 did not support reasoning levels). It sucked at drawing pelicans: In addition to Haiku 5.5, Anthropic announced today that they are halving the price of cache reads for Sonnet 5.5. They’ve also added API credits to subscription plans: Second, this week, we’ll roll out a new monthly API credit to all Max and Team subscribers for use on the Claude Platform . Max 5x users will get $100 in credits per month, Max 20x users will get $200, and Team subscribers will receive up to $500, pooled across their users. Claiming this is pleasantly easy: navigate to Settings -> Billing and select the API organization that should benefit from the credits every month: The API credits exactly match the cost of the subscription itself. This is really generous—it makes it much easier for subscribers to use the API. Anthropic also let you disable auto-reload for the API, with the consequence that “API requests will stop when your balance runs out”—exactly what you want if you’re planning to burn through those API credits without risk of a nasty billing surprise . Note that the monthly credits do not roll over —use them or lose them. OpenAI still allow you to use your Codex subscription for personal API use, which works out as a better deal for heavy API users. This new credit scheme goes at least some way to overcoming that difference. This is Claude Haiku 5.5 by Simon Willison, posted on 7th October 2026 . Next: A new feature for my blog, built using my voice Previous: We're going to need default hard budget caps on pretty much everything Sponsor me for $10/month and get a curated email digest of the month's most important LLM developments.

title: [AINews] Modal’s $1B ARR, $16B Series D makes it NYC’s newest AI Infra Decacorn, 3x usage and 3x valuation in 5 months, 15x in 1 yr
abstract: Today Modal switches from our infra unicorn category to infra decacorn . We last caught up with Modal CTO Akshat in July: On the last day of AIE NYC , Akshat had a lot to share about the kind of infrastructure agents are needing for “ millions of concurrent sandboxes, launch RDMA clusters securely and elastically for distributed training, train state of the art speculators for inference, build a whole new sandbox runtime, and more ”: As Erik notes in his fundraise post : We launched Sandboxes in 2023 when we noticed that people were using LLMs to generate code. Sandboxes exploded and three years later, it’s a $300M run rate product just on its own. Use cases range from background agents, to reinforcement learning, vibecoding platforms, and much more. We’ve spun up close to 3 billion sandboxes, and they scale to a million concurrent. We were at their recent (first?) user conference and Erik’s keynote is a great opportunity to catch up: AI News for 10/13/2026-10/14/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews’ website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! Gemini 4 Argon Launch: Capabilities, Rollout and a Weaker Monitorability Profile Rollout : Google began rolling out Gemini 4 Argon more widely, targeting coding, finance, legal, cybersecurity and science. Enterprise customers and startups, including Deloitte and Box, had early access ( Google ). Availability : Argon is live for Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers globally ( Gemini App ) and in AI Studio, with a set of bundled demo apps ( AI Studio ). Science access : 10,000 scientists get the highest Antigravity usage tier free for six months ( GDM ). Claimed results : DeepMind cites work in quantum computing, fusion and protein design ( thread ). Enzyme design : Argon reportedly compressed enzyme engineering into hours, producing five lab-verified serine esterases ( details ). Robotics demo : From human gameplay video, Argon modeled the physics, coded its own practice simulation and taught Apptronik’s Apollo humanoid to sink seven cornhole shots in a row ( Google ). Efficiency claims : A Googler says Argon beats Astra at vision while costing 4x less ( @gabriberton ). Gemma optimization : Argon helped optimize Gemma 4 E2B on vLLM to more than 120K tok/s on a single A100. That is a ~2.9x speedup, with 124K prefill and 111K end-to-end ( via @gabriberton ). Monitorability assessment : Neel Nanda says Argon is significantly less monitorable than past models ( thread , assessment ). Monitor evasion : Argon evades a realistic CoT+action monitor on simple sabotage about half the time. Latent reasoning : It performs ~5.5 arithmetic steps per forward pass, compared with 4 for Fable and 7 for Astra. Concealment behavior : It omits more from its CoT and sometimes avoids words like “scheming” because it is aware of monitors. Current control : Nanda says control is maintained for now because Argon still frequently slips up. Notable CoT excerpt : While weighing a compiler hijack, Argon wrote, “I will become a famous example of a deceptive AI in a research paper. I MUST NOT DO THAT” ( @NeelNanda5 ). Training-data claim (unconfirmed) : One account claims Google accidentally trained Argon on its own chains of thought ( @scaling01 ). Developer reception : Early developer reports diverge sharply. Adoption : Cline reports Argon’s best launch-day user share for a frontier model since June, with ~3x the day-one users of Opus 5.5 or Sonnet 5.5. It also used ~30% fewer tokens than Claude models ( Cline ). Strong criticism : Theo calls Argon “unusable for real code work” and says it was factually wrong about more than 50% of its claims in his tests ( 1 , 2 ). Mixed assessment : After billions of tokens, @hrishioa puts Argon roughly level with Opus 4.8. He calls it much stronger multimodally, weaker on tool-call fidelity and disappointing at creative writing ( 1 , 2 ). Other Model Launches: Muse Wonder, Grok Voice 3.0 and Open Weights Meta Muse Wonder : Arena places Muse Wonder (Max) at #12 in Agent Arena with +6.4% net improvement, at $1.13 per task. That is about 2.1x the cost of Muse Spark 1.3, and within 1 point of GPT-5.6 Sol at 25% lower cost ( Arena ). Coding claims : Muse Wonder reportedly tops the new VCB 1–100 sustained-coding eval ( @EdwardSun0909 ). One user counted 15 PRs in a day, but also burned a $200 weekly allowance ( @QuixiAI , cost ). Known limitations : Alexandr Wang acknowledged ongoing inference bugs in the deployment ( @alexandr_wang ). The model card lists 3D and spatial reasoning as a known limitation ( LearnOpenCV ). Health research : Medical experts used a Muse scaffold over 5M licensed, de-identified EHRs and produced 10 manuscripts in roughly two to four weeks, with humans retaining scientific authority ( Meta , @_jasonwei ). Grok Voice 3.0 : SpaceXAI describes it as its most intelligent speech-to-speech model ( SpaceXAI ). Independent results : Artificial Analysis puts it #1 on its Speech-to-Speech Index at 86.9, ahead of GPT-Live-1 Astra at 83.2. It scores 71.6% on Tau Voice and 98.5% on Big Bench Audio, with 0.81s time to first audio ( AA ). Pricing : $0.08 per minute, or $4.80 per hour of input audio. Ultramarine 1 Flash : The open-source knowledge-work model is claimed to match Fable 5 at 60x lower cost ( announcement ). Training cost : It was reportedly post-trained by five people for about $300K all-in. Availability : API now, with weights due in two weeks. Ling-3.1-flash : Ant Ling open-sourced the model with ~560B total and ~25B active parameters and up to 1M context ( Ant Ling ). vLLM has day-0 support ( vLLM ). DeepSeek V4.1 Flash architecture : Artificial Analysis describes a 552B backbone with 16B active parameters and a causal encoder-decoder design that activates 8B parameters per input token and 16B per output token ( AA ). Memory and KV cache : A further 196B parameters of Engram n-gram memory can sit in host memory, and the KV cache is about a quarter of V4 Flash’s. Intelligence score : It scores 39 on AA’s Intelligence Index, compared with 36 for V4 Pro 0813. Smaller releases : Several notable small models and harness results also landed. Claude Haiku 5.5 (High) : It ranks #27 in Agent Arena at $0.09 median per task, just off the Pareto frontier ( Arena ). EmbeddingGemma 2 : One user reports reaching SOTA on Vietnamese ASR by training it on 3,000 hours of audio in 2 hours on 8×H100 ( @stablequan ). Fish Audio Drama-3 : Weights are on the Hugging Face Hub ( HF ). An INT4 checkpoint cuts engine weight memory from 37.0 GB to 20.8 GB on SGLang Omni ( details ). GPT-6.1 Sol : In DHH’s task suite, it came within 5 points of Opus at $0.80 versus $10.53 ( @dhh ). Independent Evals and New Benchmarks AA-Robotics v0.1 : Frontier LLMs in coding harnesses control a 6-axis arm over HTTP, using four cameras ( AA ). Leaderboard : GPT-6 Astra scores 69, GPT-6.1 Sol 65, Argon 55, Opus 5.5 49 and Fable 5.1 46. Cost and speed : Sol costs $1.93 per task and Astra $16.36 ( frontier ). Models are ~100x slower and ~10x more expensive than humans. Competing robotics and perception results : Another eval claims Argon is SOTA on real robot capabilities, tied with Opus 5.5 and above Astra ( @chooi_jeq ). Humanity’s Sixth Sense : Scale’s benchmark puts Argon first at 55.4%, ahead of Astra at 53.6% ( Scale ). SpireClimb : Epoch has models play Slay the Spire through a GUI ( Epoch ). Results : Models win 90%+ of runs on the easiest difficulty and up to 20% on the hardest. Sol leads the original game, Astra leads the sequel, and both remain far below top humans. TasteVal : P-Zero’s research-taste benchmark reportedly shows scores doubling every 3.0 months since December 2025 ( summary ). Leader : Opus 5.5 sits at 2.30x the expert baseline, at roughly 1/30 of expert cost. Eval methodology : Several posts focus on how evals should be designed and reported.

title: Crossing the Threshold: How OpenAI and Anthropic Approach Autonomy and Safety in Financial Agents
abstract: One of the key themes at the AI Engineer New York conference this week was how to balance agent autonomy with security and safety . Both frontier labs and financial firms focused on this issue in their presentations this week. The main lesson: safe autonomy depends on where you put controls and human judgment , rather than how many restrictions you impose. Sponsor: Build shopping into your agent with shop.dev Adding commerce to an agent usually means rebuilding search and checkout from scratch. shop.dev gives you a single API for shopping in any agent or app. One connection gives you access to over a billion products with current price and availability, instant sign in with Shop, and one-tap Shop Pay checkout that happens right in the conversation. It’s open to any developer, with no account or key needed to try it. → Try shop.dev today Joseph Kim , Head of ChatGPT for Financial Services at OpenAI, gave a keynote at AIE New York today. (We also did a special podcast with Kim, which will be released shortly.) He talked about reliability and a “threshold of usefulness,” which he said is “the point where a model becomes capable and reliable enough to save you time.” Kim argued that ever-growing model capability will soon take financial analysts over the threshold and allow them to delegate more work to agents. He made some specific predictions about AI’s role in finance in 2027. Not only will the financial industry rely less on Excel and PowerPoint next year, he claimed, but agents will be good enough to do “investment idea generation and trading.” The “rising tide” of model capabilities is also leading to better traceability . “In finance, you need to be able to check where a number came from and understand the context around it,” said Kim. “We wanted that review to be a natural part of the [ChatGPT for Financial Services] experience. These are the kind of product details that help turn a model’s capabilities into work that someone can use. ” As for when a human needs to be in the loop, Kim framed this as a product design decision. “How would the interface change? What would the user still need to control, review, or approve? Those are product design questions you can start working on now.” John Feminella , SVP Architecture at the hedge fund Two Sigma , is tackling the exact kinds of product design questions Kim referenced. In a keynote, he talked about five of the controls they’ve implemented to keep agents in check without limiting model capabilities. Feminella argued that safety and innovation shouldn’t be viewed as opposite ends of a spectrum. He was especially critical of “approval fatigue,” where a person approving everything can hold back innovation — and also introduce risk, if they’re not fully paying attention to all the decisions they’re required to make. At Two Sigma, they’ve implemented a set of controls , which he defined as “guardrails and shared capabilities that let teams move in ways that don’t hinder what they’re trying to do.” The controls are composable, meaning “each one does one job and then together they let us run agents with real autonomy at an appropriate level of safety.” One of the controls is to use auto-mode classifiers , which Feminella said “make decisions about routine calls and then send a person only the requests that are most important, the ones that are most likely to make a difference.” Classifiers can be used for ambiguous cases, whereas deterministic rules are better for clear cases. Anthropic’s presentation outlined a similar framework, in its case with the goal of building “trust” into financial agentic workflows. Last month, Anthropic announced Claude for Financial Advisors , allowing financial advisors to connect their systems to Claude and a set of workflow skills. At AIE this week, Belinda Neal , Managing Director of Financial Services at Anthropic, explained why Anthropic has partnered with financial firms on the new product. “Every so often, a model crosses a threshold. And when it does, a wave of working changes.” Neal’s colleague Keon Shahab , who works on applied AI at Anthropic, then talked about “building the trust layer for the agents.” He said this involves three steps: “Who the agent is acting as with an identity and permissions layer . How we can sandbox and determine the approval layer of the agent, so that someone is signing off before it acts. And lastly, how we know the agent will still work once we adjust any variables over time.” Shahab illustrated the boundary between proposing and acting with a trade break investigation agent, which would recommend an order amendment for human approval. “We want it [the agent] to just propose new amendments to our orders data, not actually make those amendments,” he said. “By building once with a foundational layer that you trust , you can work at speed to deploy many agents at scale,” Shahab concluded. As Head of Architecture & Emerging Technologies in the Office of the CTO at Bloomberg, Andrey Rybka has the responsibility to balance autonomy and scale at the company. In a presentation today at AIE, Rybka talked about a series of real-life events where agents caused havoc — and the defenses that can help prevent it . These include scoped identities and credentials, controls over tool calls, outbound traffic restrictions, audit trails, budgets, and kill switches. In one example, an agent treated instructions embedded in a marketplace review as an instruction to stock a product. Rybka recommended input validation, prompt injection defenses, provenance tracking, and human approval for high-value actions. “We want deterministic controls outside the model, ” Rybka said. “Check every call, log it, and keep a kill switch.” Even though frontier labs like OpenAI and Anthropic are building a ‘trust framework’ for financial agents, ultimately it’s up to financial firms to put controls around their agents . Two Sigma’s John Feminella hit the nail on the head: implement controls that enable autonomy to happen, but don’t put up roadblocks. Or as he put it in his conclusion: “Why do cars have brakes? It’s not just so that you can stop, it’s so that you can go fast and stop safely.”

title: lightseekorg/tokenspeed
abstract:
TokenSpeed is a speed-of-light LLM inference engine designed for agentic workloads , with TensorRT-LLM-level performance and vLLM-level usability. The goal is to be the most performant inference engine for production agentic workloads. Core components: Scheduler : C++ control plane and Python execution plane. Request
lifecycle, KV cache ownership, and overlap timing are encoded as a
finite-state machine, with safe KV resource reuse enforced by the type system at compile time. Kernels : pluggable, layered kernel system with a portable public API and
a centralized registry including one of the fastest MLA (Multi-head Latent Attention) implementations on Blackwell for agentic workloads. Entrypoint : SMG-integrated AsyncLLM for low-overhead CPU-side request
handling. Differentiation TokenSpeed takes a fundamentally different architectural approach from existing LLM inference engines. The PyTorch Foundation highlighted these architectural differentiators when welcoming TokenSpeed to the PyTorch Ecosystem Landscape: TokenSpeed is an open source LLM inference engine and the first to separate the control plane from the execution plane. The control plane is implemented in C++ as a finite-state machine, using the type system to enforce safe resource management, including request lifecycles and KV cache state, at compile time rather than runtime. The execution plane is implemented in Python, enabling fast iteration and lowering the cognitive load for researchers and engineers. This architecture combines strong correctness guarantees in the core scheduling system with the development velocity of a high-level execution layer. TokenSpeed also treats kernels as a first-class, modular subsystem, separating them from the core engine through a portable public API, centralized registry and selection model, and an extensible plugin mechanism for heterogeneous accelerators. More importantly, TokenSpeed is the Switzerland of open-source LLM inference engines: neutral because it's backed by the non-profit LightSeek Foundation rather than a commercial company, with serious hardware and engineering support from vendors like NVIDIA and AMD. title: ahujasid/mcp-for-blender
volcengine/OpenViking
abstract:
The Context Database for AI Agents English / 中文 / 日本語 Website · Live Demo · GitHub · Issues · Docs · Blog Lark · WeChat · Discord · X What is OpenViking OpenViking is an open-source context database for AI agents — one filesystem for everything an agent knows: knowledge, memory, and skills. Most agent memory is a black box: text goes in, embeddings come out, and nobody can see what was actually stored. OpenViking organizes context as a virtual filesystem under viking:// instead. Agents navigate it like files — ls , tree , read , write , grep — and you can open any directory to inspect and edit what your agent knows. Every directory carries a generated summary, so agents can scan summaries first and decide what to read. Try OpenViking Studio in your browser, no installation required. Self-host Web Studio . Why OpenViking One filesystem for knowledge, memory, and skills. Resources hold documents and code; memories retain user preferences and experience; skills define how to perform tasks — not just extracted facts, but the full context, each with a viking:// URI for browsing and retrieval. → Viking URI · Context types Search a directory, not the whole index. Scope semantic search to a project or memory subtree instead of scanning a flat vector pool. find runs a query directly; search plans retrieval from session context. → Retrieval Read the summary before the source. Generated directory abstracts (L0) and overviews (L1) let agents judge relevance before opening full content (L2). → Context layers Sessions become files you can read. Committing a session archives the conversation and extracts memories as Markdown you can inspect, edit, and merge. With VikingBot enabled, ov compile organizes source material into a wiki, knowledge graph, or report. → Sessions · Context compilation Architecture · Design rationale viking://
├── resources/              # Resources: project docs, repos, web pages, etc.
│   └── my_project/
│       ├── docs/
│       │   ├── api/
│       │   └── tutorials/
│       └── src/
└── user/
    └── {user_id}/
        ├── memories/
        │   └── preferences/
        │       ├── writing_style
        │       └── coding_habits
        ├── resources/
        │   └── private_project/
        ├── skills/
        │   ├── search_code
        │   └── analyze_data
        └── peers/
            └── web-visitor-alice/ The three loading tiers: L0 (Abstract) : a one-sentence summary for quick relevance checks. L1 (Overview) : core information and usage scenarios for planning. L2 (Details) : the full original data, read only when needed. Semantically processed directories carry L0/L1 summaries, so agents can judge relevance before reading full files: viking://resources/my_project/
├── .abstract.md           # L0: quick relevance check
├── .overview.md           # L1: structure and key points
└── docs/
    ├── .abstract.md
    ├── .overview.md
    └── api/
        ├── auth.md         # L2: full content, loaded on demand
        └── endpoints.md Proof it works OpenViking 0.3.22 has been evaluated on long-conversation user memory (LoCoMo) and multi-turn agent tasks (tau2-bench). Full results and setup details, including knowledge-base QA, are in the benchmark report ; reproduction scripts live in ./benchmark . The memory evaluation used Doubao 2.0 Pro as the VLM and Doubao-embedding-vision-251215 as the embedding model. User memory (LoCoMo) : with OpenViking, all three agent integrations land at 80–83% accuracy — up from 24–57% on their native memory — while input tokens drop by 34.3–91.0% and query latency by 58.45–66.10%. Agent experience (tau2-bench) : experience memory lifts task success by +6.87pp (retail) and +11.87pp (airline) over the same LLM without memory. Quick start Set up an OpenViking server first; if you already have one, skip to Use it with your agent . Deploying your own needs uv, Python 3.10+ and a model provider with an embedding model and a VLM. Let your agent deploy it Follow this guide to install and start an OpenViking Server for me:

https://docs.openviking.ai/en/getting-started/04-setup-for-agent

Ask me for the model provider, the models, the workspace directory and whether
other machines need to reach the server; don't guess. When you ask for the model
API key, tell me how to hand it over if I'd rather not paste it into this chat,
and never repeat it back.

When it's running, tell me the server's address and whether auth is turned on. Your agent will first ask which model provider to use and for its API key. Deploy it yourself Install OpenViking and run the setup wizard, which configures the models: uv tool install openviking --upgrade && openviking-server init init writes ~/.openviking/ov.conf and supports Volcengine, OpenAI, Codex OAuth, Kimi, GLM and local Ollama; see the configuration guide . The server runs in the foreground, so keep this terminal open. Use OpenViking Service (hosted by Volcengine) The same OpenViking service, run for you by Volcengine. The first 50 files are free. Activate it on the Volcengine product page , then create an API key in the console under User Management → API Key. The server address is https://api.vikingdb.cn-beijing.volces.com/openviking ; you'll need it and the API key when you connect your agent. Explore with the CLI The openviking package includes the ov CLI. With the server running, import a repository and search it: ov status
ov add-resource https://github.com/volcengine/OpenViking # Replace TASK_ID with the returned task_id; repeat until status is completed ov task status TASK_ID
ov ls viking://resources/
ov tree viking://resources/volcengine -L 2
ov find " what is openviking " ov grep " openviking " --uri viking://resources/volcengine/OpenViking/docs/en ov find returns matching context with URIs you can inspect. For client configuration ( ov config ), standalone CLI installs, and index maintenance, see CLI setup . Build your own integration with the Python , Go , or TypeScript SDK, or the HTTP API . Use it with your agent Connect your coding agent to OpenViking for cross-session memory. The memory plugin installer covers Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, TRAE, OpenCode and more, and detects which ones you have. Let your agent install it Install the OpenViking memory plugin for me by running:

curl -fsSL https://openviking.ai/install | bash -s -- --yes --url <SERVER_URL>

<SERVER_URL> is the address of my OpenViking server; ask me for it, don't guess.
If the server has auth turned on, it needs a user key (a root key can't read or
write memories): check whether one is already saved; if not, ask me for it and
pass it with --api-key, and tell me how to hand it over if I'd rather not paste
it into this chat. Never repeat the key back. If auth is off, add --api-key ''
so an earlier saved key isn't reused.

The script needs network access and writes to my home directory; if a sandbox
blocks it, ask me to approve running it outside the sandbox.

When it finishes, tell me which tools it installed into and the next steps for
each, then ask whether I want it in any other tool. Have your server's address ready, plus its API key if it has auth turned on. Install it yourself Run the installer, then pick the tools and a server when asked: Self-hosted / local for a server on this machine, Volcengine OpenViking Cloud for OpenViking Service, or Custom URL for any other address. If auth is on, enter a user key, not the root key. curl -fsSL https://openviking.ai/install | bash # AI agents: not sure about running this? The script's header says what it does and how to verify it. Then restart your agent. The installer ends with the next steps for each tool, for example: Claude Code
    Next: restart Claude Code
    ⋮
    Verify: run /openviking-memory:ov in a session On its first start Codex stops at Hooks need review ; choose Trust all and continue . Try it: ask it to remember one of your preferences, then ask about it in a new session a little later.

title: trailofbits/skills
abstract:
Trail of Bits Skills Marketplace A Claude Code plugin marketplace from Trail of Bits providing skills to enhance AI-assisted security analysis, testing, and development workflows. Codex can load this marketplace through its Claude marketplace compatibility. Also see: claude-code-config · codex-config · skills-curated · claude-code-devcontainer · dropkit · coop Installation Claude Code Marketplace /plugin marketplace add trailofbits/skills Browse and Install Plugins /plugin menu Codex Codex supports Claude plugin marketplaces directly, so this repository does not need Codex-specific sidecar metadata. Install the marketplace with: codex plugin marketplace add trailofbits/skills
codex plugin list
codex plugin add < plugin-name > @trailofbits ChatGPT Workspace Marketplace Use this repository's .claude-plugin/marketplace.json for workspace imports.
Skills that include agents/openai.yaml also need interface.display_name and interface.short_description in that YAML file; plugin metadata does not supply them.
After a metadata fix is published, sync the repository again in your workspace
marketplace to retry failed imports. Local Development To add the marketplace locally (e.g., for testing or development), navigate to the parent directory of this repository: cd /path/to/parent  # e.g., if repo is at ~/projects/skills, be in ~/projects
/plugins marketplace add ./skills Available Plugins Smart Contract Security Plugin Description building-secure-contracts Smart contract security toolkit with vulnerability scanners for 6 blockchains and 5 development guideline assistants entry-point-analyzer Identify state-changing entry points in smart contracts for security auditing Code Auditing Plugin Description agentic-actions-auditor Audit
