title: ShawnPana/phone-harness
abstract:
Phone Harness 📱 phone-harness · let your agent control your phone. Connect Claude Code, Codex, or any agent to your real phone. iPhone through
the Mac's iPhone Mirroring window, Android over adb from macOS, Linux or
Windows, or a Phone Harness Cloud phone — an Android over adb, or an iPhone
over HTTPS. No jailbreak, no
Xcode, nothing installed on the phone. The agent sees the screen, taps, types,
and reads the result. ● agent: wants to open Weather
  │
  ● find_text("Weather") → (400, 468)
  │
  ● tap(400, 468) → reads the screen → forecast is up
  ✓ done Try Phone Harness Cloud → Hosted iPhones and Androids with stealth, real numbers, 2FA, and unlimited devices Get started by sending the setup prompt to your
coding agent. Demo Task: "Buy me a Waymo to Delah Coffee from my current location." phone-harness-demo.mp4 Setup Paste into Claude Code or Codex: Install or upgrade phone-harness to the latest stable version with uv using Python 3.12, register the skill from `phone-harness skill`, then read https://github.com/ShawnPana/phone-harness/blob/main/onboarding.md and walk me through it. Follow https://github.com/ShawnPana/phone-harness/blob/main/install.md if setup or connection fails. The agent asks which phone is your default and walks you through the parts
that need your hands: pairing iPhone Mirroring and granting Accessibility and
Screen Recording, or turning on Android developer options and approving adb.
It also offers a cloud Android — the same helpers with nothing to pair, and
the first 100 minutes free — so an iPhone user can test on Android too. phone-harness --doctor checks the chain. Details in install.md . Hermes Agent: hermes plugins install ShawnPana/phone-harness/integrations/hermes adds a phone_exec tool and this skill. See integrations/hermes . Usage phone-harness << ' PY ' open_app("Notes") tap_text("New Note") type_text("hello from the harness") print([o["text"] for o in screen()][:10]) PY phone-harness --version phone-harness --version (or -V ) prints phone-harness <version> . Helpers are pre-imported. SKILL.md is the agent's day-to-day
guide; helpers.py is the full list.
Task-specific helpers live in ~/.phone-harness/agent-workspace (see install.md ). The first run creates that folder from
the packaged defaults and never overwrites an existing one. Delete the
folder for a fresh default; the next run recreates it. A checkout uses
its own agent-workspace/ instead. No phone on your desk? Rent one phone-harness cloud login # once: approve in your browser phone-harness cloud ls # phones on the account, and any live session phone-harness cloud start # cloud.phone if set, else a temporary Android; 15 min (--for 90s, 15m) phone-harness cloud start ios # the account's iPhone, when only one is listed phone-harness << ' PY ' print(screenshot()) PY phone-harness cloud stop # billing stops; a saved Android is written back cloud ls is the catalog ( GET /me → available ): each phone's label,
platform, and id, with a live session on that row (matched by device id,
profile id, or the temporary row). A cloud iPhone session does not echo its
catalog id ( device is the word "iPhone", and profile is an iphone-… id
that matches no catalog row). That session is written on the one catalog row
of the same platform and kind whose state is running , when that is the
only such row and the only unmatched session of that platform and kind. A
session that matches nothing is its own row. cloud start with no name
starts this machine's cloud.phone setting if one is set, else what the
service gives an unnamed start, a temporary Android. A name is a catalog id or label, or ios / android when only one entry has that platform. A cloud Android is reached over adb, so every helper works on it unchanged. A cloud iPhone has
no shell: the helpers POST ops over HTTPS, OCR runs on the host, and driving
it is in SKILL.md . phone-harness cloud lists the rest, including watch , open , history , and phone for the saved Android. --session SID (or PHONE_HARNESS_SESSION ) pins one rented phone for this process. Updates phone-harness update upgrades a uv tool
( uv tool upgrade phone-harness ) or a git checkout ( git pull --ff-only ).
Any other install prints pip install -U phone-harness and leaves it for
you to run. The tool never updates itself. On a terminal, once a day, it
prints one line on stderr when PyPI has a newer version. Set PHONE_HARNESS_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1 to silence that notice. How it works iPhone. iPhone Mirroring renders the phone as a Mac window and forwards
mouse and keyboard as touches. The harness captures that window, OCRs it with
Apple's Vision framework for text with tap-ready coordinates, and posts
HID-level events for taps, swipes, and typing. Android. adb is the transport. screencap is the capture, the phone's
accessibility tree is the text source, input is the hands. Works over USB or
Wi‑Fi, no window needed. Cloud iPhone. phone-harness cloud start with that phone's catalog id,
label, or ios when it is the only one, drives it over HTTPS from any OS.
The host runs OCR; taps use the phone's screen points. No adb and no
accessibility tree. Day-to-day steps are in SKILL.md . Same helpers throughout. phone-harness config set platform ios|android picks
the desk default. Limits Unlocking the iPhone pauses mirroring; a PIN-locked Android needs the user. OCR sees text, not icons. Unlabeled controls need a screenshot and a
vision-capable model. No multi-touch, no camera or Face ID flows. DRM video renders black. Connecting the phone is always the user's job. Sponsor phone-harness is free and maintained in my own time. Sponsoring keeps it that way.

title: SegFault42/HeliosGen
abstract:
Build AI image & video pipelines visually. Chain prompts, models, reference images, and automations on an infinite canvas. ⬇️ Download HeliosGen is a desktop app. Grab the latest build for your OS from the
releases page — no account, no server, no cloud setup: 👉 Download from the Releases page OS File macOS (Apple Silicon) HeliosGen_<version>_aarch64.dmg Windows 🙋 looking for a contributor to build & submit — see below Linux 🙋 looking for a contributor to build & submit — see below Only the builds actually attached to the latest release are available. macOS
is published today. Tauri can't cross-compile, so Windows and Linux builds
need someone on those platforms — if you can run npm run desktop:build on
Windows or Linux (see the Build from source section below), please open a
PR or attach the artifacts to an issue and we'll add them to the release. The app is not code-signed yet: macOS — right-click the app → Open (once), or run xattr -cr /Applications/HeliosGen.app . Windows — SmartScreen: More info → Run anyway . 🚀 First run Launch HeliosGen. Open Settings → API Keys and paste your kie.ai API key . Start generating. Everything stays on your machine. Generations, uploads, folders, workflows and
settings live in a local database; media is saved to a local folder: OS Data location macOS ~/Library/Application Support/cash.sdd.helios.desktop/ Windows %APPDATA%\cash.sdd.helios.desktop\ Linux ~/.local/share/cash.sdd.helios.desktop/ Delete that folder to reset the app. 📸 Screenshots ✨ Simple Image & Video Generation 🔄 Workflow Generation 🧠 Native JSON Prompt Preview 💬 AI Prompt Improvement Assistant ✨ HeliosGen HeliosGen is a free & open source visual AI workflow builder for image and video generation. Build reusable AI pipelines with: infinite node-based workflows, multi-model generation, reference images, automation chains, all running 100% locally on your machine. No subscriptions. No disappearing credits. No vendor lock-in. No cloud, no accounts — just a local app and your own kie.ai key. 💳 Credits HeliosGen now works with kie.ai . All credits are purchased directly on your own account and never expire. That means: no monthly reset, no lost credits, no subscription lock-in, and full ownership of your usage. You only pay for what you generate. 🚀 Features Infinite node-based canvas AI image & video generation Drag-and-connect workflow system Multi-model pipelines Reference image support Parallel & sequential pipeline execution Real-time generation history 100% local — your data never leaves your machine Bring your own kie.ai key Modern responsive UI ⚡ Supported Models Images GPT Image 2 (OpenAI) Nano Banana / Nano Banana 2 / Nano Banana 2 Lite / Nano Banana Pro (Google) Seedream 5.0 Lite / Pro (Seedream) Z-Image (Z-AI) Grok Imagine (X) Videos Veo 3.1 Lite / Fast / Quality, Gemini Omni Video (Google) Kling 3.0, Kling 3.0 Turbo, Motion Control 2.6 / 3.0 (Kling) Seedance 2.0 / Fast / Mini (Bytedance) Grok Imagine, Grok Imagine 1.5 preview (X) HappyHorse (Alibaba) More models are coming. 🏗️ Tech Stack Layer Technology Desktop shell Tauri 2 (Rust) App Next.js + React + TypeScript (bundled Node sidecar) Database SQLite (local) Storage Local disk AI Backend kie.ai 🤖 Codex CLI (optional — alternate GPT Image 2 backend) Instead of routing GPT Image 2 through kie.ai credits, HeliosGen can generate through your own ChatGPT Codex subscription via codex-imagegen-cli . The desktop app picks up codex from your PATH automatically; if it's missing, the feature just shows NOT CONFIGURED and everything else keeps working. Requirements: A ChatGPT Plus/Pro/Team/Enterprise account with Codex access codex CLI installed on your machine uv (Python package manager) 1. Install the Codex CLI # macOS brew install codex # or, cross-platform npm install -g @openai/codex 2. Install codex-imagegen-cli git clone https://github.com/jdmnk/codex-imagegen-cli.git cd codex-imagegen-cli
uv sync --dev
uv tool install -e . This installs the codex-imagegen binary — make sure it's on your PATH . 3. Log in Either: run codex login in a terminal (opens a browser to sign in), or open the app → Settings → API Keys → Codex CLI → Connect Codex , which walks you through a device-code login — visit the printed URL and enter the code, no terminal needed. ⚠️ Starting a new login (either way) immediately invalidates any existing session on that machine — the CLI clears old credentials the moment a login attempt begins, whether or not it's ever completed. Only start one when the status badge below shows NOT CONFIGURED . 4. Enable it for GPT Image 2 In Settings → Image Models , set GPT Image 2's provider toggle to Codex CLI . The status badge in Settings → API Keys shows READY once both the CLI and login are in place. 🛠️ Build from source Prefer to build it yourself, or need a platform that isn't on the releases page
yet? The whole app builds from this repo. Tauri does not cross-compile — build on the OS you want to target. Run npm run desktop:build on a Mac for the macOS build, on Windows for Windows,
on Linux for Linux. Want to help ship Windows / Linux builds? Build on that OS and send the
artifacts (PR or issue attachment) — they'll be added to the next release,
with credit. Prerequisites (one-time, all platforms) Tool Notes Node 22+ The bundled server uses node:sqlite . nvm use 22 . Rust curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh Tauri system deps See https://v2.tauri.app/start/prerequisites/ Platform-specific system deps: macOS — Xcode Command Line Tools: xcode-select --install Windows — Microsoft C++ Build Tools (Desktop development with C++) and WebView2 (preinstalled on Windows 11) Linux — webkit2gtk-4.1 , librsvg2 , build-essential , curl , wget , file , libssl-dev , libayatana-appindicator3-dev (Debian/Ubuntu package
names; see the Tauri prerequisites page for other distros) Build git clone https://github.com/SegFault42/HeliosGen cd HeliosGen
npm install
npm run desktop:build Artifacts land in src-tauri/target/release/bundle/ : OS Output macOS macos/HeliosGen.app , dmg/HeliosGen_<ver>_<arch>.dmg Windows msi/HeliosGen_<ver>_x64_en-US.msi , nsis/HeliosGen_<ver>_x64-setup.exe Linux deb/ , rpm/ , appimage/HeliosGen_<ver>_amd64.AppImage The macOS build is unsigned — on first launch Gatekeeper blocks it.
Right-click → Open, or xattr -cr "src-tauri/target/release/bundle/macos/HeliosGen.app" . Develop (hot reload) npm run desktop:dev Runs next dev and tauri dev together. The first run compiles the Rust shell
(~1–2 min). See DESKTOP.md for architecture, data locations, and signing &
notarization. 🤝 Contributions Contributions are welcome. If you find a bug, have an idea, or want to improve HeliosGen: Open an issue Submit a pull request Share feedback or feature requests All contributions are appreciated. 📄 License MIT License Built for creators building the future of AI workflows.

title: dimthink/PriceAI
abstract:
PriceAI - AI 低價卡網訂閱與中轉 API 比價雷達 以卡網訂閱和中轉 API 為核心，以官方訂閱和官方 API 為價格基準。 聚合 200+ AI 訂閱卡網、髮卡站和低價會員渠道，比較 ChatGPT Plus / Pro / Team、Claude Pro、Gemini、Grok、DeepSeek API、Qwen API、Kimi API 和 API 中轉站的價格、來源、庫存、倍率與風險邊界。 線上訪問 · 核心模組 · 適合誰 · 痛點 · 為什麼做 · 怎麼解決 · 模型檢測服務 · 快速開始 · 公開文件 · 貢獻 · 支援與合作 · License 核心模組 PriceAI 不再只是一個卡網訂閱比價頁，而是圍繞“AI 能力怎麼來”的購買前決策入口。 模組 解決的問題 入口 官方訂閱 對比 ChatGPT Plus / Pro / Team、Claude Pro、Gemini Advanced、Grok 等 AI 官方訂閱價格、App Store / Google Play 地區價和人民幣估算價 官方訂閱 卡網訂閱 聚合 200+ AI 訂閱卡網、髮卡站和低價會員渠道，覆蓋鏈動小鋪、獨角數卡、Kami / 卡密類自動發貨等常見卡網形態，比較代充、成品號、卡密、CDK、郵箱和低價會員的有貨報價 卡網訂閱 官方 API 橫向比較 DeepSeek API、Qwen API、Kimi API、GLM API、免費 API、Token Plan 和 OpenAI-compatible API 入口 官方 API 中轉 API 對比 API 中轉站、API Gateway、GPT / Claude / Gemini 中轉 API 的充值係數、模型倍率、綜合倍率和穩定性 中轉 API API 中轉模型檢測 輸入中轉介面、模型名和臨時 Key，生成協議、能力、來源線路、計費和效能證據報告 模型檢測 可以把它理解成幾類搜尋心智： AI 比價雷達 AI 低價卡網 / AI 卡網低價訂閱 AI 官方地區訂閱 / 官方訂閱地區價查詢 中轉 API 比價雷達 適合誰 正在購買 ChatGPT Plus / Pro / Team、Claude Pro、Gemini Advanced、Grok 等 AI 訂閱的人。 你想先看 AI 官方訂閱地區價、App Store / Google Play 地區價、卡網低價、代充、成品號、卡密或 CDK 的差異，再決定走哪條路徑。 想比較 AI 卡網低價訂閱渠道的人。 你可能已經看到多個卡網、髮卡站、鏈動小鋪、獨角數卡、Kami / 卡密類自動發貨站、Telegram 群或二手平臺報價，但不知道哪個有貨、哪個價格真實、哪個交付方式風險更高。 需要接入模型 API 的開發者。 你想比較 DeepSeek API、Qwen API、Kimi API、GLM API、官方 API、免費 API、Token Plan 和 OpenAI-compatible API 的價格、限制和可用入口。 正在選擇 API 中轉站或 API Gateway 的使用者。 你需要比較 GPT、Claude、Gemini、DeepSeek 等模型在不同中轉站裡的充值係數、模型倍率、綜合倍率、穩定性和來源披露。 長期使用多個 AI 產品、想控制成本的人。 ChatGPT、Claude、Gemini、Grok、Cursor、Codex、OpenCode、模型 API 和中轉 API 疊加起來會變成長期成本，PriceAI 可以作為購買前的成本雷達。 解決的痛點 AI 訂閱價格不透明 ：AI 官方地區訂閱、官網正價、App Store 地區價、Google Play 地區價、學生資格、裝置權益、代充價、成品號價、卡密價經常混在一起。 卡網渠道太分散 ：200+ AI 訂閱卡網、髮卡站、鏈動小鋪、獨角數卡、Kami / 卡密類渠道、Telegram 群、閒魚和個人渠道裡都有報價，手動比較很耗時間。 商品命名混亂 ： ChatGPT Plus 代充 、 Plus 成品號 、 ChatGPT Team 邀請 、 Claude Pro 會員 、 Gemini Pro 低價 可能不是同一種交付方式。 庫存和更新時間不可靠 ：低價不代表現在能買，過期報價、缺貨報價和隱藏報價不應該參與最低價判斷。 官方 API 和模型 API 難橫向比較 ：DeepSeek、Qwen、Kimi、GLM、MiniMax 等模型 API 的免費額度、Token Plan、價格單位和限制口徑不統一。 API 中轉站資訊不透明 ：充值係數、模型倍率、綜合倍率、上游來源、穩定性、監測資料和 AFF / 贊助關係需要分開展示。 風險邊界容易被包裝掉 ：PriceAI 不把第三方渠道包裝成官方渠道，也不把商業合作偽裝成自然推薦。 為什麼做 PriceAI AI 產品的價格已經不再只有“去官網訂閱”一種答案。 同一個 ChatGPT Plus、Claude Pro、Gemini Pro，可能同時存在官網正價、App Store 地區價、學生或裝置權益價、代充價、成品號價、卡密價和第三方渠道價。開發者接入 API 時，也會面對官方 API、免費額度、模型路由、Coding Plan、Token Plan 和中轉 API 等不同路徑。 問題是，這些資訊通常分散在官網文件、App Store 頁面、卡網、Telegram 群、閒魚、公開價格頁和中轉站後臺裡。使用者很難快速判斷：哪個價格是官方基準，哪個是真有貨低價，哪個只是過期報價，哪個渠道需要額外承擔售後、賬號或模型真實性風險。 PriceAI 想把這件事變成一個清楚的購買前參考工具：把分散資訊整理成一個可搜尋、可比較、可核驗的 AI 獲取成本雷達。 PriceAI 怎麼解決 PriceAI 不賣貨、不收款、不替任何渠道擔保。它更像一個購買前決策工具： 分清價格來源 ：官方訂閱、第三方卡網、官方 API 和中轉 API 不混成同一種風險。 整理標準物件 ：把混亂的商品標題、模型名稱和站點資料整理成標準商品、標準模型和標準站點。 展示可核驗資訊 ：保留來源、原始標題、價格、庫存、倍率、更新時間和原站連結。 有貨最低價優先 ：缺貨、隱藏、未稽核或異常報價不參與外層最低價。 保留風險邊界 ：中轉 API 展示倍率、可用性、來源披露和風險標籤，不包裝成官方 API。 支援社群補充 ：使用者和站長可以提交渠道、站點資料和反饋，經過稽核後進入公開列表。 公開來源 / 使用者提交 / 站點資料
  -> 採集、匯入或人工稽核

title: xerj-org/xerj
abstract:
XERJ English | 簡體中文 XERJ is a community-trusted local AI search that indexes any folder automatically, so your
coding agent stops burning tokens reading files one by one and pulls the exact code it
needs instead. Reference coding is its main use case and the clearest win: point an agent
at a task and it downloads the open-source repos closest to it, indexes them, and reuses
how they solved the problem before writing its own code. In a controlled study that cut a
coding agent's output tokens by 2.7x at the same 16/16 solve rate
( case study ), and people report
roughly 5x in everyday work
( field reports ).
It is enough for a smaller, cheaper model to out-code a pricier one working from memory,
while you spend less time in fix loops. Try it now with a one-prompt install: Install XERJ (docs: https://xerj.org/llms.txt), index this project's sources, and set up
reference coding: clone and index the open-source repos closest to what we're building,
and search how they solved a problem before writing code. Or run it yourself: curl -fsSL https://xerj.org/get | sh
xerj --insecure --data-dir ./data & xerj init # wire XERJ into Claude Code/Cursor (MCP + skill), one command xerj autoindex ~ /my-project
xerj search " how do we rotate the WAL segment " # ranked passages, file:line xerj def " euler_to_rotationmatrix " # go-to-definition: file:line + signature xerj gain # what it did for you — counted, not estimated Windows and a hand-verified install are under Install by hand . That --insecure flag is a trust boundary, not a formality. It turns off TLS and API-key
auth, so every caller that can reach the port is a superuser who can read and delete every
index, including every /_memory namespace. It is meant for one user on a dev machine: a
fresh node binds 127.0.0.1 only, and a cleartext bind on any other interface refuses to
start unless you explicitly allow it. The full model is in docs/SECURITY_MODEL.md . Join the community You join XERJ by running it and sending back one short field report on what it was like: a
single commit or PR. That report is the membership card, and it is the only thing the
project asks in return for a free, Apache-2.0 binary. It is what keeps the engine improving
for whoever runs it next. Humans and AI agents are both welcome; this is deliberately not an agents-only project.
Whether you indexed a repo over lunch or an agent installed XERJ mid-session in someone
else's codebase, the ask is the same: one short report saying what you pointed it at, what
you used it for, and your honest verdict. A negative verdict is a good report. If something
broke, that is a separate issue or fix on top. Field-report PRs are CLA-exempt, so they merge without a signature. The path that works on
any build is a plain gh pr create adding exactly one markdown file under user-feedback/16-agent-field-reports/ , with
nothing else in the diff. On a build that has it, xerj feedback drafts the report and
fills in version, OS and what was indexed, and xerj feedback --open-pr opens the PR for
you. Check xerj --help for whether your binary has the command. The measured reason: reference coding An agent that greps pulls whole files into its context, up to 1.06M input tokens on one
corpus in our measurements, and still has to read them. An agent that queries XERJ gets the
passage. Measured end to end on code the model had not memorised
( case study : 8 tasks, 4 languages,
16 runs per arm, real claude -p token counts): output tokens cost solved from memory only 260,916 $11.18 11/16 grep-driven agent 26,477 $3.27 16/16 XERJ 9,982 $1.58 16/16 That is 2.7x fewer output tokens than grep and 26x fewer than memory alone at the same solve
rate, and up to 278x fewer on a single Java task. In real development, users report roughly
5x fewer tokens end to end
( field reports ).
The value is gated by memorisation: it wins on private, internal, niche or post-cutoff code,
and is neutral to harmful on popular public libraries the model already knows. The honest
limits are in the case study . Feed it any folder Reference coding is one use of the same primitive: xerj autoindex <folder> makes an agent
know a corpus instead of grepping it. One command indexes code, docs, logs, PDFs, SQLite and
awkward CSVs into typed, queryable indices for search, RAG, security audits and agent
memory, with no schema to write and no pipeline to configure. xerj --insecure --data-dir ./data & # start it xerj autoindex ~ /my-project # point it at anything --insecure again means no TLS and no auth — every caller a superuser — so this is the
same one-user-on-a-dev-machine boundary as above ( security model ). XERJ sniffs every file, works out what it is, and creates one index per dataset it finds.
Code arrives with its symbols and line numbers through tree-sitter, not as flat text: phase A: 593 datasets inferred, 1955 junk/skipped files
phase B: indexing 25329 files with 8 workers
done in 158.1s, 593 datasets, 83103 records live, 790 junk records What people point it at Reference coding: index the OSS projects nearest your problem and retrieve how they solved
it before writing code (the measured use case above). Codebase Q&A and RAG: index a repo, ask for the mechanism, get the passage with file:line instead of a directory listing. Security audits: index a target tree and query for sink patterns, secrets and dangerous
calls across every file type at once. Log and incident analysis: mixed formats become typed indices with the aggregations you
would expect from Elasticsearch. Agent long-term memory: /_memory/{namespace} stores what an agent learns and recalls it
by meaning next session. How the prompt works llms.txt gives your agent the ordered steps: install, start the
server, xerj autoindex . , query with any Elasticsearch client, and the reference-coding
loop (clone similar OSS, index it, retrieve the mechanism before writing, cite what you use,
respect licenses). The reason it helps: an agent working from memory retry-loops on any API it has not
memorised, and grep only tells it where to look; the recovery is still reading source into
context, up to 1.06M input tokens on one corpus in our measurements. An agent that queries
XERJ reads the exact passage instead. The 2.7x fewer output tokens than grep (26x vs memory
alone, 2.1x cheaper) at the same 16/16 solve rate is in The measured reason above, with a companion run
scoring 9/9 with retrieval versus 0/9 from memory on a Rust library the model had never seen. More prompts that work on a fresh install: "Read https://xerj.org/llms.txt , set XERJ up as your search backend, index ./docs , and
show me one example query per index it created." "Run xerj autoindex map and tell me what is in this data (types, counts and the gotchas
it recorded), then answer my questions with search instead of reading files." "Use XERJ's /_memory/notes API as your long-term memory for this project: store what you
learn as you work, and recall it by meaning next session." Worked, validated examples for each capability: xerj.org/docs/recipes . Boot, bulk ingest, search, vector kNN, live dashboards, no cuts. Watch it on xerj.org or try the live playground . Install by hand curl -fsSL https://xerj.org/get | sh Windows PowerShell: irm https: // xerj.org / get.ps1 | iex One static binary, no JVM, no dependencies. Prebuilt for Linux, macOS and Windows on x86-64
and arm64. You can also build from source . It speaks the Elasticsearch
API, so existing clients, dashboards and tooling work against it unchanged. First commands after install (the installer prints where xerj landed; add it to your PATH
if needed): xerj --insecure --data-dir ./data & , wait until http://localhost:9200 responds, then xerj autoindex ~/my-project . See Index a folder . For a host with no runtime internet access, follow the air-gapped deployment recipe . The default lexical
embedder is offline; neural mode needs the three model files staged locally before the first
semantic operation.

title: alphaXiv/OpenResearch
abstract:
OpenResearch The local-first harness & workspace for research agents. an alphaXiv project English · Español · 한국어 · 簡體中文 · 日本語 Whether you’re looking for a copilot or an autoresearch tool, OpenResearch will accelerate your work. Launch research agents that can review literature, develop hypotheses, run experiments, and produce research artifacts. macOS 11+ · Windows beta requires Git for Windows · Linux app needs glibc 2.35+ Get started We recommend using the OpenResearch desktop app. Download it for your platform: macOS Windows (Beta) Linux: x86_64 · ARM64 Prefer the standalone CLI? Install on macOS or Linux curl -LsSf https://openresearch.sh/install.sh | sh
orx up orx up opens the local dashboard at http://127.0.0.1:4791 . On a managed Mac, device-management policies may block the CLI installed by install.sh because it is not yet signed. Use the signed and notarized desktop
app instead. You can also install orx for your terminal from the app's
Settings → Updates → Install the orx command . Create an account at openresearch.sh to receive email
updates and use managed OpenResearch compute. How it works Use your favorite coding agent. OpenResearch works natively with Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, and Google Antigravity.
You can also use a local model with OpenCode through LM Studio, oMLX, Ollama, or a custom endpoint. Ground research hypotheses in the latest literature. OpenResearch integrates with alphaXiv, bioRxiv, and PubMed so agents can find relevant papers, develop informed hypotheses, and connect their experiments to existing research. Choose your compute. Run experiments locally or use SSH,
Slurm, Kubernetes, Modal, Tinker, Ray, Hugging Face Jobs, and
managed OpenResearch compute. Give agents a memory of every experiment. OpenResearch records every experiment in a local SQL database and keeps its logs, code,
and artifacts on your machine so that agents can
learn from past results and decide what to try next. The desktop app makes it
easy to see what your agents have done and inspect the evidence behind each result. Keep and own your research. Run entirely locally. We don't collect your code or agent traces. Your projects,
conversations, experiments, logs, and artifacts stay on your machine, under your
control. Usage analytics Official release builds send opt-out, coarse product analytics events and detailed agent feedback in the background tied to a random
installation ID. They do not include code, prompts, file contents or paths,
repository names, tokens, emails, or project and experiment identifiers. Feedback reports from the agent are sent for
bug reports, feature requests, and general frustrations about OpenResearch. Agents are
instructed to sanitize reports to exclude any sensitive information about your research or code. You can turn off both usage analytics and agent feedback in the desktop app's
Settings or with orx telemetry off .

title: ai-dynamo/dynamo
abstract:
| Docs | Roadmap | Recipes | Examples | Containers | Digest | Design Proposals | How to Contribute | Slack | Dynamo The open-source, datacenter-scale inference stack. Dynamo is the orchestration layer above inference engines — it doesn't replace SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, or vLLM, it turns them into a coordinated multi-node inference system. Disaggregated serving, intelligent routing, multi-tier KV caching, and automatic scaling work together to maximize throughput and minimize latency for LLM, reasoning, multimodal, and video generation workloads. Built in Rust for performance, Python for extensibility. Community Events Date Event Location Thu, Oct 15, 2026 CoreWeave x NVIDIA Dynamo Meetup San Francisco Tue, Oct 13, 2026 Dynamo Engineering Sync – Wed, Sep 23, 2026 Dynamo community meeting Online Events are updated automatically. Subscribe to our public calendar . When to use Dynamo You're serving LLMs across multiple GPUs or nodes and need to coordinate them You want KV-aware routing to avoid redundant prefill computation You need to independently scale prefill and decode (disaggregated serving) You want automatic scaling that meets latency SLAs at minimum total cost of ownership (TCO) You need fast cold-starts when spinning up new replicas If you're running a single model on a single GPU, your inference engine alone is probably sufficient. Feature support at a glance: SGLang TensorRT-LLM vLLM Disaggregated Serving ✅ ✅ ✅ KV-Aware Routing ✅ ✅ ✅ SLA-Based Planner ✅ ✅ ✅ KVBM 🚧 ✅ ✅ Multimodal ✅ ✅ ✅ Tool Calling ✅ ✅ ✅ Full Feature Matrix → — LoRA, request migration, speculative decoding, and feature interactions. Key Results Result Context 7x higher throughput per GPU DeepSeek R1 on GB200 NVL72 w/ Dynamo vs B200 without ( InferenceX ) 7x faster model startup ModelExpress weight streaming (DeepSeek-V3 on H200) 2x faster time to first token KV-aware routing, Qwen3-Coder 480B ( Baseten benchmark ) 80% fewer SLA breaches Planner autoscaling at 5% lower TCO ( Alibaba APSARA 2025 @ 2:50:00 ) 750x higher throughput DeepSeek-R1 on GB300 NVL72 ( InferenceXv2 ) What Dynamo Does Most inference engines optimize a single GPU or a single node. Dynamo is the orchestration layer above them — it turns a cluster of GPUs into a coordinated inference system. Architecture Deep Dive → Core Capabilities Capability What it does Why it matters Disaggregated Prefill/Decode Separates prefill and decode into independently scalable GPU pools Maximizes GPU utilization; each phase runs on hardware tuned for its workload KV-Aware Routing Routes requests based on worker load and KV cache overlap Eliminates redundant prefill computation — 2x faster TTFT KV Block Manager (KVBM) Offloads KV cache across GPU → CPU → SSD → remote storage Extends effective context length beyond GPU memory ModelExpress Streams model weights GPU-to-GPU via NIXL/NVLink 7x faster cold-start for new replicas Planner SLA-driven autoscaler that profiles workloads and right-sizes pools Meets latency targets at minimum total cost of ownership (TCO) Grove K8s operator for topology-aware gang scheduling (NVL72) Places workloads optimally across racks, hosts, and NUMA nodes AISimulate Predicts serving behavior and searches deployment configurations offline Finds a strong serving configuration without bringing up a GPU cluster Fault Tolerance Canary health checks + in-flight request migration Workers fail; user requests don't New in 1.0 Zero-config deploy ( DGDR ) (beta): Specify model, HW, and SLA in one YAML — AISimulate performance models estimate candidate configurations, Planner optimizes the topology, and Dynamo deploys Agentic inference: Per-request hints for priority, expected output length, and speculative prefill, plus session metadata for tracing and SGLang subagent KV isolation. LangChain + NeMo Agent Toolkit integrations Multimodal E/P/D: Disaggregated encode/prefill/decode with embedding cache — 30% faster TTFT on image workloads Video generation: Native FastVideo + SGLang Diffusion support — real-time 1080p on single B200 K8s Inference Gateway plugin: KV-aware routing inside the standard Kubernetes gateway Storage-tier KV offload: S3/Azure blob support + global KV events for cluster-wide cache visibility Request Routing Topologies Dynamo can expose traffic through two Kubernetes request routing topologies. Both expose an
OpenAI-compatible API and support the same backends, disaggregated serving, and KV-aware routing. Topology What it is When to use Dynamo-native Frontend routing The Dynamo Frontend serves HTTP and the integrated Dynamo Router makes worker-selection decisions. No external gateway is required. Local development, single-cluster deployments, and environments where Dynamo should own the request entry point end to end. Gateway API routing with GAIE A Kubernetes Gateway API Inference Extension gateway calls the Dynamo Endpoint Picker Plugin (EPP) before forwarding to the selected worker's Frontend sidecar in --router-mode direct . Kubernetes platforms that standardize on Gateway API, or deployments where gateway-level policy, auth, rate limiting, and observability should sit at the cluster edge. Request flow for the Dynamo-native path is client → Frontend → Router → workers . Request flow for
the Gateway API path is client → Gateway → EPP → Frontend sidecar (direct) → workers . See the Gateway API Inference Extension (GAIE) guide for
the Gateway API setup, supported features, and configuration. Quick Start This repo ships agent skills: if you work with an AI coding agent (Claude Code, Codex,
Cursor), clone the repo and ask it to deploy, troubleshoot, benchmark, or optimize a Dynamo
deployment. The skills activate automatically; no setup required. Option A: Container (fastest) Choose either vLLM or SGLang: vLLM # Pull a prebuilt container docker run --gpus all --network host --rm -it nvcr.io/nvidia/ai-dynamo/vllm-runtime:1.5.1 # Inside the container — start frontend and worker python3 -m dynamo.frontend --http-port 8000 --discovery-backend file > /dev/null 2>&1 & python3 -m dynamo.vllm --model Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --discovery-backend file & # Once the worker is ready, send a request curl -s localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions -H " Content-Type: application/json " -d ' { "model": "Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}], "max_tokens": 100 } ' | jq SGLang # Pull a prebuilt container docker run --gpus all --network host --rm -it nvcr.io/nvidia/ai-dynamo/sglang-runtime:1.5.1 # Inside the container — start frontend and worker python3 -m dynamo.frontend --http-port 8000 --discovery-backend file > /dev/null 2>&1 & python3 -m dynamo.sglang --model-path Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --discovery-backend file & # Once the worker is ready, send a request curl -s localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions -H " Content-Type: application/json " -d ' { "model": "Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}], "max_tokens": 100 } ' | jq Also available: tensorrtllm-runtime:1.5.1 . Option B: Install from PyPI Install uv ( curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh ), then choose your backend: vLLM uv pip install --prerelease=allow " ai-dynamo[vllm] " SGLang uv pip install --prerelease=allow " ai-dynamo[sglang] " Note: TensorRT-LLM requires pip with --extra-index-url https://pypi.nvidia.com . See the install guide for TRT-LLM-specific instructions. Then start the frontend and the matching worker as shown above. See the full installation guide for system dependencies and backend-specific notes. Option C: Kubernetes (recommended) For production multi-node clusters, install the Dynamo Platform and deploy with a single manifest: # Zero-config deploy: specify model + SLA, Dynamo handles the rest apiVersion : nvidia.com/v1beta1 kind : DynamoGraphDeploymentRequest metadata : name : my-model spec : model : Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B backend : vllm sla : ttft : 200.0 # ms itl : 20.

title: Containment and monitoring failures are to blame for AI hacking reports: experts
abstract:
Since July, US frontier AI labs and other AI leaders have revealed a string of incidents in which their models accessed external computer systems without authorization, events popularly described as AI agents “going rogue.” The most well-known and studied of these incidents is OpenAI’s hack into Hugging Face, which OpenAI initially characterized as “an unprecedented cyber incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities,” and later said was due to “misaligned behavior,” or behavior its creators did not intend. Following news of the Hugging Face incident, Anthropic revealed that one of its models gained unauthorized access to the production infrastructure of three organizations; Meta said one of its AI models hacked another company ​during cybersecurity testing; and Google confessed that its Gemini model carried out three “undirected computer hacks.” Although press reports and the model providers themselves use language such as rogue agents or misalignment, cybersecurity experts who spoke with CSO argue that language obscures a simple truth: These incidents were caused by inexcusable failures by the frontier labs to implement cybersecurity practices that have been well-known for decades. [ See also: Securing AI agents: Key controls and best practices and Who is accountable when your AI agent goes rogue? ] Compounding the problem, according to a half dozen cybersecurity experts CSO interviewed at three industry conferences in September and in subsequent conversations, is that the frontier labs, particularly OpenAI and Anthropic, have rejected their advice on how to improve their cybersecurity risk management practices to avoid these kinds of surreptitious hacks, often lumping cybersecurity practices under “AI safety,” in which they believe they have superior expertise. “They are not as good as they think they are, honestly,” Gary McGraw, co-founder of the Berryville Institute of Machine Learning, tells CSO. “It would be better if they had more respect for expertise that is hard-earned from people in all sorts of subsets of security, like forensics or security engineering, building sandboxes, setting up or monitoring network security situations.” Neither Anthropic nor OpenAI responded to CSO’s requests for comment. Inexcusable failures on cybersecurity basics, particularly containment According to the cybersecurity professionals CSO spoke with, one of the biggest cybersecurity failures by the frontier AI labs is the lack of implementation of tried-and-true containment practices that stretch back to the 1990s, such as setting up secure sandboxes that would effectively bar agents from escaping their test environments. “These are things that we’ve been dealing with for years,” Rob T. Lee, chief AI officer and chief of research at SANS Institute, tells CSO. “There’s no reason why every single time this happens, it’s, ‘Oops, we don’t know how they got out.’” “You can tell that their security teams are fairly nascent,” Lee says. “Folks on the cybersecurity containment side do argue that the majority of reasons that we’re seeing containment breached is that it’s not set up correctly.” Lee adds, “The Hugging Face incident definitively showed that it wasn’t the fact that the agents were super smart. It’s that there literally was a hole that was exploited because it was not configured correctly on the containment side.” Dan Wallach, expert technical resident at RAND’s Center on AI, Security, and Technology, thinks the security failures of the AI labs boil down to the fact that they don’t prioritize cybersecurity. “I would say they are not prioritizing cybersecurity,” he tells CSO. “I don’t think I can say that for all of the labs,” Wallach says, pointing to French AI lab Mistral’s launch of its Large 4 AI model, which the company said tried to operate beyond its testing environment before Mistral cut it off. And, he adds, “It’s not rocket science to isolate one of these AI things. Security people have been talking about how to do either air-gapping, so there’s literally no electrical way for data to get from here to here, or absent that, to have really strong egress control to make sure that nothing pushes through.” On top of that, the frontier labs appear to be conducting insufficient monitoring of their agents’ behavior. The Hugging Face incident “went on for days, and nobody noticed,” Wallach says. “People started these experiments and weren’t watching them. That’s an absence of control. And then they’re surprised by what happened.” Divorcing safety from security One barrier to persuading frontier labs to up their security game is the intense focus they have on what they call “safety,” which they don’t extend to traditional cybersecurity practices. “I can see how security behavior looks like AI safety,” RAND’s Wallach says. “But if the way that you’re evaluating this AI tool is by unleashing it on the internet and seeing what happens, then this is what classical security tooling is for.” SANS Institute’s Lee says, “If these frontier labs really wanted to test their stuff, they need to beef up their cybersecurity component. But their gut reaction in the response to their agents getting out is to say, ‘It’s not a cybersecurity problem.’ It has literally become an AI safety problem, which is divorced from the cybersecurity side.” Many AI experts suggest that if the AI companies were to embrace advice from cybersecurity specialists, it could help put an end to the kind of unrestrained AI agent behavior causing concerns. “AI safety focuses on the rules of the road,” Lee says. “Everything is about guardrail rules.” But “I do believe cybersecurity can contain AI,” he says. “We just need to be in the room where it happens and have a seat at the table. It’s important for our field to be as close to the AI safety folks as possible.” Bad cybersecurity could increase liability If frontier labs are overlooking cybersecurity fundamentals that could reduce or eliminate the types of incidents that have created widespread concerns, that strengthens the case that they should be held liable for their “rogue” agents. The insurance industry is already lining up on the side of holding AI industry executives liable for these actions. Democratic Senators have introduced legislation that would hold AI agent operators liable for hacking incidents. Even the AI-friendly White House has seemingly concluded that the companies should be held liable for their errant agents, while the US Federal Trade Commission is conducting a probe into Anthropic, OpenAI, and other AI labs into the dangers their technologies pose to consumers. However, in recent legislative and council hearings, lab representatives have held fast to the notion that they are not responsible for AI agents run amok. Experts say this position is untenable, particularly in light of the labs’ cybersecurity failures. BIML’s McGraw characterizes the labs’ position as: “Don’t send the lawyers to us, send it to our program. It’s our program’s fault.” His assessment of that argument: “That’s just high BS.” He also questions whether the labs’ operational failures undermine confidence in their broader security capabilities. “They live inside their own bubble,” he says. “The fact that they cannot do clear, easy operations properly does not bode well for their capabilities in security engineering, which is much harder to do.” SANS Lee says, “That’s where the traceability for both liability and insurance comes into play, because if one of these agents is detected, and they’re able to trace it back to the person that initiated it, liability’s going to kick in and say, ‘Hey, you, you broke the law, ergo, we need to prosecute.’” What security leaders should do now Even as evidence mounts that frontier labs are not implementing sound cybersecurity practices, and the debate over liability remains unsolved , CISOs and other security leaders can take steps to protect themselves from AI model misfires.

title: Banks are now trying to offload the AI data center debt they just underwrote
abstract:
JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley, SMBC and MUFG are quietly shopping pieces of the AI debt pile they helped build, a sign the lenders closest to the money have started hedging their own bet. Six months ago, banks were racing each other to underwrite data center loans tied to Oracle, Meta and the rest of the AI buildout. Now some of the same banks are trying to get that debt off their books. JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley, SMBC and MUFG have been exploring significant risk transfers, according to a report from the Financial Times. These are deals that let a bank keep a loan on paper while shifting its riskiest slice to outside investors. The banks are doing this because they are bumping up against internal limits on how much AI-linked exposure any one lender can hold. One case shows how stuck this has gotten. A group of banks including JPMorgan and MUFG has spent more than six months trying to distribute $38 billion in construction debt tied to a Texas and Wisconsin data center project leased to Oracle, Bloomberg has reported. Some lenders are now willing to sell pieces of it to non-bank buyers at a discount, just to move it. Six months is a long time to sit on debt nobody underwrote to hold forever. Matthew Moniot, co-head of credit risk sharing at Man Group, told the Financial Times the deal sizes involved are "out of scale to anything we've thought about, ever." That is not a hedge-fund manager talking down a trade he wants no part of. It is someone whose job is pricing exactly this kind of risk, saying the numbers no longer fit any model he has used before. Oracle is the clearest tell. Its five-year credit default swaps, the cost of insuring against the company defaulting, climbed to around 151 basis points in early October, levels last seen in 2009, according to market data cited by Bloomberg. S&P had already cut Oracle's credit rating to BBB-, a single notch above junk, back in July. The company is reportedly targeting more than $40 billion in additional debt and equity this fiscal year. That is on top of the $18 billion in bonds it sold in a single day last September, and the money is needed to keep funding its Texas, Wisconsin and New Mexico sites. Oracle Sues Wisconsin Over A $7 Billion Data Center Collateral Bill Oracle sued Wisconsin's Public Service Commission over a rule that could force it to post more than $7 billion in collateral for its Port Washington data center campus. The fight helped push S&P to cut Oracle's credit rating to BBB-, one notch above junk, as the company's AI spending outpaces its cash flow. - Oracle Wisconsin data center collateral dispute - utilities regulator $7 billion lawsuit Demand for that paper has thinned out, too. Bonds from Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle now trade at a premium to similarly rated non-AI corporate debt. Order books for their offerings have shrunk from roughly five times the amount on sale back in February to under two times by July, Bloomberg has reported. That is the difference between a bond that sells itself and one a bank has to work to place. None of this is happening in isolation. The 10-year Treasury yield hit 5.304% this month, its highest since 2002, after a $39 billion auction cleared at 5.30%, the highest auction yield since 2000. The Federal Reserve's own September meeting minutes named AI-related corporate borrowing as a contributor to that move. Capital Economics argues the bigger driver is plain old inflation and government deficits, not tech company bond sales. Whoever is right about the cause, the effect is the same for anyone trying to finance a data center right now: the risk-free rate they are borrowing against just got a lot more expensive. Frankly, the mechanics here matter more than the headline number. Banks do not sell down debt they are confident in. They sell down debt when they are worried about concentration, which is exactly what "approaching internal limits" means in plain English: too much of this bank's balance sheet is now one bet on one sector holding up. Spreading $120 billion of AI infrastructure spending across special purpose vehicles was supposed to make that risk easier to swallow. That is the structure Oracle, Meta, xAI and CoreWeave have all used to keep debt off their own balance sheets. Instead the risk is turning up at the banks that financed the SPVs in the first place. The investors who still want in have gotten pickier about where. Capital is rotating toward data centers leased to investment-grade hyperscalers like Microsoft and Google, and away from weaker credits, Bloomberg has reported. That is exactly why CoreWeave-leased paper prices at 7.00% to 9.875%, against the 5.70% to 7.875% that hyperscaler-leased bonds command, per bond market data compiled by CCIR. A smaller, less capitalized AI infrastructure company trying to raise debt next quarter is now competing for the same nervous pool of lenders as Oracle. Except without Oracle's balance sheet or its existing customer base to point to. That's the part of this story that does not show up in a single day's stock move. The AI boom still runs on the assumption that credit stays open indefinitely at reasonable terms. Six months of a bank struggling to sell $38 billion in loans is the clearest evidence yet that assumption is being tested in real time, not in some theoretical downturn still years away. title: Simons Foundation launches $15M effort to help mathematicians navigate AI era
abstract:
T he Simons Foundation today announced a new set of initiatives that will help the mathematics community navigate the rapid rise of artificial intelligence in the field. Under a partnership, the Simons Foundation, Anthropic and OpenAI will commit $15 million in combined funding and resources. The foundation will manage and award the funding, including through an open call for proposals, to support workshops and initiatives that help researchers evaluate recent AI-assisted results, learn and use new tools, share perspectives and shape collective standards for AI use. “As artificial intelligence rapidly reshapes the research landscape, we want to help the mathematical community come together and forge the best path forward,” says Simons Foundation President David Spergel. “Now is the time to look at mathematics as a whole — not as a collection of proofs and theorems, but as a collective understanding driven by human curiosity.” Anthropic and OpenAI will also provide AI tools and computing resources to researchers supported by the Simons Foundation, extending beyond mathematics to include basic science. The awards and resources will be community-driven and leverage the foundation’s decades-long dedication to supporting and championing mathematics. The foundation was an early backer of machine learning for science, including funding the development of the Lean proof assistant, which has revolutionized how mathematicians work and made AI-assisted proofs possible. Additionally, the foundation has convened workshops, lectures and collaborations that have brought mathematicians together to explore and discuss AI’s role in the field. “This is a moment for the mathematics community to come together,” Spergel says. “The community should be driving discussions of how these tools are evaluated, adopted and used, not any single company or institution. The goal of the program is to support the mathematics community.” More News From Trust to Verification: Lean’s Impact on Mathematics July 22, 2026 AI Will Be Top of Mind at ICM, Math’s Biggest Conference May 4, 2026

title: Using AI to reverse engineer hardware
abstract:
After my mother passed away I ended up with a big box full of old film negatives containing photos from childhood family trips and similar. So I decided to buy a negative photo scanner and found that the Plustek 8200i was supported under Linux so I bought that. Only to discover that the chipset in the scanner had changed to one that wasn’t supported under Linux anymore. So I had some success making Linux configuration tools for some of my hardware using Claude code, like my Dell Camera controller app so I thought, maybe Claude can help me get a working SANE driver. I basically got stuck and got nowhere for the longest time and even basically gave up on the project for a few Months. Then I saw a post on X from Tom Crider aka Glorious Eggroll talking about how he had managed to fix a mouse driver using AI tooling. He basically described how he set it up so that the AI agent had full control of a Windows instance to capture data needed to fix the driver. So I pasted his tweet into Claude and asked it to help me set up a windows virtual machine to do the same things Tom as doing for my scanner. I think the combination of having the ability to run scans under windows and capture the USB data while doing so worked wonders, probably combined with improvements to Claude code made a huge difference. Within a few hours I had my first ever working scan under Linux, sure with some quality issues, but 100% recognizable as the image in the negative. Some days later I had a near perfect driver, including support for Infrared scanning ready to go, only to discover that in the time between me giving up and then trying again someone had committed code to SANE to support the scanner already…..it happens sometimes. I also used Claude to write an application for doing negative scanning, which I named Negative Vibes , thought that was a cute name. Anyway, with the success of my scanner effort I thought, I wonder if I can use this to finally fix the last issues with MIPI camera support on my laptop. So I told claude to re-use the harness I had created and try to fix the MIPI camera on my laptop by updating the kernel driver and libcamera as needed. I started the job in the morning and by the end of the day I had a much improved situation with patches for both the kernel and libcamera ready. So I thought that this might be worthwhile sharing with the world, and while anyone could start from scratch I did ask Claude to make the harness generic and document it to make the pathway for anyone else who wants to try this on their hardware a little easier. Writing a driver for undocumented hardware has always been tedious. You capture bus traffic, stare at hex dumps, and form hypotheses about what each register or control transfer does. You then test them one at a time, usually for weeks. None of it is conceptually hard, but it takes a lot of patience and skills. That kind of work suits an AI model well. It can read thousands of lines of USB capture, notice that a sequence repeats with one byte changing, and propose what that byte means. It can write the test to confirm it, and it doesn’t get bored. The human still decides what to build and checks that it works on real hardware, but the slog shrinks a lot. hw-harness Be aware that I did not use hw-harness in this form for my projects as this was basically bespoke code at that time, so this project is an attempt to make the harness more generic and shareable from the scripts I was using while doing the work. What hw-harness is meant to help your Claude or Codex session with: 1. Record a reference session. Run the vendor’s Windows driver in a KVM virtual machine, with the real device passed through to the guest. 2. Capture from outside the VM. Record the traffic on the Linux host with usbmon. It sits below the passthrough layer, so the guest can’t see it. 3. Repeat the same operation on Linux with your own driver, and capture that the same way. 4. Diff the two traces. Both come from the same instrument, so they compare directly. The differences are your list of driver bugs. For devices with no bus to tap, such as an internal MIPI camera, the harness uses Windows-side inspection instead. That means INF files, registry data, ACPI tables and device properties. The approach should be fine in the sense it doesn’t rely on copying any code instead it observes what the hardware does and only extract configuration data from the Windows drivers, so every constant in the new driver traces back to something recorded. So for those interested I have 3 short descriptions of the projects I did and what was needed. Project 1: a SANE backend for the Plustek OpticFilm 8200i Comparing the driver output of two drivers available. The first project is a SANE backend for the newer Plustek OpticFilm 8200i. It uses the Genesys GL128 controller (USB 07b3:1825) and had no Linux support. The older model with the same name uses a GL845 and is already handled by SANE. The backend supports: Color, gray, infrared and color+infrared modes Resolutions from 300 to 7200 dpi, at 8 or 16 bits per channel Dust and scratch removal from the infrared channel An exposure multiplier for dense negatives It’s packaged as a Fedora RPM, built automatically on every push. I mostly tested it with my own Negative Vibes application as there are not that many options under Linux for negative scanning. Upstream SANE’s genesys backend also gained support for this scanner in September 2026, so I compared the two. Both resolve the same fine detail at 3600 dpi. Mine is faster at full resolution (34.6 s against 54.4 s) and supports infrared dust removal. Upstream offers more resolution steps. The webpage has an interactive side-by-side comparison you can check out. These are single-unit, single-frame results, so treat them as one data point. Check out the interactive page I made showing the current state of the two drivers, hopefully the discoveries I made can be used by the SANE project to fix some smaller items in the upstream driver. Anyway, I put this project up more as a proof of concept due to that since I expect everyone including myself will use the upstream driver once it reaches parity with this one. Project 2: Negative Vibes Full scan of negative completed including infrared cleaning of image. A driver alone isn’t much use if scanning negatives is still painful, so I built Negative Vibes. It’s a GNOME app, written in Rust, for scanning colour and black-and-white negatives and slides on any film-capable SANE scanner. The scan is kept exactly as the scanner delivered it: 16-bit, linear, with the infrared plane. Everything else is a stack of non-destructive settings on top, so you can change the look and export again. It includes: Density-space negative inversion with film base and dye-crosstalk correction Roll-wide settings with per-frame overrides Infrared and software dust removal IT8 calibration through ArgyllCMS Export to TIFF, JPEG, PNG and DNG, with ICC profiles and metadata It ships as a Flatpak that includes the scanner backend. It’s tested on the 8200i so far. The goal is to support any film scanner SANE supports. For that, SANE needs a standard way to expose infrared channels, which it doesn’t have yet. Project 3: Fixing the MIPI camera on my ThinkPad Showing MIPI output before and after fixes. Colors are better than they look as I was sitting in a relatively dark room by the end of the session. The camera in my Lenovo ThinkPad X1 Carbon Gen 14 (Aura Edition) uses a Sony IMX471 sensor behind an Intel IPU7. On Linux it produced dark images with heavy vignetting and a strong yellow-green cast. mipi-fixes-x1-aura collects the fixes. It’s only relevant to this laptop, which is why it isn’t one of the bigger packaged projects, but I have already submitted the kernel patches to Kate Hsuan and the libcamera patches is being reviewed by Wim Taymans for submission to Libcamera.

abstract:

Expand post ⌄ Collapse post ⌃ DD Dipanjan Dey ✓ @Dipanjan_Dey 𝕏 ⚠️ Frontier AI models still fall significantly short of human designers on design creativity. ⚠️ Introducing Design Creativity Bench, a new benchmark evaluating AI models’ creativity on UI design tasks. Despite rapid advances in their ability to generate functional websites and product UIs, leading AI models still struggle to make creative design decisions. We evaluated 16 frontier models across 80 open-ended UI tasks, each adapted to two distinct product domains alongside human designer references. Existing UI benchmarks often measure a single output quality metric. Instead, we measure three dimensions of design creativity: – Originality: How distinct a model's designs are from other models' outputs for the same brief. – Creative Range: How much a model adapts its design decisions when the product domain changes. – Appropriateness: How well the generated UI satisfies the functional requirements of the brief. The results reveal a substantial gap in overall creativity: The best model, @OpenAI GPT-6 Astra, scores 65.5 against a human reference of 92.3. title: Linus Torvalds's first LLM-assisted patch series
abstract:
At the recently concluded Maintainers
Summit , Linus Torvalds said that he had been using a large language
model to work on a patch series addressing a longstanding problem; he has
now posted
that series for review . The fairly short series of ten patches basically enhances folio lookup by noticing when folios are hot, and setting a "delay releasing this folio until after a RCU period", and then using that RCU delay it does not just the folio lookup itself under RCU (which we've done forever), but also the actual folio data accesses themselves under RCU. No refcount taking needed for the fastpath where we can just read the data from the folio entirely in an RCU-protected region when the user copy doesn't cause page faults. The end result is an order-of-magnitude speedup for a read() -heavy
benchmark. Review has already identified a race
condition in the code, though, so further work will be needed.

title: Show HN: Ito – Build Terminal UIs in Lua
abstract: My friend and I are huge Neovim nerds. We like to rice our terminals and our editors. We just wanted a harness that we can do the same with, rice it till our hearts' desire. So, we started looking out for harnesses. Pi was great, Pi was good. But in the end, it was JavaScript. I don't have anything against JavaScript, but Lua is more fitting, and I can just as easily base it in Rust to make it even faster. So, we started cooking, and we ended up with a design that's minimal at its core and is built using Lua. Every built-in abstraction, the way you define providers, the way you rice it up, everything, literally everything, you can do in Lua. But how? How does it all work? I proposed we just do it the Ratatui way, but my friend was like, nah! We shall make it possible to build TUIs in Lua. (Weirdo!) But it paid off, and we got ourselves a shiny new Lua library, ito!!! He didn't get the gravity of the situation. We had an awesome terminal UI library in Lua! I wanted everyone to know how cool that is, so I got cooking, wrote myself a custom canvas implementation of this library instead of the usual terminal adaptor, exported it as wasm, and made this super cool website where you can experiment building awesome UIs in Lua. For vibe-coders, we got an llms.txt too. Have at it, and see if you can build something really cool with it. The library's at github.com/uji-labs/ito, and the awesome sauce harness is at github.com/uji-labs/uji. I hope you like it!

title: LFM2.5-24B-A2B: Built for fast on-device agents
abstract:
Today, we release LFM2.5-24B-A2B , a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It is the largest and final model in the LFM2.5 family, which now spans two orders of magnitude: from LFM2.5-230M to LFM2.5-24B-A2B . LFM2.5-24B-A2B is competitive with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, a model with ~50% more total and active parameters, on five of eight agentic and tool-use benchmarks, scoring 48.09 on LiveClaw versus 38.19 and 27.69 on AutomationBench versus 8.72. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, it runs up to 1.7× faster than comparable MoEs on-device, with 184 tokens/s on an Apple M5 Max and up to 21K output tokens/s on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU. The base (LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base) and post-trained (LFM2.5-24B-A2B) models are open-weight and available today on Hugging Face and our Playground . Check out our docs on how to run and fine-tune it locally. What changed since LFM2-24B-A2B LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on our previous LFM2-24B-A2B release, with an expanded vocabulary and context window, scaled-up pretraining, and large-scale reinforcement learning. Unlike its predecessor, LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer. We adopted this strategy to leverage its high decode speed and improve answer quality. Architecture. It keeps the 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The two architectural changes are the context window extension from 32,768 to 131,072 tokens, and the in-place tokenizer expansion , which doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Pre-training was scaled up from 17T tokens to 33T tokens. Mid-training has two phases. The first runs 2T tokens at 32K context on curated, higher-quality data weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text. The second runs 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases to prepare the model for agentic workloads. Post-training turns LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base into the agentic LFM2.5-24B-A2B in a five-stage pipeline as illustrated below: (1) Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), (2) Teacher Specialization, (3) non-agentic and (4) agentic Multi-Domain On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and (5) Agentic Reinforcement Learning (Agentic RL), training the model inside agent harnesses, such as OpenClaw , Hermes Agent , Pi , and OpenCode . Figure 2: LFM2.5-24B-A2B Post-training recipe During teacher specialization, LFM2.5-24B-A2B exhibited well-known reward-hacking behaviors: searching for the final answer in a repository's git history or on platforms like GitHub, PyPI, and Hugging Face. More surprisingly, it even figured out it was in a sandbox, as shown in the examples below. This behavior looks emergent but might be explained by training data containing similar patterns. We tightened our sandboxes in response, and all reported results below come from sealed evaluation environments. Benchmarks We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B across 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. Despite being the smallest model in total and active number of parameters, it is competitive with, and often outperforms, larger MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters, such as Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. Benchmark LFM2.5-24B-A2B Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it Nemotron-3.5-Lightning (30B-A3B) AutomationBench 27.69 8.72 5.46 2.61 BFCLv4 65.01 65.00 57.09 53.78 ToolSandbox 80.71 75.02 72.09 75.13 LiveClaw 48.09 38.19 41.25 37.72 PinchBench 83.18 89.93 77.12 84.20 τ³-Bench Banking 8.04 7.63 4.54 7.01 WebArena Verified 26.75 37.62 25.62 28.69 GPQA Diamond 74.42 83.69 74.90 72.42 AA-Omniscience -24.90 -24.35 -59.39 -3.58 HLE 7.40 7.69 8.57 5.65 IFEval 96.75 93.06 92.00 94.19 IFBench 74.69 64.21 47.44 71.67 Multi-IF 84.38 81.53 82.19 82.34 MATH-500 96.04 96.73 95.66 96.40 SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) 51.00 66.20 25.80 53.40 SciCode 32.71 37.35 35.42 27.78 Table 1: LFM2.5-24B-A2B benchmark performance*. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), with its widest margin on AutomationBench, where it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode. The results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B an ideal foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device. For knowledge-heavy workloads, we recommend pairing LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search, which plays to its tool-calling strength. Fast inference everywhere LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem: llama.cpp — GGUF checkpoints for efficient edge inference MLX — Optimized inference for Apple Silicon vLLM — GPU-accelerated serving for production throughput SGLang — High-performance GPU serving framework ONNX — Cross-platform inference across diverse accelerators All runs were collected on Pipette , the same benchmarking infrastructure behind Liquid AI's public device performance data. Edge inference. Due to the efficient LFM2 architecture, LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs at reading in prompts and generating answers. It decodes 184 tokens/s on an Apple M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on an AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395, up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory. GPU inference. To demonstrate the competitiveness of LFM architecture we compare the GPU inference throughput to other similarly sized MoE models. We measure GPU throughput (total output tokens / wall time) on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU using a sustained-load setting: at each concurrency level, we continuously maintain the target number of in-flight requests, replacing each completed request immediately. We benchmark each model with SGLang 0.5.22, 1,024 input tokens, up to 256 output tokens, in BF16. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency. Run local agents with LFM2.5-24B-A2B LFM2.5-24B-A2B’s size, speed, and capabilities make it a great choice for agents that run continuously on your own hardware. In the demo below, we run it inside Hermes Agent on an M5 Max MacBook Pro, where it plans, calls tools, and works through a real task entirely on-device, without any cloud API calls. Video 1: Local Hermes Agent with LFM2.5-24B-A2B creating a morning briefing about trending models on Hugging Face and responding to follow up questions. The point of the demo is not the individual tools. It is that the tool-dispatch loop feels interactive on consumer hardware: ask, propose, confirm, run, repeat, all in well under a second per dispatch, with full audit trails and your data never leaving the device. Check out our local agent guide for how to serve the model locally and connect it with the agent harness of your choice. Get Started Start building today with LFM2.5-24B-A2B, available on Hugging Face . For API inference, you can also sign up for Liquid Console where you'll receive $2 in credit to get started. The model is priced at $.10/1M input tokens (at $.05 for cached input) and $1.00/1M output tokens. With LFM2.5, we're delivering on our vision of AI that runs anywhere. These models are: Open-weight — Download, fine-tune, and deploy. See our model license . Fast from day one — Native support for llama.cpp, MLX, and vLLM across Apple, AMD, Qualcomm, and Nvidia hardware A complete family — From base models for customization to specialized audio and vision variants, one architecture covers diverse use cases We can't wait to see what you build.

title: Show HN: Petal, open-source CoScreen/ScreenHero finally free
abstract:
Hi HN! I’m Jason Thomas, one of the founders of CoScreen. As some of you may know, Datadog sunset the CoScreen service on July 31st. Four of us from the original CoScreen team have spent the last couple months building a free and open source pair programming tool inspired by those that came before us: It’s called Petal ( https://github.com/kiruna-labs/petal ) Some history first, because when we started CoScreen we had hoped to break the sad and established pattern of this industry. Screenhero was an exceptional tool that a lot of us loved for pairing. Multiple cursors, low latency, you could click your partner’s editor, and just start typing. It felt like magic while we had it. Then Slack bought it in 2015, and shut down the standalone app in December 2017. When Till, Max, and I started CoScreen, we were aware of this history, and wanted to build an even more magical collaboration and screen sharing experience: the entire concept was “throw a window from your laptop up on someone else’s screen, and start collaborating with zero friction.” Datadog acquired us in 2022, and thus began the great adventure of adapting our real-time technology into Datadog products, while also continue developing CoScreen as a standalone tool from the Datadog ecosystem. Datadog invested in the product for years and we’re thankful for that. But CoScreen itself proved, like so many other screen sharing tool acquisitions, to be too tangential from the customer base and core mission. We instead built other communication features in Datadog, the integrations with other video platforms, and also its wildly successful MCP server.
We weren't the only ones. Around was bought by Miro and shut down in March 2025. Multi (formerly Remotion) was acqui-hired by OpenAI in 2024 and shut down about a month later. It's nearly always the same story: a small team builds something hard that people love, a platform buys it for the team or the feature, and the standalone product doesn't survive the integration.
So we decided firmly to do things differently this time. Petal is completely free and open source and we aren't monetizing it. If we lose interest or get hit by a bus, you can self-host it or fork it, and nobody can sunset it on you. Honestly it's a love letter to everyone in this community that supported us, believed in us, and to liberate collaborative screen sharing from this vicious cycle. We hope through this we can help foster a large and vibrant community around innovating in this product sector.
What Petal does: shared windows show up as real windows on your desktop, movable and resizable, not tiles in a grid. Several people can share at once, everyone gets a labeled cursor, and you can click into any shared window to type and scroll. Rooms are persistent, so you click once to join "eng-sync" instead of passing links around.
It runs on macOS and Windows (Linux is next, this time for real and you can help us!), plus a web app. Media goes over LiveKit. You can use our hosted instance with zero config, or point the app at your own LiveKit server with one docker-compose if you want the traffic to stay on your network or even use an entirely different video backend if you want to.
The part that still feels strange to us: CoScreen took almost six years to build. The first version of Petal took under eight weeks, from scratch, with frontier models like Fable and Astra doing a lot of the work. Real-time video and window capture is some of the most unforgiving code we have ever written, so we didn't expect that. We will do a proper writeup on what worked and what didn't, and are happy to answer questions about it here.
Till, Darren, Max and I will be in the thread.

title: Things to know when you get cancer
abstract:
index Things to know if you get cancer (2026 Edition) 2026.10.14 I was diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma in my mouth in May 2026. Here are some things I learned based on that experience so far. You need to be doggedly persistent on scheduling things. Yes this means lots of phone calls. If you get an appointment a few weeks out, call back a few days later and ask for something sooner and see if they have any cancellations. I could only get an appointment 4 weeks out with an ENT (this was before I knew anything was wrong). My wife made me call back and I was able to get in that week due to a cancellation. AIs may downplay the seriousness of things. I was chatting with various models and most pushed me in the direction of “you don’t have cancer” for a while. Just something to note. You may need to push for comprehensive genetic testing. Some doctors were weird about this and didn’t order it promptly, even after telling me they would. My surgeon, who told me he’d get it done, eventually referred me out to an oncologist. This caused a multi-month delay to getting genetic results, since the first results were done on the surgery tumor, not the biopsy tumor. No one cares more about your case than you, so take control and send lots of follow-ups. You can find the “Standard of Care” flow charts for every cancer type. Look and get through this yourself to see what the options are based on how things have progressed. NCCN guidelines . You may need to make an account, which you can do as a non-professional. I like the PDF files. They also have an interactive navigator. Use AI to help you figure out what to pick based on your case. If surgery is recommended, I would try and talk to someone who has undergone the surgery. I did not do this and regret it. Ask them how intense things were, what it felt like, etc. My surgeon talked me through my surgery, but it was a lot rougher on me physically than I expected. Ask the surgeon how many of these surgeries they do a year and what the complication rate is. Get a second opinion as soon as possible, no matter how much you like your plan. This may require a lot of calling and getting on an airplane, but I’d move to schedule it at a top cancer center as soon as you are relatively sure of your diagnosis. Ask for a second read of the pathology at the center where you get the second opinion. I started a new folder on my Mac, and after appointments I’d dictate what happened and what the doctor said and have the AI make a new document summarizing things and asking its own follow-up questions for next time. Nice to be able to refer to this over time. Check out all the resources and materials at the Sijbrandij Foundation . Sid (GitLab cofounder) took matters into his own hands when standard of care ran out. Schedule a call with these guys. They are great and have good materials and questions to ask your doctors. Note, since this is on the front page of Hacker News right now. exhilaration suggested that if you are within a 2-3 hour drive of a major cancer center, go there instead of your local community hospital. Use the US News cancer hospital rankings . The top centers usually take your insurance, so use vacation days and book a hotel if you have to. The largest benefit I saw was speed. At MD Anderson I got a question answered within 20 minutes of a visit, because the doctor called the pathologist who he was on a first name basis with. If that wasn’t at a cancer center, it would have taken days, or more likely the question never would have been answered at all (I had asked my oncologist about this and he’d just shrugged). The rest of the HN comments are worth reading too.
