title: Wayland desktop for Linux with skeuomorphic design
abstract:
English | 日本語 DEsk v0.1.2 (BETA) -- v0.1, the first public release, with fixes and an installer for Fedora. See RELEASE-NOTES.md . I've created a Discord server!
You can also report bugs and submit ideas for new features here!
link : https://discord.gg/xR5f7Xs49 DEsk is D esktop E nvironment and desk in one word -- a
name that came from the Reddit community. It used to be called DeskWM:
the commands are now desk , desk-session , desk-settings and so on, and
what was set up for DeskWM (its settings, its data, DESKWM_* variables)
carries over by itself. A Wayland desktop for Linux in realistic skeuomorphism -- the kind iOS 6
had, where everything on the screen is drawn to look like the real thing.
Here the desktop is a desk. Windows are sheets of paper on a walnut desk. The dock is a drawer, your
apps are filed in binders on a bookshelf behind the desk, notifications
arrive in a post box, and the system controls are a panel built into the
back of the desk. The room is ray-traced, and one desk lamp lights all of it. Status: beta. DEsk is used day to day on its author's machines and has
been checked carefully (see docs/ARCHITECTURE.md ,
section 9), but this is its first release: expect rough edges, and expect
things to change. Your settings and data will be carried forward. Install Download the latest release from the Releases page and unpack it (or
clone this repository). Then, in its folder, run the line for your system: Debian 13 sudo sh scripts/install_debian.sh Ubuntu 24.04 / 26.04 (and Linux Mint, Pop!_OS) sudo sh scripts/install_ubuntu.sh Arch Linux (and EndeavourOS, Manjaro) sudo sh scripts/install_arch.sh Fedora 43 / 44 (and Nobara) sudo sh scripts/install_fedora.sh Then log out and choose DEsk on the login screen. It shows what it will install and asks first. --yes takes the suggested
answers; --no-apps installs DEsk without the recommended programs. The first login draws the room once: a few seconds on a GPU, longer
without one. After that it starts at once. To update, get the new release and run the same line again. Your settings
are kept. Something went wrong? See Reporting a problem . More options, building by hand and running DEsk in a window are under Build and Run . What's on the desk Nothing here is a symbol for a thing on a desk. As in the realistic
skeuomorphism of iOS 6, each is drawn to look like the real thing set down
there -- its material, the light on it, its shadow and the wear of use. Windows are paper. Each window sits on a cream sheet with real fibre,
thickness and a dog-eared corner. Hold the pointer on the corner and it
lifts to show what is printed on the back: Fold (minimize: folded
like a letter and left on the desk, under the windows as paper put down
is), Unfold / Refold (maximize and restore), and Discard (close:
crumpled into a ball and tossed).
Dragging an edge pulls more paper out from behind the sheet. The drawer is the dock. Pull the brass handle (or press Super+D ).
It holds the things you put in it: any app, or a folded window. Out of
the box it holds DEsk's standard programs (below) and a screwdriver that
opens Shell Settings. The bookshelf holds your apps ( Super+A , or the ALL APPS plate).
Each category is a ring binder whose sheets fan from a single ring.
Take a sheet and it is carried down to the desk, where the app's window
opens on it. At the end of the row stands an ALL APPS index book :
every program from A to Z, with thumb tabs and a line at the top of the
page to type into (input methods via IBus work). The post box is the notification centre ( Super+N ). Letters show the
sender and subject, and a letter taken out lies on the desk. The Control Panel ( Super+C ) is a valve-era machine built into the
back of the desk: real meters, a volume knob, network and Bluetooth
levers, a fader for the room's lamp and one for the screen's own
backlight (on a laptop, through logind; the brightness keys work too),
a key to unlock the power buttons, and the system tray as paper slips
under it (more than fit, and the wheel slides the row along). A desk calendar, a desk memo pad and a clock stand on the shelf. The
calendar has a notebook of plans and to-dos, and notes are peeled off and
stuck onto the day. The memo pad is taken down the same way and written
on (IBus works there too); its sheets turn over the wire. The clock
shows the seconds small beside the minutes, under two lamps that light
only while a camera or a microphone is in use. The front door is out in the real world. The lock screen's door has
the hour's light -- the sun worked out from your time zone's city, the
porch lamp coming on at dusk -- and, if you let it ask open-meteo.com for
that city's weather (only its latitude and longitude are sent), the
weather: rain darkening the brick and streaking past the lamp, snow
settling on what faces up, fog, lightning. And on certain days of the
year the door and the clock have something more for you -- there is no
setting for it; what it is, you will see on the day (give Shell Settings
your birthday, and that is one of them). Esc stops it. Light. The room (desk, shelf, console, post box) is ray-traced on the
GPU (GLES 3), with a CPU tracer as the fallback, and cached per screen
size. Everything drawn over it is lit by the same lamp. At login the room
starts dark and the lamp comes up as the room is made, while the clock
counts how far in glowing red. Sizes are in points. A bigger screen is a bigger desk, not bigger
things. More than one screen. The desk is on one screen; every other shows
more of the desk's boards, running on from it, for windows to lie on. A
new window comes onto the screen the pointer is on, Unfold and full
screen fill the screen the window is on, and nothing the desk's own
screen does -- the drawer, turning to the bookshelf -- moves what lies on
the others or takes it out of reach. A screen taken away puts its
windows on one that is left. X11 apps run through Xwayland, and windows that draw their own frames
sit on paper too. The screen lock is the front door ( Super+L , or logind): you walk
up to it at night, close enough to touch, traced in 3D with its own
lamps and soft shadows. Your picture and name are on the board hung on
it, the password goes in at the brass plate, the key beside it; on
Return (or a click on the key) you lean in and turn the key. Let in, it
goes round, the door swings open, you walk through into the room and sit
down at the desk; told no, it will not turn. Locking is the same run
backwards -- out of the room, the door shut, the key turned -- from Super+L or the blue LOCK button on the Control Panel. Checked with
PAM, as at login. Seven languages. Everything DEsk prints itself, and the names of
programs, are in English, Japanese, Chinese (simplified), Korean,
Spanish, French or German: the locale's, or language = en | ja | zh | ko | es | fr | de in ~/.config/desk/shell.conf (or the Shell Settings
app), and switch live. The calendar is printed as one sold there is,
and Chinese and Korean are set in their own cut of the CJK faces. Standard programs DEsk is meant to be installed as a whole desktop, like GNOME or KDE, so it
picks a standard program for each job the desk has: a terminal, a web
browser, a file manager and a text editor. The drawer's things and Super+Enter open them. For each job, the first of these that is there: app.terminal , app.browser , app.files , app.editor in shell.conf (a .desktop id), the default-applications lists in the freedesktop.org order: ~/.config/desk-mimeapps.list (DEsk only), ~/.config/mimeapps.list (what Shell Settings' Default programs, xfce4-mime-settings, writes), and
the same two in the system's folders, ending with the desk-mimeapps.list installed with DEsk -- the same answers xdg-open
and GIO give, the standard set, classic GTK programs first: Xfce Terminal, Firefox
ESR, Thunar, Mousepad (then MATE Terminal, Caja, Pluma, and so on), any program filed under the right category.

title: Neckbeard – A DevOps/platform/SRE plugin for your agent
abstract:
neckbeard A plugin for your coding agent that turns an app into cloud infrastructure you
can actually review, with the monthly bill attached. Coding agents are great at application code and weirdly confident about
infrastructure. Ask one to "deploy this to AWS" and you'll get three hundred
lines of plausible HCL, a security group open to the world, an IAM policy with
a star in it, and no idea what any of it costs. It reads like the work of
someone who has absorbed every blog post and never once been paged. The model
isn't lying to you. It has simply never seen the invoice. neckbeard splits the job. Humans maintain a catalog of OpenTofu modules that
are versioned, tested in CI on every change, and scoped to one honest workload
shape: a container image, up to ten HTTP, worker, and cron processes, Postgres,
object storage, secrets. The agent reads your repo, works out what the app
needs, asks you the questions code can't answer, and maps the answers onto
catalog inputs. Everything in between is deterministic Go. The planner writes a
hash-verified blueprint.yaml , the renderer is a pure function of it, and
regeneration refuses to overwrite a file you've touched. The agent never
invents infrastructure. If your app needs Redis, you get a named finding that
says the catalog doesn't do Redis yet, rather than a module that looks like it
might. It covers AWS, GCP, and Azure, with GitHub Actions or GitLab CI, as serverless
containers (Cloud Run, ECS Fargate, Container Apps) or Kubernetes (EKS, GKE,
AKS). The plugin shape is borrowed from ponytail , which proved a plugin
can be mostly one good prompt. Install Claude Code, as two separate prompts: /plugin marketplace add bealesh/neckbeard /plugin install neckbeard@neckbeard Then open your app's repo and run /neckbeard:analyze . Your first neckbeard
command installs the small CLI the plugin drives (a sha256-verified release
binary, or go install if you have Go around), and that's the whole setup.
Cost estimates and validation lean on tools you may already have, namely
Infracost, OpenTofu, and Checkov. /neckbeard:doctor tells you what's missing
and what each one buys you. Codex, Cursor, or anything else that reads a SKILL.md : see INSTALL.md . What it's like to use You run /neckbeard:analyze and the agent reads the repo the way a careful
new hire would. Dockerfiles, exposed ports, environment variables, health
endpoints, the Procfile, the corner of settings.py where Django quietly
reads DATABASE_URL . It writes an app profile in which every fact carries a
file and line number, every inference carries a confidence, and every
assumption is loud. Then it asks you the things it genuinely can't know: how
much traffic to expect, how much downtime you'll tolerate, whether that
Postgres is one you already run or one you want built, what the worker is for.
Your answers get recorded next to the assumptions they resolve, and planning
refuses to run while any of them is still open. /neckbeard:estimate plans against the catalog and shows you the bill before
anything exists. /neckbeard:sync scaffolds the infrastructure, the
pipelines, and on Kubernetes the cluster manifests, then validates them and
tells you precisely what it did and didn't prove. From there you review the
files like any other pull request and follow the generated docs/bootstrap.md once per environment, with real credentials in your own hands. The agent never
gets those. Command What it does /neckbeard:analyze Read the repo into an evidence-backed app-profile.yaml , ask the open questions, propose neckbeard.yaml . /neckbeard:estimate [comparison] Plan against the catalog and show the monthly cost table, including everything that couldn't be priced. serverless vs kubernetes or solo vs smallteam runs both. /neckbeard:sync Plan, estimate, scaffold, validate. Your edits are never silently overwritten. Ends with PASSED, FAILED, or NOT EXERCISED for each check. /neckbeard:doctor [plan|estimate|validate|all] Install the CLI if it's missing and report which tools are present. /neckbeard:help The short version of this page. The bill Nobody tells you what infrastructure costs until the invoice arrives, which is
a strange way to make an engineering decision. So neckbeard asks Infracost
first. Same reference app (an HTTP service, a worker, a cron job, Postgres),
smallest tier, all three environments, live prices: Cloud Run Container Apps ECS Fargate EKS GKE (regional) AKS monthly $77 ~$98* $250 $396 $754 ~$801* The asterisk matters. Infracost can't price Container Apps compute yet, and
the honest move is to say so rather than let a low number lie, so the report
lists every resource it couldn't price right next to the total. The rest is
what you'd want from anyone who has read a cloud bill with their name on it:
the idle baseline separated from usage, the usage assumptions written down
where you can edit them, low, expected, and high scenarios, and a footer saying
where the numbers came from. The table is also how the tool argues. When a solo
developer asks for Kubernetes, the numbers say "not yet" so nobody else has to. What it will and won't claim Infrastructure tooling has a long tradition of implying more than it has
proven. A passing tofu validate has never once meant a thing deploys.
neckbeard reports in three levels and insists on showing you the third: V0 PASSED tofu validate [prd]
V0 PASSED checkov policy [prd] every skip carries a written reason
V0 PASSED kubeconform (clusters/)
V1 NOT EXERCISED authenticated plan requires cloud credentials
V2 NOT EXERCISED deployment verification requires cloud credentials V0 is syntax and policy. Every Checkov skip in the generated config carries a
written reason, because a skip without one is a lie about your security
posture. V1 is an authenticated plan and V2 is a verified deployment; both
need credentials, and both stay NOT EXERCISED until a human runs them. When
live runs break, the failures go into the public findings ledger and from there into the catalog. The first
real deployment produced ten of them, and five became module fixes the same
afternoon. Degraded paths say why: an Azure plus GitLab merge-request plan
can't federate, so the generated pipeline says that out loud instead of
failing in a way you'd lose an evening to. What's in the box Three isolated environments with their own state, sized by tier presets that
spell out traffic, availability, recovery objectives, and how many people are
actually around to operate the thing. Every preset value is visible and
overridable within the catalog's tested envelope, and anything outside that
envelope is marked rather than blessed. Pipelines come from one internal model
for either CI: test, build, scan (Trivy blocks HIGH and CRITICAL), push, plans
on pull requests under a read-only identity, applies on main under a write
identity, production gated behind environment protection. There are no static
cloud keys anywhere. It's OIDC federation end to end, and a test fails the
build if a rendered pipeline so much as mentions AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY .
Networks are private by default, secret managers hold the names the operator
fills in (values never pass through neckbeard, its state, or your git
history), and managed WAF rules switch on where the tier calls for them. Money
gets two controls that are never confused with each other: monthly_budget_alert renders a real cloud budget per environment that notifies people, and monthly_ceiling is the one that actually refuses, enforced at the only point
a limit can be enforced, before the resources exist. Where it actually stands Pre-alpha, and specific about which parts.

title: I designed a nose guard for my dog and gave it away. Now 500 dogs wear one
abstract:
I designed a nose guard for my dog and gave it away. Now 500 dogs wear one Author Omri Hillel Designs, prints and packs every SnoutCover in his shed. Also the guy holding the ointment. Chief Nose Officer Billie Tested all thirteen prototypes. Reviewed this article and approved it for one treat. Did not lick the screen. Mostly. Omri Hillel · Reviewed by Billie October 15, 2026 · Signed off with one lick SnoutCover mode On Billie's nose is covered in every photo, stitches and all. Tap any photo to peek, or switch off to see them uncovered. A year ago, I didn't know this would become a business. Here's how we got here. It starts with Billie, my pitbull, a dog who lives for lying in the sun. When she was diagnosed with DLE, discoid lupus erythematosus, an autoimmune condition where the immune system attacks the skin on the nose and sunlight makes it worse, the vet laid it out plainly: there's no quick fix, only management. Ointment on her nose twice a day, keep her out of the UV, and expect flare-ups for the rest of her life. Tap to peek Cover again Billie's nose after surgery, and Billie doing her favorite thing. That sounded manageable until the first evening I tried it. You put the ointment on, and she licks it straight off. You can't hold a dog's tongue away from her own nose for ten minutes, twice a day, forever. And you certainly can't explain to a sun-loving dog why the yard is suddenly off limits. Tap to peek Cover again Tap to peek Cover again Tap to peek Cover again Billie's nose in spring 2024. So I did what I always do when something bothers me. I sat down and designed something. I called it Doguard. It took thirteen prototypes, a lot of evenings and a very patient dog, but eventually it worked. Billie could wear it, the ointment stayed where it belonged, and she got her sunbathing back. Billie in the first version. The truth is, I never planned to sell it. I made it for Billie. Once it worked, I uploaded the file to MakerWorld and wrote the whole process up on Reddit , free for anyone to print. I remembered how lost I felt in those first weeks after the diagnosis, and I figured if even one other dog owner found it and had a solution, that was worth it. Then the messages started. Could I sell them one? At first I tried to help people make their own. I'd help them find someone who could print it locally, explain how to scale it for their dog, walk them through putting the webbing straps together. Some did it beautifully. But slowly something sank in that seems obvious now: not everyone is a creator. Most people just love their dog and want to get a solution, fast. And if I was the one who could make that happen, it felt wrong not to. So on October 1st last year, I built a small website . Sixteen days later, my first customer placed an order. The first site, back when it was still called Doguard. I wish I could tell you I celebrated. I panicked. I had no inventory. I ran to print everything I could. Then I ran out to find webbing, suddenly worried about the next two or three orders that hadn't even happened yet. Then it dawned on me that a package has to be packed! That the moment someone opens it counts too. Then that packages go to a post office, and post offices have queues. Remember, I never set out to sell these, so I hadn't given a single thought to any part of that cycle. Two days later a second order came in. On the 24th, two more. A few weeks in, I decided to give it a new name: SnoutCover. That was the beginning. Designing the cover in Onshape, getting it ready in Bambu Studio, and printing it in the shed. From one dog to 500 Not much about how SnoutCover is made has changed. I still print every SnoutCover myself, on one printer in my studio shed. I still cut and assemble every strap, pack every envelope, and hand each week's batch to the Sunday pickup. What's changed is how far those envelopes travel. As of today, SnoutCover has helped more than 500 dogs. Most of them wear a cover I made myself - 395 orders, to 16 countries - and the rest wear covers their owners printed and assembled themselves. I still find that hard to believe. Just a few of the dogs now living a better life with the help of SnoutCover. It wasn't all smooth. Getting parcels across the world turned out to be the hardest part of the whole thing, and when some got stuck along the way, I sent them again at my own cost. I know how stressful it is to watch a tracking page that won't move while your dog's nose needs help, so sometimes I just sent a second one while the first was still on its way. What the clients taught me The first year was also one long round of fixes. Every email, every photo of a dog in a cover that didn't sit quite right, went straight back to the bench. The straps changed the most. A cover that slid up on every lick looked like a sizing problem, but it almost never was. The real fix was where the collar fasteners sat, so I kept reworking the strap design and the way I assemble it, until the cover stayed put without being pulled tight against a sensitive nose. The model changed too. When enough dogs got a paw under the Shield and pulled until it tore, I stopped treating it as a training issue and reinforced it where it flexes and where the straps pull. And some dogs simply don't fit a standard size. A Bull Terrier's long, curved nose needs coverage much further along the bridge than any stock cover gives, so I designed one from scratch, shaped from photos of that one dog. Custom models like that have become part of the work: when the standard sizes don't fit a dog's needs, I build one that does. The custom Bull Terrier cover, fitted on a model of the dog's head. And some of it wasn't about the product at all. Plenty of dogs freeze the first time they wear one - head down, waiting it out. That's normal, and it passes with a lick mat and a week of short, easy sessions. So I wrote it all down: tutorials for fitting, for training, for those first few days. None of it is finished, and I don't think it ever will be. The goal hasn't changed since the first prototype: every cover a little better, and a little more reliable, than the last. How the Care version was born In late May, a shipping issue put everything on hold for about two weeks. It felt like terrible timing. It turned out to be the best thing that happened to the product, because for the first time since launch, I had nothing to pack. Just a bench, a printer, and a problem that had been quietly piling up in my inbox. Some dogs needed something for the other twenty-two hours of the day. Not sun protection, just a gentle barrier during ointment time, or for noses so sensitive they couldn't be licked at all and had to stay protected while fully ventilated. The clearest case came from Stephanie and her husky, Iris. Iris's nostrils sat low compared to the openings on her cover, so every lick knocked it out of place. Her nose was raw enough that any movement hurt, and in the videos Stephanie sent I could hear that a fully covered nose was stressing her out. We tried every strap position and size. Two other owners were writing to me about the same thing. Eventually I understood that Iris didn't need a better rigid cover. She needed less cover. Getting there was a slog. The first versions simply wouldn't come out the way I pictured them. Then came the balance: too much material and it may as well be solid, too little and it stopped being a barrier at all. Then shapes that looked perfect on the bench and gave up the moment they met a warm nose. Breathing room came last, and it's the whole reason the model exists. A few of the Care prototypes. And then, after a long stretch of nothing, the idea just arrived - a completely different way of thinking about how the whole thing comes together. It solved most of those problems at once, and turned out far more durable than the original, too. The Care. Billie tested it first, on a walk home from the vet. She wore it the whole way without a fuss.

title: Suicide rates highest ever among middle-aged men
abstract:
Michael Searles Deputy Health Editor. Ben Butcher Data Editor Updated 13 October 2026 5:22pm BST Published 13 October 2026 5:05pm BST Suicide rates among middle-aged men are higher than ever, new figures have revealed. Men in their early 50s were more likely to die by suicide than anyone else last year, according to data from the Office for National Statistics . There were also increases in suicides among pensioners, with the biggest rise among those aged 75 and older, while the rates among men under 45 fell slightly. Mark Winstanley, the chief executive of Rethink Mental Illness, said the rate of deaths by suicide remained “stubbornly high”. He said: “Every suicide is a devastating tragedy, and these figures are a stark reminder that many people are reaching crisis point without getting the help they need.” The reasons behind suicide were “complex”, he said, but added that many people were “facing significant pressures in their lives, including financial issues, job insecurity, rising housing costs, loneliness and poor mental health ”. Suicide rate highest on record Mr Winstanley added: “While these factors affect everyone differently, they can contribute to distress and overwhelm, and leave people at risk of suicide.” The data, which cover England and Wales, showed that 6,162 suicide deaths had been registered in 2025. This was down from 6,190 last year, but the overall rate remained broadly the same at 11.3 deaths per 100,000 people. The stats watchdog uses deaths per 100,000 people to calculate changing rates while accounting for changes in the size of the population. Almost a third of the deaths were among men aged 45 to 64, which was up by 49 compared with 2024. The rate increased to 23.8 per 100,000, up from 23.2 the year before and the highest on record since data collection began in 1981. For men aged 50 to 54 specifically, the rate increased to 28, suggesting this group was at the highest risk. Men continued to be more than three times as likely to take their own lives as women overall. Among middle-aged women, there were 553 deaths – a rate of seven per 100,000, which was the same as 2024. Sonya Trivedy, the executive director of external engagement at Samaritans, said the figures “show that suicide rates are among the highest recorded rates this century”. She said: “The evidence is clear that successive governments have failed to deliver on their promise to reduce suicide rates and make suicide prevention a priority. Today must act as a wake up call. The current approach is not working; we need meaningful action and proper funding if lives are to be saved.” The data show a growing gap in suicide rates between middle-aged men and those aged 25 to 44. Recommended Simon Reeve: 'I was a whisker away from taking my own life' Read more There were 19.5 deaths per 100,000 men aged 25 to 44 last year, which is the widest gap since 2009, when middle-aged male suicide rates overtook those of younger adults. The rate increased from 14 to 14.4 per 100,000 for those aged 65 to 74 and from 13.2 to 15.4 among those aged 75 or older. Marjorie Wallace, the chief executive of mental health charity Sane, said she was “not surprised” by the data. She said: “Analysis of the contact we receive reflects this – almost 60 per cent of our callers now talk about suicide or self-harm, a very different picture than 10 years ago. “While middle-aged men in their forties and fifties still remain at greatest risk, our other concern is the number of young people, particularly girls and women aged 16 to 24, who report anxiety and depression on a scale not experienced before.”

title: America didn't lose its rare earth industry, it sold it
abstract:
Kirsten Asdal Tom Koch Tao Tan Meet The Authors Subscribe to Lawfare In October 2025, Beijing imposed sweeping controls on its rare earth exports. Since then, those controls have been suspended one short reprieve at a time , in the latest instance until Nov. 10 , with a broader trade truce through Jan. 10, 2027 . The reprieves have repeatedly come only after American concessions, demonstrating China’s leverage in the export fight. Yet China has constricted sales even during the truce, as buyers have few options but to take what they can get. In June, with the suspension in force, Beijing placed MP Materials and USA Rare Earth, the two companies the U.S. is counting on to build an alternative supply to China, on an export control list . Washington’s effort to rebuild the supply chain, meanwhile, has not yet reached the scale or durability the problem requires. With up to $100 billion in loan authority specifically earmarked for critical minerals in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the capital undoubtedly exists. What is missing is alignment of interests among the parties that would supply and benefit from it, and a political system patient enough to hold a course for the decade or more that rebuilding a supply chain takes. This article’s authors work at the intersection of finance and national security. Between the three of us, we have watched the same on-again, off-again rhythm play out in both Chinese statecraft and U.S. budget fights. A consistent pattern plays out: Capital markets are good at financing efficient supply but are not good at financing a binary outcome, such as insurance against a monopoly state seller that can manipulate both price and availability. And subsidies alone will not close that gap. We have seen firsthand that what the U.S. government has to offer right now insufficiently incentivizes private investors, because its tools are market tools deployed in an environment of market failure. Instead, we propose a financing instrument that could clear both economic and political hurdles: a contingent convertible security that converts into ownership if Beijing weaponizes supply. Rare Earths Are a Market Failure The history of how we got here is well known, but worth retelling briefly. The Chinese Communist Party inherited its strategic focus on building industrial capacity from the Soviet Union. In 1964, Deng Xiaoping inspected an iron ore mine near the Mongolian border holding the world’s largest rare earth deposit. He ordered the engineers to develop steel and rare earths alike. Since then, as technologies have increasingly relied on specialized materials, the Chinese Communist Party under successive leaders has deliberately invested in and consolidated control over the rare earths industry. China refines more than 90 percent of the world’s rare earths and close to 99 percent of heavy rare earths today. It processes nearly all the heavy elements that go into precision-guided weapons and advanced chips. When Beijing tightened export controls in October 2025, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent characterized it as “pointing a bazooka at the supply chains and industrial base of the entire free world.” Remarkably, the entire market for rare earth oxides is worth less than $10 billion. That a $10 billion market can grind to a halt trillions in global gross domestic product is the definition of a chokepoint. Beijing controls this chokepoint today by design. Decades of state policy work laid the groundwork for the Chinese Communist Party to enact an international licensing system by 2025. General Secretary Xi Jinping himself openly speaks about the importance of maintaining global dependency on China’s industrial supply chains. Hindsight treats this as neglect, something policymakers lost sight of and let slip during the U.S.’s unipolar moment. That is a necessary, but only partial, explanation. The truth is the United States did not lose its rare earth industry due to carelessness. Private American companies willingly sold it, for reasons that made perfect economic sense at the time and still do. China bought it for reasons that were never purely economic. That mismatch explains why, after years of investment and policy attention, the dependency remains. Until the late 1980s, the United States was the world’s leading producer and refiner of rare earths. But it was a dirty business: The Mountain Pass mine in California leaked roughly 600,000 gallons of radioactive and other waste into the Mojave. As cleanup and regulatory costs mounted and profits fell, the mine shut down in stages starting in the 1990s until it was fully idle by 2002. Meanwhile, the work moved to China, where the state subsidized unprofitable operations, tolerated pollution, and sold the processed oxides back to the U.S. at rock-bottom prices. The same thing happened to the magnets: In 1995, General Motors sold Magnequench , its magnet unit, to a Chinese-backed consortium. By 2006, the last U.S. plant had closed, and the machine tools and equipment had been shipped to China. Economists would say this was the right move for a free market economy. Comparative advantage did what it was supposed to do, and a dirty, low-margin business left a wealthy country for a developing one. There was even a strategic rationale: Drawing China into the trading system, the wishful thinking went, would also make it a responsible stakeholder rather than a rival. The category error was to conceive rare earths as a market, rather than recognizing it as a geostrategic industry. A market solves for the lowest cost. To be sure, Chinese producers competed on cost, and they rode a tech boom with surging demand for their product. But a state will pay almost any price to control a chokepoint, because tolerating a money-losing business pales in comparison to the geopolitical leverage that it brings. Over time, China has become less market driven, not more. Meanwhile, the U.S. continued to treat as a market what the Chinese Communist Party came to appreciate as a strategic program. Control over the chokepoint gives Beijing a switch. When it lets the material flow, no private interest will build alternative supply chains at scale, because Chinese state-funded producers can sell at or below cost indefinitely, and no rational private investor will willingly sign up to lose money. When China cuts off the flow, the incentives reverse overnight, but capacity cannot follow overnight, because standing up the full supply chain and rebuilding the lost know-how can take a decade or longer. This is classic market failure in which the same critical material can become worthless or priceless on command. In 2010, during a maritime dispute with Japan, Beijing reportedly halted rare earth shipments , and Tokyo quickly conceded. The short-term truces of the past year, each struck around contentious but episodic trade disputes, further entrench that market failure. Each successive loosening and tightening seems designed to keep the United States and its allies off balance and frustrate any long-term plan to reduce Beijing’s leverage. Government Money Has to Survive Politics If the market will not rebuild the rare earths supply chain, the government must do so. Administrations under both parties have tried, and their attempts have run into a predictable morass of misaligned interests. The parties to government financing all want different things. Private investors want attractive returns in fat years, while having the government carry losses in lean ones. Commercial lenders want years of fully contracted offtake to guarantee interest payments, while Congress typically appropriates money for the next year. Markets want flexibility while Congress wants tight oversight and guardrails. Washington often wants to be the last (and lightest) money in, which signals to investors that the government is hedging. And cheap, open-ended financing is exactly the wrong signal to send to management teams.

title: Virtual Oxide Labs: Emulating a Full Oxide Rack
abstract:
14 Oct 2026 Virtual Oxide Labs: Emulating a Full Oxide Rack Steve Karam Product Assurance The trouble with testing and developing for rack-scale hardware is that rack-scale is
not all that easy to come by. I mean, nevermind the whole DDR5-as-a-currency thing;
even if all the parts were available in abundance, any completed racks go swiftly
to the front lines (AKA our customers' data centers). As a member of the Product Assurance Team at Oxide, I find that totally unfair
yet completely reasonable. And so we have to get a bit creative. We have to be
able to: Replicate diverse customer networking topologies Run our actual control plane Test up to date versions of our software Represent the hardware components (we make racks, after all) including our switches and microcontrollers And the cherry on top: we need to do that without cutting special "test version" releases.
Because we want to keep our CI sleek, but also because that wouldn’t be playing fair. Now, don’t get me wrong — we’re not without our tricks. When I joined Oxide last year,
one of the first things I was introduced to was our racklettes ; that is, smaller
than average racks of four sleds and two switches each. These racklettes can be
initialized and run just like a real rack, precisely because they are a real rack.
Just not in any form factor it would be economical to sell. But for testing they
work like a charm. We have four of them today, soon to be eight, where we can test
any combination of hardware/software requirement. We also have our various simulated methods of running Omicron. You can read more about
those at How to Run Simulated and the full(er) How to Run Guide . I
won’t go into a ton of detail here, but suffice it to say that most parts of our control plane (and more) can be run independently, in tandem, and in various degrees of simulation. What’s a Voxel? Do you remember the game Q*bert? It was one of the first wildly popular isometric
games, and looked a little like this: Why am I showing you a ridiculously small game screenshot? Well, each cube in that
image represents a 'voxel,' or a point in 3D space. It’s actually the 3D version of a
pixel. Volume Element + Pixel = Voxel. Neat, right? Anyway, for Oxide, Virtual OXidE Labs (or Voxel) means an incredible amount of
fidelity packed into a single piece of hardware. It is the spiritual successor to
our prior virtual labs (known as a4x2) which allowed us to hack out decent racks
running in VMs. Pay attention to that word "fidelity" by the way.
For it is, as Bryan Cantrill puts it, the Prime Directive : labs should use
stock Oxide software without hack or modification. This is what Voxel gives us. A complete software emulation stack, built on illumos
in Rust, where we can build and test a variety of realistic configurations: Sled virtualization provided by Propolis BGP (numbered and unnumbered) or static networking with Debian and FRR P4-powered switches via Oxide’s own SoftNPU, a software P4 switch Microcontroller simulation and emulation for our Service Processor (SP) and Root of Trust (RoT) And what’s more, it gives us all these features in a fairly small footprint. At home,
I run Voxel labs on a Minisforum MS-A2 mini-PC with a 32-thread AMD Ryzen 9 9955HX and
96GB RAM. On that computer, I can spin up 6 sleds with ease, either in the form of
one rack or in a multirack configuration (two separate racks, one management plane). All
it requires is Oxide Helios and a decently
fast NVMe drive. Launch, and in about 10 minutes you have a full Oxide rack with each "sled"
in its own Propolis VM — alongside switches (also in Propolis) and other infrastructure. Image Creation Remember how I said we have to use stock Oxide software? That actually makes things
easier. The first thing we do (following a common practice in hypervisor tooling) is
to create a reusable snapshot. Oxide sleds are only ever one of two things: a normal
sled (a "gimlet" for the first generation, "cosmo" for the current) or a "scrimlet,"
which is a sled wired to the sidecar switches that runs a switch zone. It’s all
amazingly elegant in its complexity, you should read more about it in our networking docs . To create a snapshot for Voxel, all we must do is create a "sled" (virtual machine),
install our control plane (Omicron) on it, snapshot it before the point of configuration,
et voilà: a ready-to-launch sled. The control plane can be installed one of two ways: From source Voxel clones the Omicron repo on GitHub (or uses a locally defined source for rapid development) and uses cargo to compile From TUF repo We use Tufaceous to package Omicron releases using The Update Framework (TUF) and our CI tool Buildomat Using the second option as an example, here’s the beginning of the process where voxel image create pulls out the key pieces that make up the sled config: $ pfexec ./target/debug/voxel image create --from-tuf ../5d176e0be7e5cc0d3288c1bef10005ec31f2cd7c.zip 5d176e0be7e5cc0d3288c1bef10005ec31f2cd7c [ voxel ] TUF source ../5d176e0be7e5cc0d3288c1bef10005ec31f2cd7c.zip: system version 23.0.0-0.ci+git5d176e0be7e, omicron 5d176e0be7e [ voxel ] extracted 12 zones from ../5d176e0be7e5cc0d3288c1bef10005ec31f2cd7c.zip [ voxel ] extracted 3 measurement corpus artifacts [ voxel ] extracting host artifacts - > /export/home/helios/voxel-rawfix/target/debug/../../voxel-image/.tuf-host [ voxel ] host boot image 1258295296 bytes, phase 1 rom 33554432 bytes [ voxel ] extracted SP/RoT firmware - > /export/home/helios/voxel-rawfix/target/debug/../../voxel-image/.tuf-fw/ca9184058bd7 After a decent amount of unpacking and staging, it will launch a VM that everything
gets written/installed to. And finally: [voxel] ready: voxel-cp version=unknown unpacked_artifacts=18 built=2026-09-06T21:37:58
[voxel] clearing device-instance map, halting
[voxel] flushing, up to 25s
[voxel] stopping hypervisor
[voxel] writing voxel image voxel-cp-5d176e0be7e-tuf That image is a zfs snapshot which can be used and reused to create our rack. Ready for Launch Launching the rack uses a similar process, except the control plane is already
installed. All we need at this point is: An "frr" image (the Debian VMs for networking) A control plane image (like the one we just created) The voxel-init agent that gives each virtual sled its assignment The log output is pretty long, but you can scroll through it if you’d like. I’ll
recap after. $ pfexec ./target/debug/voxel launch --emu [ voxel ] sled-agent config schema ( image properties ): data_links = Tagged disks = Hardcoded Writing key pair to "./cargo-bay/sprockets/test-root-a.key.pem" Writing key pair to "./cargo-bay/sprockets/test-signer-a1.key.pem" ... Writing certificate to "./cargo-bay/sprockets/test-root-a.cert.pem" Writing certificate to "./cargo-bay/sprockets/test-signer-a1.cert.pem" ... Writing pki path to "./cargo-bay/sprockets/test-sprockets-auth-0.certlist.pem" Writing pki path to "./cargo-bay/sprockets/test-alias-0.certlist.pem" ... add net fdb0:a840:2500:1::/64: gateway fdb0:a840:25ff:0::2 add net fdb0:a840:2500:5::/64: gateway fdb0:a840:25ff:0::4 [ sp-emu ] instance state dir: /export/home/helios/voxel-unzip/sp-fleet/r0/sp-emu/state/33300 [ identity ] seed = 0x2aac7ae3f8cfbb1e ( 3074967765137734430 ) [ identity ] SP UID 13120858064df80da1642f2b, RoT UUID 00a94a8e206f3f138a790fba1b12db36 [ flash ] Hubris archive /export/home/helios/voxel-unzip/sp-fleet/r0/sp-emu/sidecar.archive - > /export/home/helios/voxel-unzip/sp-fleet/r0/sp-emu/state/33300/archives/sp.zip flashed 786688 bytes into slot A (base 0x08000000, reset PC 0x080002e8 ) of /export/home/helios/voxel-unzip/sp-fleet/r0/sp-emu/state/33300/sp-flash.bin [ sp-emu ] instance state dir: /export/home/helios/voxel-unzip/sp-fleet/r0/sp-emu/state/33310 [ identity ] seed = 0xa65abed0e20d08d1 ( 11987103162554976465 ) [ identity ] SP UID 72a3c3327682e0df38de478a, RoT UUID fcb600f7322f3393899f72036aa2b4fd [ flash ] Hubris archive /export/home/helios/voxel-unzip/sp-fleet/r0/sp-emu/gimlet.

title: Anthropic's Scion is heavily inspired by Mononoke
abstract:
Update 2026-10-15: I wrote a followup to answer questions and concerns. Discuss on Hacker News or Lobsters . Here is Anthropic describing ( archive link ) yesterday how their new version control system, Scion, uses a concept called “derived data” to make operations like blames more efficient: How Anthropic describes Scion’s derived data. Here is me, back in 2022, describing in my Oxide candidate materials how the Mononoke source control server I helped build uses a concept called “derived data” to make operations like blames more efficient: How I described Mononoke’s derived data. I think the level of imitation goes well beyond having similar insights 1 . The fact that Sapling was only credited for “hard-won lessons”, and that Mononoke was not mentioned at all, borders on plagiarism. The post comes off as Anthropic claiming that Claude designed all this, while the reality is that our (extraordinary) team at Meta came up with many of the insights that Claude dutifully applied almost a decade later. (We looked at plenty of prior art for Mononoke and Sapling too, from Google’s SrcFS to write-ahead logs in databases.) I am very glad that the vision our team had back in 2017-18 was so powerful and enduring — when you go against the grain, you’re always a bit unsure if what you’re doing is genius or madness, and I think Mononoke’s design has stood the test of time. And, to be clear, I do not have a problem with Anthropic copying Mononoke’s design. (This is part of why we put out open source — to benefit humanity through the spread of good ideas.) But as LLMs continue to assist in designing new systems, they are likely to index heavily on existing designs. Mononoke is open source and in every LLM’s training set. If you ask Opus 5.5 or GPT-6 Astra (thanks Matthew Fowle ) about prior art, they both immediately point out the similarities to Mononoke. Giving credit to those that came before us is now easier — and more important — than ever. There is no longer an excuse. For an example of a system with similar insights but many key design differences, see Vicent Marti’s blog post for Cursor . ↩︎

title: Federated Generation and Fusion for Privacy-Preserving Cross-Domain Optic Disc and Cup Segmentation in IoT-Enabled Healthcare
abstract: Ocular diseases are a leading cause of permanent blindness worldwide, making early and accessible screening critical for vision preservation. Fundus imaging, increasingly deployed through Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) devices, offers a noninvasive and cost-effective modality for large-scale retinal screening in community and remote settings. AI-driven segmentation of the optic disc and cup from fundus images enables automated quantitative assessment for disease diagnosis. However, existing models suffer from severe performance degradation across heterogeneous imaging devices and raise substantial privacy concerns when centralizing multisite data for training. To address these intertwined challenges, we propose a federated generation and fusion framework for privacy-preserving cross-domain optic disc and cup segmentation in IoMT environments. The framework jointly addresses three complementary challenges: domain discrepancy is mitigated through generation-based image translation, privacy preservation is achieved via a Gaussian perturbation-based image fusion mechanism, and cross-site collaboration is enabled through federated optimization without raw data sharing. At each local site, a generative model bridges the domain gap via an ensemble of losses, including a fast Fourier transform (FFT)-based high-frequency loss for texture preservation, a multilayer contrastive loss for region-focused style transfer, a feature-matching loss for semantic alignment, and an adversarial loss, which are balanced through multitask learning. To protect local data privacy, a Gaussian perturbation-based, privacy-preserving image fusion strategy combines real and generated images using perturbed weights. The global segmentation model is then obtained via federated weighted averaging across distributed sites without raw data exchange. Extensive experiments on four public fundus datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves competitive or superior segmentation performance across diverse target domains while providing empirical privacy protection. Results are reported as the average of three independent runs to ensure statistical reliability. The code is available at: https://github.com/JRHU0048/FundusGAN

title: Diffusion-Collaborated Text--Visual Multimodal Guidance for Image Manipulation Localization in IoT Supply Chain Systems
abstract: AI-powered supply chain systems, a critical component of IoT, leverage automated image verification for deliveries but face vulnerabilities such as image manipulation, which can introduce false data and security risks. With advancements in generative AI, attackers can now manipulate logistics images more convincingly, altering goods’ status, concealing damages, or even erasing items entirely, making detection increasingly difficult. Previous research addressing this issue has typically encountered a decrease in performance when confronted with a variety of manipulated images in real-world situations. To address this issue, in this article, we propose an image manipulation localization framework based on multimodal feature guidance collaborating with advanced latent diffusion models (LDMs). By reconstructing rich intermediate feature representations of images under fake-oriented conditions using diffusion, we combine multimodal fused high-level semantic information to guide the segmentation process, achieving state-of-the-art performance. We further propose a high-quality image manipulation dataset tailored for supply chain scenarios, filling the gap in this field. Extensive experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of identifying forged images.

title: A GenAI-Powered Authentication Protocol for Secure Monitoring of Hajj/Umrah Pilgrims Using Cinematographic Drones
abstract: Maintaining safety in crowded events with more than 4.5 million Hajj and Umrah pilgrims becomes a very challenging issue in terms of crowd security. While occlusion occurs in traditional closed-circuit television (CCTV) systems, drone-based crowd surveillance is still susceptible to threats like spoofing, command injection, and video replay attacks. This article proposes generative AI (GenAI)-powered authentication protocol, which provides both mutual authentication and an intelligent threat detection module based on GenAI between three entities. The proposed scheme provides security under the random oracle model (ROM), offers perfect forward secrecy, and resists a replay attack using SHA-256, xor, and concatenation. The key revocation and desynchronization attack countermeasures have been proposed and verified formally through ProVerif and Burrows–Abadi–Needham (BAN) logic proof techniques. Furthermore, the vision–language model (VLM) detects any stampede hazard, fire outbreak, or medical emergency based on the analysis of authenticated video frames with a 91.7% success rate. The computational cost for Core i7, Galaxy A07, and Raspberry Pi 4 processors at $40~{^{\circ }}$ C is 3.8, 13.1, and 10.5 ms, respectively, with 1984-bit overhead and 32.4 mJ of energy expenditure.

title: Ensemble LLM Consensus Architectures for Deterministic Trade Signal Generation: An Empirical Study of Multi-Persona AI Panels in Retail FinTech Applications
abstract: This paper presents an empirical study of a multi-persona large language model (LLM) consensus architecture deployed in a live retail FinTech platform for equity and options trade signal generation. Grounded in a prior quantitative trading framework (Anton, 2025) and building upon academic antecedents in multi-agent LLM systems (Xiao et al., 2024), the Edge Stack Trading platform deploys a six-persona AI analyst panel producing structured, constrained verdicts across a real-time multi-signal scoring architecture. Analysis of nine live trade reports generated between April and May 2026 reports a preliminary 87.5% directional accuracy rate across eight assessable signals in an exploratory proof-of-concept evaluation, with unanimous panel consensus strongly correlated with system confidence extremes. Inter-model disagreement functions as an auditable risk signal, and model API failures produce identifiable, recoverable degradation patterns consistent with graceful degradation requirements for financial AI systems. The architecture addresses the 2026 conference theme of Reliable and Deterministic AI for Financial Systems through structured verdict formats, role-constrained persona prompting, and explicit multi-signal deterministic scoring as mechanisms for AI governance in retail financial decision support. One incorrect signal (Palantir) reveals a boundary condition in which extreme valuation risk overrides technical alignment, informing a specific architectural recommendation. Implications for HBCU financial technology education, democratized institutional-grade AI analysis, and regulatory auditability are discussed.

title: Deep Learning-Based Signal Detection With Denoising and Temporal Sequence Structuring for Molecular Communication in Vessel-Like Channels
abstract: Molecular communication via diffusion (MCvD) in vessel-like channels is strongly affected by laminar flow, diffusion-induced dispersion, and severe intersymbol interference (ISI). These challenges are even more pronounced in scenarios with multiple transmitters, where molecules of the same type released from multiple transmitters overlap at the receiver, giving rise to accumulated interlink interference (ILI). However, existing signal detection studies have mainly focused on the release of different types of molecules or single-symbol detection. In this article, we propose a Transformer-based sequence detector with a denoising and temporal sequence structuring (DTSS) strategy for multiple transmitters that release the same type of molecules in vessel-like MCvD channels with Poiseuille flow. The proposed approach structures raw molecular sequences into consecutive segments and uses a self-attention Transformer to model long-range ISI and ILI, thereby enhancing robustness to multiple transmitters superposition. Simulations show that the proposed Transformer-based model with the DTSS strategy converges the fastest and achieves the best detection performance among the baseline deep neural network (DNN) and Transformer models, the Transformer with Denoised and Grouped strategies, and the DNN with DTSS preprocessing.

title: Engaging HBCU Students in Active Learning for Blockchain, FinTech, and Generative AI: A Human-Centered Pedagogical Framework
abstract: The convergence of blockchain, financial technology, digital assets, and generative artificial intelligence creates important opportunities and challenges for undergraduate education, especially at Historically Black Colleges and Universities. Students preparing for careers in business, computing, analytics, cybersecurity, and financial services need more than exposure to emerging technologies; they also need confidence, collaboration skills, ethical awareness, computational fluency, and experience applying tools to realistic problems. This paper proposes a human-centered pedagogical framework to engage HBCU students in active learning about blockchain, FinTech, and generative AI. The framework synthesizes classroom-tested strategies from computer information systems, business analytics, programming, mathematics, and interdisciplinary student research. It emphasizes structured collaboration, low-stakes practice, role rotation, peer evaluation, reflective learning, responsible use of generative AI, reproducible computational notebooks, and applied problem contexts such as credit risk, fraud detection, investment analysis, digital trust, and smart financial systems. The paper presents an evidence-informed model that instructors can adapt across introductory and advanced undergraduate courses. The framework suggests that active, collaborative, and AI-supported pedagogy can increase student participation, reduce anxiety around technical topics, support inclusive learning, and strengthen workforce readiness for emerging blockchain and FinTech ecosystems.

title: CASSIS: An LLM-Driven Framework for Sensitive API Identification in Cyber–Physical System Software Repositories
abstract: As cyber–physical systems (CPSs) are increasingly deployed in critical infrastructures, the misuse of CPS-sensitive (safety-critical) data can compromise device safety and even endanger human life. In this article, we focus on identifying repository-specific sensitive APIs that manipulate CPS-sensitive data along sensor-to-actuator data paths in CPS software repositories (“CPS repos”). These APIs are critical to downstream tasks related to CPS-sensitive data operations, such as vulnerability detection, access control, and privacy protection. Existing static and dynamic program analysis tasks typically assume a repository-specific list of sensitive APIs as input. However, such lists are usually hand-crafted or derived from ad hoc pattern-matching rules. Therefore, they are difficult to reuse across repositories. Moreover, in large CPS repositories, where physical semantics are often abstract and documentation is scattered, these lists are prone to omissions. To address this issue, we propose a CPS-aware Source and Sink identification system (CASSIS), an LLM-driven framework that automatically identifies sensitive APIs in CPS repos without model fine-tuning. CASSIS constructs a CPS-aware code–documentation index, prunes unlikely candidates, and iteratively labels the remaining functions with an LLM without updating model parameters. On two real-world CPS repos—Genesis and ArduCopter, CASSIS reduces the number of functions requiring LLM-based classification by more than 80% while preserving high recall for I/O-related functions. Overall, CASSIS achieves function-level Accuracy/Macro- $F1$ of 80.4%/77.8% on Genesis and 82.0%/80.8% on ArduCopter, demonstrating its effectiveness for practical CPS code auditing and security assessment.

title: Fed-DAPT: Federated Dynamic Alignment and Prompt Tuning for Efficient Personalized Vision Transformers
abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables multiple clients to collaboratively train a model without exchanging raw data, making it attractive for privacy-sensitive edge computing where edge devices are constrained by bandwidth, energy, and computation. Personalized FL (PFL) further addresses client heterogeneity by learning personalized models; however, deploying large-scale vision transformers (ViTs) in PFL remains challenging under non-IID data due to prohibitive communication and computation costs. To tackle these challenges, we propose Fed-DAPT, a lightweight framework that decouples communication cost from backbone size by freezing the vision–language backbone and communicating only global prompt parameters. Fed-DAPT further integrates variational adaptive inference (VAI) into early-exit transformer blocks on easy samples and an unbalanced optimal transport (UOT) module to align heterogeneous feature distributions across clients for improved robustness. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet-100 show that Fed-DAPT consistently outperforms strong personalized FL baselines while substantially reducing both communication and computation overhead. In particular, Fed-DAPT achieves up to 87.84%, 58.86%, and 76.72% Top-1 accuracy, improving by up to 3.48 percentage points over the strongest baseline, while reducing per-round communication by over 99% and lowering inference cost by approximately 40% in GFLOPs.

title: A Unified System for Intelligent Financial Fraud Detection
abstract: Modern financial ecosystems require real-time, transparent, and trustworthy fraud detection systems capable of processing massive transaction volumes while meeting regulatory and auditing requirements. This paper presents a unified, modular system integrating four layers: (a) a blockchain-based transaction logging mechanism, (b) an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) fraud detection engine, (c) a Mistral large language model (LLM) client for natural-language reasoning, and (d) an AI agent for orchestration. A Python-based prototype demonstrates the complete pipeline—from transaction ingestion to fraud scoring, explanation generation, and immutable blockchain storage. The system serves as an educational and experimental platform for research and development, offering flexibility and extensibility for future enhancements.

title: Building Financial Resilience at HBCUs through Generative AI, FinTech, Blockchain, and Cybersecurity Education
abstract: Financial resilience has become an urgent educational priority as individuals face increasingly complex decisions involving budgeting, debt, credit, retirement planning, digital payments, online fraud, artificial intelligence tools, and rapidly changing financial technologies. Historically Black Colleges and Universities are well-positioned to advance financial security education by integrating financial literacy, FinTech, blockchain, cybersecurity, and generative artificial intelligence into interdisciplinary learning experiences. This paper proposes a human-centered framework for building financial resilience at HBCUs through technology-enhanced financial security education. The framework is organized around six connected pillars: financial foundations, FinTech literacy, blockchain and digital trust, generative AI-supported decision learning, cybersecurity and fraud prevention, and community-centered financial resilience. Using a conceptual design-science methodology, the paper synthesizes literature on financial literacy, digital financial capability, AI risk management, cybersecurity education, and HBCU-centered pedagogical innovation. It also builds on prior work in AI-supported learning, investment decision-making, blockchain education, and human-centered cybersecurity. The paper contributes a scalable curriculum model, sample learning modules, implementation strategies, and assessment measures for HBCU programs in business, computer information systems, cybersecurity, data science, and interdisciplinary fields. The framework positions financial resilience as a lifelong learning outcome and connects HBCU-centered financial education with digital trust, cybersecurity awareness, and responsible use of emerging financial technologies.

title: PaCR: An Agentic Preference-Aligned TAP Conflict Handling
abstract: With the increasing complexity of smart home environments, trigger-action-program (TAP) conflicts have emerged as critical issues, occurring when multiple automation apps compete for control over shared devices or interact in unintended ways. While existing approaches detect and resolve such conflicts using predefined rules or expert knowledge, they fail to account for the significant variability in individual pReferences for conflict resolution and significantly degrade the automation-system utility. To address this gap, we propose a preference-aligned conflict resolution (PaCR), a novel agentic framework that resolves conflicts while aligning with users’ personalized preferences for automation behavior. PaCR employs a two-step conflict resolution process: first, it interactively gathers contextual information from smart home configurations to generate conflict resolution agents (CRAs) with user profiles that accurately depict user preferences and characteristics; then, the agents, acting as users, utilize the semantic reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) to assist in generating personalized conflict detection and resolution strategies. Due to the agentic conflict-resolving feature, we evaluate the effectiveness of PaCR with existing datasets at scale. PaCR demonstrates strong capabilities in addressing conflicts based on users’ needs and significantly improves conflict resolution efficacy and interpretability, offering a user-centric approach to managing smart-home automation conflicts.
